title: Hands Calloused, Heart Worse
author: Lunaeryi
summary: Phainon's just a broke, country-bred good guy trying to survive city life, charm old ladies, and maybe flirt with the man who keeps stealing his coffee. He wasn't planning on falling for him. And he definitely wasn't planning on him being the CEO of the company merging with his. Mydei's been doing just fine ignoring his feelings and hiding behind overpriced coffee and his resting bitch face, thank you very much. But somehow, this annoyingly charming man with calloused hands and a sunshine grin keeps getting under his skin.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: You Stole My Coffee, Asshole
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Phainon spends his morning corralling gossiping grandmas, playing café janitor for free, and nursing existential dread—only for his fancy seasonal latte to get swiped by the city’s mystery man, sparking the most petty coffee-shop feud this side of the skyline. Cats are fed, baristas are judged, and one very annoyed hayseed vows revenge.

Chapter Notes

Finished this during a picnic with my friends😭

The corner café on Grove Street was a city institution, though no one would ever admit it out loud. It had no name—just a weathered wooden sign over the door with the faded outline of a coffee cup—but at any given hour, you’d find the same cast of characters rotating through its cramped little interior.

Students hunched over half-dead laptops and overpriced study guides. Office workers pretending to take client calls while texting their exes. Cranky freelancers arguing over who’d stolen their usual window seat. And, of course, Mnestia’s Book Coven—a gaggle of old ladies who met every Thursday afternoon to tear through spicy fantasy novels and roast the protagonists’ life choices over lemon muffins. They wore too much perfume, claimed the corner table like royalty, and left baristas clutching their pearls in their wake.

It was exactly the kind of place Phainon loved.

He nudged the door open with his shoulder, a box of supplies balanced in his arms—Anaxa’s latest demand, because apparently ‘if you’re gonna squat here, make yourself useful’—and stepped inside, straight into the crush of mid-morning chaos.

Someone immediately shouldered past him without so much as a glance.

Another guy in a sleek suit cut the line with all the entitlement of a man who thought “networking” was a personality trait.

Phainon still held the door open for a woman with a stroller, even as she breezed through without a word. Not even a nod.

And from behind the counter, Anaxa’s familiar voice drifted over the hiss of the espresso machine, dry as the goddamn desert.

“You’re too glamorous for this city, hayseed.”

Phainon grinned. “Yeah, yeah. Good to see you too, professor.”

Anaxa, as usual, looked like he regretted every decision that had led him to this point in his life. Sharp-boned, sharp-tongued, and perpetually dressed like a noir detective off-duty, he barely spared Phainon a glance as he wiped down the counter.

“If you’re gonna loiter, at least stay out of the way. I got students stress-buying caffeine and old ladies arguing over dick sizes in chapter twelve.”

“I brought your stuff.” Phainon hefted the box onto the counter with a thud.

“Congratulations, you’ve earned the right to breathe my oxygen a little longer.”

The café was packed, tables full, a line stretching to the door. Somewhere in the back, one of the book club ladies cackled loud enough to make a barista jump.

Phainon rolled his shoulders out, warmth settling over him like a well-worn jacket.

Yep. Welcome to his life.

“Phainon, darling!”

The chorus hit him the moment he turned around. He barely had time to brace before four perfume-clouded hurricanes descended on him from the book club’s corner table.

“Merope, careful,” one scolded, but Merope had already grabbed a fistful of his sleeve. “Where’ve you been, sweetheart? We haven’t seen you in weeks.”

“It’s been three days,” Phainon laughed, easy and warm as a sun-drenched porch swing. “Miss me that bad?”

“Oh, hush,” complained Alkippe, the one with the crimson lipstick and earrings shaped like tiny swords. “You promised you’d pick a book for next month and then vanished into thin air.”

Another hand—Clio, forever in pastels and scandalized expressions— reached up to pinch his cheek. “Look at this face. Wasting it on spreadsheets and coffee. A tragedy!”

Phainon ducked away with a grin, but let them tug him down for a quick, smothering hug that left him smelling like lavender and powder. “You know you’re my favorite part of this city, right?”

“Flatterer,” muttered Merope, pretending not to preen.

“Anaxa, we’re stealing your boy,” Alkippe called toward the counter.

Anaxa didn’t look up from his espresso shot. “Take him. Leave the box. And don’t get any perfume on my beans.”

The old ladies cackled like crows over a carcass, and Phainon managed to extricate himself with promises of visiting their next meeting and bringing better muffins.

Once they were distracted by a fresh round of speculation over the protagonist’s bedroom skills, Phainon slid into the empty stool by the counter, dropped his elbows onto the polished wood, and—with all the grace of a man whose soul had left his body several hours ago—let his head fall forward with a dull thud.

Anaxa didn’t even flinch. He just kept polishing a glass.

“Rough day?”

Phainon groaned without lifting his head. “You have no idea.”

Anaxa set the glass down with a soft clink, grabbed a clean towel, and went right back to ignoring him like a professional.

Phainon stayed like that, forehead against the counter, for a long, blessed moment. The warmth of the wood, the hum of the café, the distant shriek of a milk frother. A cozy little pocket of misery.

“You’re not even gonna ask?” he mumbled.

“No,” Anaxa said flatly, flipping a page in some battered old paperback he kept stashed under the counter. “But you’re gonna tell me anyway.”

Phainon sighed, sitting up halfway. “Rude.”

“Order first,” Anaxa muttered without looking up.

“Alright, alright. I’ll take a—”

“Yes, I know, you order the same shameful nonsense every time,” Anaxa snapped, slapping a hand on the counter. “‘Oat milk, cardamom, lavender syrup, double shot, extra foam, sprinkle of nutmeg on top, because you’re a delicate fucking flower.’”

A few patrons glanced over. Phainon shot them a thumbs up. “It’s a good drink.”

“It’s a crime against god and coffee,” Anaxa grumbled, scribbling the order down anyway. “Now vent. Get it over with.”

Phainon huffed out a laugh, propping his chin on one hand as he watched Anaxa work.

“I got called in early. Again. For another ‘company culture revitalization’ meeting.”

“Oof.”

“Which is code for some middle manager telling us to smile through the crushing existential dread of late-stage capitalism.”

Anaxa grunted, setting a mug under the espresso machine.

“And then,” Phainon went on, “I found out they’re probably getting bought out by some corporate juggernaut. Which means new management. Which means layoffs. Which means my broke ass gets to polish my résumé and pray to the god of LinkedIn connections.”

“Guess you should’ve gone to law school like your mama wanted.”

Phainon snorted. “My mama wanted me to marry a preacher’s daughter and take over the family farm.”

Anaxa smirked. “Poor woman.”

“Don’t you dare feel bad for her, she’s thriving.”

They both lapsed into a familiar, easy silence as the espresso machine hissed.

It was stupid, but in moments like this—watching the same old people cycle through, the scent of burnt coffee and pastry sugar in the air, Anaxa’s relentless bitching—the city almost felt like home.

Almost.

The café TV—one of those ancient flat screens bolted into the corner with a crooked bracket—droned softly above the hum of conversation. Normally tuned to whatever sports highlights or cooking competition Anaxa could stomach, but today it was stuck on some 24-hour business news channel.

Phainon wasn’t paying attention until the scrolling ticker caught his eye:

“Castrum Kremnos rumored to acquire Okhema Tech in Q3 corporate merger shakeup.”

And of course, right on cue, a perky, too-polished anchor appeared on screen, voice syrupy-smooth and detached from the impending corporate bloodbath she was reporting.

“Sources close to the matter suggest that Castrum Kremnos, one of the city’s most prominent financial conglomerates, is finalizing negotiations to acquire Okhema Technologies in a multi-million dollar merger projected to reshape the regional tech landscape. The acquisition is expected to trigger a series of departmental restructurings, with analysts forecasting a significant workforce reduction in non-essential roles.”

Phainon groaned, dragging both hands down his face.

Anaxa slid his drink across the counter without a word.

“I swear to god,” Phainon muttered into his palms, “if I get laid off and end up working some gig where my uniform involves a visor and a name tag, I’m jumping off the 5th Street bridge.”

“You’d survive,” Anaxa said, deadpan. “You’ve got country boy resilience.”

Phainon peeked through his fingers. “Would you hire me? If I got fired?”

“No.”

“Seriously?”

“You practically work here already. Only difference would be me having to actually pay you.” Anaxa smirked over the rim of his coffee. “And I’m not about to shell out payroll for Aglaea’s stray charity cases.”

That one hit a little to the left of petty and straight into personal.

Phainon leveled a half-hearted glare at him. “You’re still mad at her for that book fair thing?”

Anaxa didn’t even blink. “She knows what she did.”

“Dude, it was ten years ago.”

“She alphabetized poetry under nonfiction.”

“…Okay yeah, that’s fair.”

They let that sit a beat, the anchor still babbling about fiscal quarters and restructuring forecasts like she wasn’t announcing the potential end of Phainon’s rent-paying existence.

Phainon tipped his head back. “Guess I better start brushing up my fry cook skills.”

Anaxa snorted. “You’d set yourself on fire inside a week.”

“Maybe I’d like the flames,” Phainon sighed.

From across the room, one of the old book club ladies shouted, “Stop feeling sorry for yourself, sugar, and come say hi before we die!”

Phainon gave Anaxa a weary look. “See? My public demands me.”

“Go get your cheeks pinched, hayseed.”

The next hour passed in the lazy, haphazard rhythm that made this place feel more like a community center than a café.

Phainon made the rounds without meaning to—holding the door for a guy juggling a tray of muffins, helping a frazzled student reconnect to the café’s eternally spotty Wi-Fi, and untangling a set of earbuds for a kid who looked two seconds from tears. Every time Anaxa passed behind the counter, he’d grunt a new order at him: “Move those crates. Tighten that loose table leg. Tell book club they can’t bring in outside pastries.”

And every time, Phainon grumbled back but did it anyway.

Somewhere between refilling napkin holders and rescuing a barista who’d dropped an entire tray of spoons, the Book Coven finally snagged him, pulling him in with the kind of matriarchal gravity no mortal man could resist.

“Sweetheart, come here and settle something,” one of them demanded, waving a half-eaten muffin like a gavel.

“Which one of these fictional hunks would you marry?” another asked, thrusting an open book under his nose. The page in question involved a shirtless warrior prince with brooding eyes and an attitude problem.

Phainon laughed, played along, let them tug at his sleeves and pinch his cheek and slip him a contraband strawberry bar under the table.

Across the café, Anaxa watched it all with his usual expression of mild, pained irritation. But when no one was looking, he quietly refilled the glass of water by Phainon’s usual spot at the counter. Topped it off with ice, too. And when Phainon came back to set down a handful of stray menus, Anaxa didn’t say a word—just shoved it toward him with a grunt.

Eventually, the midday lull started to settle in. Conversations dropped to murmurs. The line shrank to a trickle. The sunlight through the windows edged toward gold.

And then—

“Order for Phainon!”

His name, called sharp and clear from behind the counter.

He perked up immediately, a deep, heartfelt sigh escaping him like a man rescued from the edge.

“Thank god,” he muttered, rubbing the back of his neck as he straightened up from where he’d been crouched, adjusting a stubborn table leg.

A few of the old ladies chuckled knowingly as he made his way toward the counter, threading through scattered chairs and half-finished conversations, already picturing the first perfect, scalding sip of—

The cup disappeared.

Right off the counter.

Before his fingers could even brush the cardboard sleeve.

Phainon stopped mid-step. Blinking.

Someone else’s hand was already around his drink.

And just like that—the universe had decided to screw him again.

Phainon closed his eyes. Took a long, steady breath in through his nose. Counted to three like his grandma used to tell him when he was about to put someone through a wall.

Then he opened them.

“Are you fucking kidding me.”

The words came out low and flat, the kind of tone that made nearby conversations stutter and pause. A few heads turned. One of the old book club ladies made a delighted little ooh sound.

Standing there, smug as sin, drink already halfway to his mouth, was him.

Mydei didn’t even blink. Took a slow, infuriatingly casual sip of Phainon’s overcomplicated, shamefully indulgent seasonal drink—oat milk, cardamom, lavender syrup, the whole overthought mess—and let out a content little hum like he’d been served nectar from the gods.

“Hmm?” Mydei tilted his head, playing mock-confused. “Oh… was that yours? Thought it was mine. Rookie mistake.”

The air between them went tight as a wire.

Phainon’s glare could’ve cracked glass.

A few tables over, Anaxa didn’t even look up. Just muttered, “And there goes my peaceful afternoon.”

“Give it back.”

Phainon’s voice had dropped to a warning growl, but Mydei just raised a brow, unhurried as ever, taking another pointed sip of the drink. The smug little ahh sound he made after could’ve gotten a lesser man killed.

“Make me.”

It was always like this. Sharp words exchanged like blades, tight smiles masking the constant simmer of irritation that flared whenever they shared air. It wasn’t even about the drink anymore—hadn’t been for months.

The rivalry had started when Phainon, bleary-eyed and sleep-deprived, grabbed a drink off the counter that wasn’t his. Took a huge swig expecting bitter coffee and got walloped with something so aggressively sweet and floral he damn near spat it back into the cup. The memory still haunted him.

Turned out it belonged to this asshole.

Mydei, naturally, took that as a personal offense. So, of course, the next time Phainon’s order was called out, Mydei snagged it and sauntered off like nothing had happened.

And now here they were. Every time they crossed paths, it was open season.

Phainon’s jaw ticked. His hand flexed at his side, tempted to snatch the cup back, but…

Goddamn it.

He looked good today.

He hated to admit it—would sooner eat glass—but fuck. Mydei was standing there in a black sleeveless turtleneck that clung to his frame a little too well, and over his shoulders hung this soft pink sweater, casually draped like some careless afterthought. His hair was slightly mussed from the wind, sharp features calm and unbothered as ever.

For anyone else, Phainon would’ve started a bar fight over this. Made a damn expedition out of reclaiming his drink and ending this dumb little war.

But for him…

Well.

“You gonna keep glaring at me or actually do something about it?” Mydei asked, voice mild as ever, but there was a glint in his eye. A challenge.

Phainon gritted his teeth. “One of these days, pretty boy.”

Mydei smirked, stepping just slightly closer, lowering his voice. “Promises, promises.”

A chair scraped somewhere. The low hum of conversation returned, but the air between them stayed tight as ever.

Phainon reached for the cup—and Mydei smoothly shifted it to his other hand.

Fucker.

Phainon’s jaw flexed. His patience—already paper-thin—finally gave.

“You keep this up, and I swear to god I’m gonna—”

Mydei, deadpan and far too calm for his own good, cut in smoothly. “You’ll what? Use those big, calloused hands on me?”

The words hit the air like a lit match.

Phainon’s mind blanked for a beat, then snapped into motion.

In a sharp, graceless motion, he grabbed a fistful of Mydei’s sweater, spun him around, and pinned him against the nearest patch of wall—not hard enough to hurt, but enough to startle a few patrons and knock a flyer loose. His other hand planted firm beside Mydei’s head, caging him in.

The café dropped a few decibels. Even Anaxa glanced up from behind the counter with a sigh, already done with this bullshit.

Phainon tilted his head down, leaning in close, just enough for Mydei to catch the glint in his eye and the barely-suppressed smirk threatening at the corner of his mouth.

“Careful what you wish for, sweetheart.”

And god, the way Mydei’s smug little eyes didn’t falter—if anything, it sharpened.

Somewhere off to the side, a student with a laptop muttered under their breath, “Jesus christ, just fuck already.”

Neither of them moved.

Phainon’s pulse kicked in his throat.

Mydei’s eyes flicked down to his mouth, then back up like he was absentmindedly judging him.

Phainon grinned, sharp and wolfish, and stepped back just enough to let him go.

“Asshole,” he muttered.

Mydei smoothed his sweater like nothing happened and raised the drink in a mock toast. “See you tomorrow.”

Phainon let out a long, exhausted sigh as the door swung shut behind Mydei. He leaned back against the counter like the wind had been knocked out of him, scrubbing a hand down his face.

From the book club table, Merope let out a delighted giggle.

He practically snapped his head in her direction, glare sharp enough to cut glass. “What.”

She only grinned wider, undeterred. Another one of the ladies elbowed her, both of them dissolving into gleeful whispers.

Anaxa from where he was wiping a glass dry, muttered under his breath, “They’re not wrong.”

Phainon scowled. “What was that?”

“Nothing.”

“Yeah, that’s what I thought.”

He pushed off the counter and made for the register again. “Alright, fine, hit me. One more of those ridiculous oat milk, cardamom—”

“Yeah, yeah, I know your shame order,” Anaxa cut him off flatly. “You’ve ordered the same thing for a year, don’t act like you’re surprising me.”

Phainon grumbled, pulling out his phone to check his rapidly dwindling bank account. He winced. “Jesus, how is this shit eight bucks? What’s it brewed with, liquid gold and student tears?”

Anaxa snorted. “Nah. You’re just broke.”

“I hate you.”

“You wish you could.”

Phainon eyed the menu board again, sighed, then shoved his phone back in his pocket. “You know what, forget it. Coffee’s a scam anyway.”

“Coward.”

“I said I’m good.”

Anaxa grunted, set down the glass, and grabbed a small paper bag from behind the counter. Without ceremony, he lobbed it at Phainon, who barely caught it in time.

“You’re off shift. Get out of my café.”

Phainon blinked down at the bag—fresh pastries, still warm.

“…You’re a softie.”

“Eat shit.”

A few of the regulars called out their goodbyes as he made for the door. One of the students gave him a lazy salute. The book club people waved their hands, rings glittering.

“See you next week, darling!”

Phainon grinned, adjusting the bag under his arm. “You know it.”

And with that, he stepped back out into the city’s chill, the door shutting behind him with a soft jingle.

Phainon stepped out into the street, the cool air hitting his face like a wake-up slap. He sighed, rolling his shoulders, the weight of the day settling in again now that the brief chaos had passed.

A flicker of movement by a lamppost caught his eye.

There, crouched in the shadow of a trash bin, a scrappy gray cat watched him with wary yellow eyes. One ear was nicked, its fur a little patchy, but it held itself like a tiny, threadbare king.

Phainon huffed a soft laugh, crouched down, and tore a corner off one of the pastries in the bag. “You’re out here hustling too, huh?” He tossed the bit of pastry toward the cat, who eyed it, sniffed, then devoured it like it might be his last meal.

“Yeah,” Phainon muttered, straightening up. “I get it.”

With a final glance at the café—still bright, still loud, still carrying on without him—he adjusted the strap of his bag, stuffed his hands in his pockets, and made his way toward work.

chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Phainon and Mydei accidentally go to dinner together, swap shitty date stories, and somehow don’t kill each other. Phainon nearly bankrupts himself, gets saved by a friendly waitress, simps over Mydei under moody streetlights, and gives him a crumpled pressed flower like a Victorian maiden. An Uber driver named Sal (allegedly, maybe) ships it immediately. Neither of them admit they’re having a good time.

Chapter Notes

I need sleep, but the yaoi won me over. Why do I always post these mf’s so late😭

The city at night was a living thing.

Neon signs flickered in storefront windows, throwing lazy, half-hearted glows against rain-slicked concrete. Somewhere in the distance, a late-night bus groaned around a corner, headlights washing over puddles and uneven sidewalks. Distant club basslines bled into the streets—low, thrumming reminders that somewhere out there, people were still awake, still dancing, still doing something other than working themselves into the ground.

Phainon could hear his own footsteps.

Heavy. Unsteady. Bone-deep tired.

The streetlights hung in hazy halos, a pale gold cutting through the blue-black of the city’s late hours. A stray cat darted under a parked car. Teenagers loitered by a shuttered store, passing a vape back and forth, the thin stream of it catching in the light before vanishing into the damp air.

Phainon adjusted his grip on the strap of his bag, the leather biting into his shoulder through the thin fabric of his shirt. Said shirt was a mess— crumpled, sleeves pushed up to his elbows to reveal forearms marked with faint old scars and a faint spatter of blue pen ink from somewhere around hour ten of today’s corporate hellscape. His tie hung loose and lopsided around his neck, long since given up on being anything more than decorative.

He could still hear his supervisor’s voice ringing in his skull.

“We need this cleaned up by the end of the day.” “But it’s already the end of the day.” “Then stay late.”

That was fourteen hours ago.

A logistics crisis some other department had caused had landed in his lap, and of course the higher-ups at Okhema—eager to look competent ahead of the impending merge—had decided to drop it squarely on his department. Fix it. Damage control. Make them look good, or don’t come back Monday.

And Phainon wasn’t stupid. He wasn’t deaf to the murmured talks of restructuring, of trimming the fat, of redundancies when Castrum Kremnos finally sank its teeth into Okhema’s throat. Like he’d talked about with Anaxa before, layoffs would be coming. And people like Phainon, people without seniority, without anyone watching their back?

They’d be the first to go.

So he stayed late.

Worked through lunch, through dinner, drank shitty office coffee until his hands shook, watched the sun set through the crack in the blinds. And when it was done—when the files were patched and the numbers were spun into something the investors could stomach—no one even thanked him.

“We knew you’d pull through,” was the closest he got.

Phainon let out a long breath, dragging a hand down his face. He didn’t bother fixing his tie. Didn’t bother rerolling his sleeves. His shoulders ached from hours hunched over his desk, from carrying a department’s worth of fuckups on his back, and now all he wanted was food cheap enough to pay for with pocket lint and pride.

A dollar slice. A shitty diner. Hell, maybe just a coffee he didn’t have to expense.

A man on a bike zipped past, delivery bag bouncing against his back. Someone shouted from a fourth-floor window. The smell of hot garbage and fresh rain lingered like an old, stubborn bruise.

Phainon squared his shoulders.

“Okay,” he muttered to no one. “Food. Then sleep. Then do it all over again.”

He forced a long breath in through his nose, jaw tight.

Think about something good.

It was a trick Cyrene taught him back home, one of those old things that stuck no matter how many years you spent scraping by. Count your blessings, no matter how rotten the day.

He dug for them.

Okay—he hadn’t gotten fired.

The crisis hadn’t sunk the department.

The overworked printer in his office hadn’t caught fire this time.

Someone in HR had brought in stale muffins. He’d managed to steal two.

Was that four? That was four. Not bad.

And… okay. That one old lady at the boutique store this morning had called him “handsome in a scruffy way,” which technically counted. Five.

Phainon let out a huff of a laugh at that, soft and tired, his steps falling into a slower rhythm as he rounded the corner onto a quieter stretch of street. The city dimmed a little here—neon signs sparse, the shops all shuttered, only the occasional glow of a distant window or flickering streetlamp.

His stomach grumbled, a reminder that muffins weren’t a real dinner.

He passed a shuttered bodega, metal grate halfway drawn, the flickering light inside catching on rows of dusty snack bags and sun-faded lottery ads. In the window, a cat sat perched on a stack of cardboard boxes, one paw tucked under its chest, watching the world with the unbothered detachment only cats and the very rich ever managed to pull off.

Phainon slowed, pausing in front of the glass.

The cat blinked at him. Yellow eyes, slitted and disinterested. Its ear twitched once.

“Lucky bastard,” Phainon muttered.

The cat yawned, wide-mouthed and unconcerned, before curling deeper into itself and turning its gaze elsewhere.

Phainon huffed, a threadbare smirk tugging at the corner of his mouth. He adjusted the strap of his bag and kept moving, his footsteps the only thing marking time against the hush of the street.

And then, as he rounded the next corner—

He almost plowed straight into a silhouette standing dead-center beneath a streetlamp’s halo.

Phainon’s foot caught on uneven concrete, his balance tipping forward fast enough that his stomach dropped, the world tilting with it. He barely had time to hiss a curse through his teeth before a hand caught him—firm, steady, a palm pressed against his chest and fingers curling tight around his upper arm.

“Woah, hey—”

“Shit, sorry—! Fuck, I wasn’t—” Phainon scrambled, the strap of his bag sliding off his shoulder as he instinctively grabbed the stranger’s wrist to steady himself. “Didn’t see you, I wasn’t—walking, just—I mean, I was, but not like at you, I—”

“Are you oka—”

The voice stopped.

Phainon’s words tangled in his throat as he looked up, gaze colliding with a pair of sharp, gold-shot eyes. Not amber, not hazel, but that unmistakable glinting, metallic warmth that looked downright supernatural under the streetlamp’s glow.

His stomach flipped.

Oh, fuck me.

It was him.

For one long, stifling moment, neither of them moved. Phainon still half-bent from the fall, a fistful of the other’s wrist, the stranger’s—Mydei’s— hand braced against his shoulder like he was debating whether to shove him off or steady him again.

Phainon’s brain supplied details against his will.

The cigarette, unlit but half-raised, still smoldering faintly between Mydei’s fingers where he must’ve just sparked the lighter. The slim band of a simple, worn signet ring catching the light. Red nail polish—a sharp, deep crimson—slick and immaculate on blunt, elegant fingers.

The shirt was black. Mandarin collar. Off-center button closure that ran in a precise line down the side of his chest. Tapered trousers, cut so well they probably cost more than Phainon’s rent. Black leather ankle boots with a slight heel that clicked faintly against the sidewalk when Mydei shifted his weight.

Phainon was… leaning. And looking. And if his stomach did a weird little dip about it, that was the exhaustion talking.

Neither of them spoke.

Somewhere in the distance, a car horn blared. The world thinned to the ring of streetlights, the haze of rain-damp air, and the relentless, shared oh-god-it’s-you moment stretching thin between them.

Mydei’s gaze dragged over Phainon’s face, down to the loose tie, the ink stains, the crumpled shirt, then back up. His expression barely flickered, save for the smallest, impossible-to-read lift of one brow.

Phainon’s brain cells screamed in union, move, say something, stop standing here like an idiot.

He cleared his throat. “Of course it’s you.”

The words came out rougher than intended.

Mydei’s mouth curled at the corner—not a smile. Something far more sardonic. The cigarette flared to life between his fingers, a brief halo of orange-red glow that painted the edges of his cheekbones and made the gold in his eyes catch like a predator’s.

“Likewise,” Mydei said, smoke curling from the corner of his mouth.

They separated like someone had cut a wire between them. Phainon dropped his hand, jerking his bag back up onto his shoulder with a sharp motion. Mydei casually stepped back a pace, like gravity itself was a minor inconvenience to him.

Phainon turned on his heel, scowling hard enough to sour milk, and muttered, “Just my fucking luck.”

Behind him, the soft click of a boot heel on wet concrete and a quiet exhale of smoke.

Neither of them left.

Somewhere down the block, a drunk laughed too loud. The cat in the bodega window pawed lazily at a moth.

Phainon adjusted his bag higher on his shoulder with an exaggerated motion. He wasn’t leaving. He could feel the expectant weight of Mydei’s stare, like the bastard was waiting for it—for him to slink off first, to be the one who relented. Phainon planted his feet harder, jaw set, scowl sharp enough to cut glass.

He wasn’t the one walking away first.

Across from him, Mydei took a long, unhurried drag from his cigarette. The ember flared, catching red against the damp-dark curve of his cheekbone. Smoke slipped from between his lips in a lazy ribbon, and he made a show of exhaling like he didn’t have a single care in the world.

But he wasn’t leaving either.

They stood there like two storm fronts refusing to break, both too spiteful to retreat.

Phainon’s patience snapped first.

“Should’ve let me faceplant,” he muttered, glaring at some imaginary spot over Mydei’s shoulder. “Would’ve improved my night.”

Mydei didn’t miss a beat. His gaze cut sideways, sharp and impossible to read.

“And rob myself of the entertainment?” Another drag. “No thanks.”

The nerve of him.

Phainon scoffed, a disbelieving huff that was half laugh, half threat. “Didn’t peg you for a sadist, but I guess I should’ve known.”

Mydei’s mouth twitched—not quite a smirk, but god, it wanted to be. “You assume I’m not already one. How sweet.”

“Trust me,” Phainon shot back, stepping a fraction closer, “there’s nothing sweet about me.”

“That look might work on softer men,” Mydei said, flicking ash to the curb. “But I stopped pitying creatures like you years ago.” A pause, eyes catching Phainon’s for a beat too long. “Shame, though. I imagine you’ve still got a line of them, hoping for a turn.”

Phainon’s heart did something awful in his chest—a sharp, traitorous stutter —but his mouth was faster.

“Bet you’re at the front of that line.”

It landed like a thrown glove.

Mydei’s eyes snapped back to his, pupils sharp slits in the gold. The tension wound itself tighter, something electric and crackling in the scant inch that separated them now. They’d both shifted without realizing it, the place narrowing to a single, suffocating point of contact. Phainon could smell the smoke on Mydei’s breath, could see the sharp gleam of red polish on his fingers where they held the cigarette, could hear his own pulse in his ears.

Neither of them moved again.

“You couldn’t handle me,” Mydei accused.

Phainon didn’t lean in, but

he didn’t lean back either. He huffed a quiet, humorless laugh.

“Wouldn’t have to,” he said automatically. “You’d fall apart first.”

The city noise blurred.

The distance between them was paper-thin.

Phainon clicked his tongue, sharp and annoyed, and finally stepped back a pace. His nose wrinkled, waving a hand as if to clear the thin coil of cigarette smoke hanging between them.

“Hate the smell of smoke,” he muttered, pointed and petty, like the problem was the cigarette and not the man holding it.

Mydei hummed, utterly unbothered, taking one last drag before flicking the half-finished cigarette to the curb. He ground it out under the heel of a black boot, the sharp click of sole to pavement louder than it should’ve been in the hush between them.

“Tragic,” he murmured.

Phainon’s jaw clenched. He shifted his bag higher on his shoulder and muttered, half to himself, “I need to find something to eat before I chew through my own goddamn hand. Shame that sandwich place closed up...”

“Same,” Mydei replied, smooth and light, like this wasn’t the worst coincidence imaginable.

They both turned, sharp little movements like dueling cats, heading off in separate but unfortunately mirrored directions—only to realize, a few paces in, that it was the same one.

A pause.

Both stopped, turning just enough to look at each other.

“Which way,” Phainon ground out, already knowing the answer.

Mydei lifted a brow, and without a word, pointed down the street.

Phainon pointed too.

They stared. No blinking. No flinching. Just the unspoken, bone-deep of course sinking between them.

Phainon dragged a hand down his face. “The place down the street?”

Mydei gave a soft, disbelieving laugh through his nose. “You’re kidding.”

Phainon shot him a glare. “Do I look like I’m in a joking mood?”

“Never,” Mydei deadpanned, lips curling just enough to count as a smirk.

Another beat. Another unspoken fuck you.

“Well,” Phainon sighed, starting down the street with grim resolve, “don’t walk too close. People might think we’re friendly.”

Mydei fell into step beside him anyway. “Unlikely.”

They walked in silence for maybe half a block. The damp air stuck to Phainon’s skin, heavy with rain and exhaust, and his stomach growled again —loud enough this time for him to sigh, more annoyed than embarrassed.

He sighed, “if I don’t eat in the next ten minutes, I might actually start gnawing on a street sign.”

Mydei snorted, not even looking his way. “Might improve your face.”

Phainon shot him a glare. “You’re one to talk. You’ve got the kind of face that looks like it’s used to getting slapped.”

“Funny,” Mydei said, flicking a glance sideways, the corner of his mouth tilting. “You strike me as the type who’d ask for it.”

“That supposed to be a kink thing or are you just bad at insults?”

“Why not both?”

Phainon let out an amused scoff, surprised it escaped him. He caught Mydei watching him then—not obvious, just a sliver of gaze from the corner of those sharp gold eyes, like he was filing the sound away.

The street dipped a little ahead, light pooling in uneven patches. From the corner of his eye, Phainon spotted a drunk couple halfway through an argument, voices sharp and slicing through the quiet. The guy gesturing too wide, the other’s face pinched in frustration. Instinct kicked in—Phainon edged closer to Mydei’s side without thinking, angling his body just enough to put himself between the man’s flailing arm and Mydei’s path.

He didn’t say anything about it.

Mydei either didn’t notice or was too proud to. He kept walking half a step ahead, still picking up the thread of their argument like it hadn’t skipped a beat.

“… and for the record,” Mydei was saying, “that sandwich place didn’t close. It moved two blocks down.”

“Bullshit.”

“I had lunch there last week.”

“Yeah, well, maybe the food’s fine if you’re the type who thinks truffle oil makes up for a dry bun.”

“Ah,” Mydei sighed, mock-sympathetic. “A man of low standards.”

“Hey now,” Phainon grinned, adjusting his grip on his bag. “I’ll have you know, I’m a man of simple pleasures. Good bread, strong coffee, a halfway decent sunset—that’s it. Not all of us need gold flakes on our fries to feel something.”

Mydei made a soft noise at that. Not quite a scoff, not quite a laugh. More intrigued.

“Country boy wisdom,” he said dryly. “Touching.”

Phainon smirked. “Don’t act like you aren’t charmed.”

“I’d rather gnaw on a street sign.”

And for reasons neither of them would admit, they both kept close.

Because at 11PM in a city like this, even the worst company was better than none.

Eventually, in the middle of humming some old tune to pass the time— Phainon realized they’d stopped.

He glanced up, expecting some flickering diner sign or a ratty awning half-hanging off a corner pizza joint. Something cheap, grimy, familiar.

Instead, glass.

Tall, sleek panels stretched up into the night like sheets of dark water, catching the city lights in smooth, liquid reflections. Warm, understated lighting spilled from inside, painting the sidewalk gold. And then—the name. Etched in clean, elegant lettering above the door.

Phainon’s brain hiccupped.

Wait a second—

He knew that name.

Twilight & Courtyard.

Not because he’d ever set foot in the place, but because some executive at the office once bragged about dropping a casual three grand there on “a light evening out.” It was the kind of place where the menu didn’t have prices, where everything came in portions small enough to insult your grandmother, and where they probably charged extra if you had the nerve to ask for tap water.

And here it was. Right in front of him. Right where they’d apparently been walking this whole time.

What the hell—

“Didn’t know this was here,” he muttered without thinking, the words slipping out numbly.

In his head, they were both heading for the same late-night dive. Greasy noodles. Shitty coffee. A place where it wouldn’t matter that he looked like hell. He figured they’d pass this place, maybe trade a cheap shot about pretentious rich assholes, and move on.

Except Mydei didn’t stop.

Didn’t even hesitate.

Like it was nothing, like he’d done it a hundred times, Mydei stepped forward and pushed through the heavy glass door. A suited host looked up from his podium, expression smoothing into polite recognition.

Phainon’s stomach dropped.

Oh, oh no.

He was still standing there when Mydei glanced back over his shoulder, one brow faintly arched. “You coming, or planning to admire the sidewalk all night?”

His tone wasn’t condescending. Like he genuinely thought they’d been headed to the same place this whole time. Which somehow made it worse.

For half a second, Phainon considered cutting his losses. Making up some excuse about needing to take a call, fake-limping away, getting hit by a bus —literally anything but walking into a place where his whole month’s rent probably wouldn’t cover the bread basket.

But then his gaze snagged on Mydei’s face in the glow of the glass doorway —those sharp features softened in the warm light, gold eyes catching like the city itself had made a home in them. And for reasons he would never, ever say out loud, Phainon’s spine stiffened.

His brain screamed oh fuck oh fuck oh fuck, but his feet moved anyway.

Maybe it was stubbornness. Maybe it was pride. Maybe it was that deeply stupid part of him that couldn’t back down from a pretty face if it tried.

So he squared his shoulders, forced a smile over the rising panic, and followed.

His stomach was somewhere around his ankles, his wallet preemptively sobbing, but screw it—if he was going to die financially, he wasn’t about to do it looking like a coward.

Inside, the air changed. Gone was the grit and damp of the city, replaced with soft amber lighting and a scent like clean linen and expensive liquor. Crystal glasses caught the glow in delicate prisms. A pianist somewhere in the back let notes of slow, unobtrusive jazz drift through the room like smoke.

Phainon was already recalculating his life choices when the host approached.

“Sir Mydeimos,” the man greeted smoothly, giving a polite nod that Phainon swore bordered on deferential. “Your table’s ready.”

Mydei gave an absent wave of acknowledgment, leaning in just enough to mutter, “My contact bailed. I’ll be dining with him instead.”

A tilt of his head toward Phainon.

Phainon’s brows shot up. Him?

Okay, so maybe his company wasn’t entirely repellent. Huh.

Not that Mydei gave him even a flicker of attention—already dismissing the moment like it meant nothing. Which, sure. Fine.

Phainon went to make some offhand comment, but then the host gestured, and instead of heading toward the modest scattering of well-dressed tables like normal people, they were led down a short, narrow hallway lined with glass that seemed to dim the world outside.

And into a separate dining area.

Not a backroom, not a corner booth. This was some VIP, no-price-listed, jazz-playing, waiters-who-look-like-they-commit-clean-hits-on-weekends type shit.

Phainon’s jaw nearly hit the floor.

There were maybe four tables in the whole space, each glowing under its own delicate ring of light. The walls were dark wood, and somewhere overhead hung a chandelier that probably cost more than his annual salary. Menus were already placed at their table, printed on paper so thick it felt illegal to touch. No prices. Because if you had to ask, you couldn’t afford it.

Phainon’s stomach dropped straight to his shoes.

He opened his mouth—already halfway through the mental drafting of actually, hey, I just remembered I have to go wrestle a raccoon or pay rent or cry in a corner somewhere—when Mydei gestured smoothly to the opposite seat.

“You’re already here,” he said, tone light but leaving no room for argument. “Sit down.”

The way the amber light caught in his hair, those long fingers resting against the crystal glass like he belonged in a noir film or some doomed love story—it framed him in a way that made something low in Phainon’s chest twist.

This was a bad idea.

A horrible idea.

So of course he coughed, adjusted his sleeves like he did this shit every night, and dropped into the chair.

“You better be picking up the check,” he muttered, snatching the menu open only to immediately regret it when he couldn’t pronounce a single thing. It wasn’t even a menu, it was a test. A fucking tax bracket IQ test.

His brain whimpered.

Still—he flicked a glance up at Mydei, letting a crooked grin tug at the corner of his mouth. “Fair warning, though. If any of this turns out to be snails or foam pretending to be food, I’m ordering a burger on the way home.”

A few minutes passed. Phainon kept his eyes trained on the menu, or what he assumed was a menu, though most of it wasn’t even in English. A delicate, serif font spelled out words in French, Italian, maybe ancient Latin for all he knew, while his brain gamely tried to translate crème de something-something into ‘probably soup.’

He was sweating.

His palm dragged against the thick, linen napkin in his lap as he hunted for anything that didn’t sound like it required a black market organ sale to afford. Mydei sat across from him, the very picture of disinterest, one elbow propped on the table, head tipped back just enough for the warm light to catch the edges of his sharp cheekbones. His eyes flicked lazily over the drink selection.

Neither of them spoke.

Phainon was halfway through internally debating whether it was more shameful to fake a phone call or just bolt when a soft voice cut through the tension.

“Good evening, gentlemen.”

He glanced up—and his stomach did a spectacular somersault.

Why?

It was Hyacine.

Hyacine, as in Anaxa’s Hyacine, the one he’d helped move a busted futon up three flights of stairs a month back. Anaxa’s assistant, med student, soft-spoken and genuinely sweet in a way that always made him feel like a crow sitting next to a dove.

She stood there in tailored black, a notepad in hand, hair back neatly. A small silver pin gleamed at her collar. For a second, she didn’t register him. She was too busy doing her job, giving the same warm, polished smile every waiter in this place had to have patented.

Then she did a double take.

Her brow furrowed, head tilting, recognition sparking behind those bright eyes.

“Phainon?”

His name came out soft, surprised. She blinked, as if mentally recalculating what the hell he was doing in a place like this.

Phainon felt the color drain from his face. He sat up straighter, his hand flattening over the menu like he could hide behind it. “Uh—hey.”

Her gaze flicked to Mydei, then back to Phainon. The pieces clicking. A bright little smile tugged at the corners of her mouth. “Oh… are you two —?”

“No,” both men said at once.

Too quick.

A heavy pause dropped between them.

Phainon ran a hand through his hair, scowling at his own knee. Mydei didn’t even look up from the drink options. It would’ve been funny if it wasn’t mortifying.

Hyacine, to her credit, smoothed right over it. She gave Phainon a subtle, wordless look. The kind that translated across rooms and lifetimes.

Baby, what are you doing here?

Phainon’s lips twitched in a helpless grimace.

I can’t pay for this.

One brow quirked. A tiny head tilt.

I got you, idiot.

His soul all but floated out of his body in sheer, unholy gratitude.

And with a pro-level smoothness that would’ve impressed an actual hitman, Hyacine turned to Mydei like none of it had happened. “Our chef’s special tonight is a seared lamb with saffron couscous and roasted heirloom vegetables,” she said lightly, “but if either of you prefer something off-menu, we’re happy to accommodate.”

Phainon didn’t even pretend to look at the menu again.

“Yeah, uh—sure,” he said, gesturing vaguely. “Whatever’s good.”

Hyacine’s mouth twitched. She knew. God, she knew.

“And for you, sir?” she asked Mydei.

Mydei glanced up, finally, golden eyes catching hers. “The special’s fine.”

“Excellent,” she said, scribbling it down. She glanced back at Phainon one last time, amusement flickering behind her polite professional veneer. “I’ll make sure they don’t poison it.”

Phainon snorted, his tension breaking just a fraction.

As she walked away, Phainon slumped back against his chair, casting a sideways glare at Mydei who reached for the glass of water in front of him like this wasn’t the most bizarre, financially ruinous night of Phainon’s life.

Phainon tapped a fingertip against the base of his glass. Mydei leaned back in his chair, one arm hooked lazily over the backrest, his expression unreadable in that maddening way Phainon was already learning to despise.

“So,” Phainon started,“You eat at places like this often, or is this a ‘make your enemies feel poor’ sort of thing?”

Mydei snorted, lips quirking. “Not usually. Was supposed to be a work dinner.”

“Ah,” Phainon said, nodding slowly. “So I’m the charity case.”

“More like a contingency plan,” Mydei replied, glancing sidelong at him. “Didn’t want to waste the reservation.”

“Yeah, heaven forbid you lose your preferred spot in the bourgeoisie feeding trough.”

That earned a quiet, breath-of-a-laugh sound from Mydei, the kind Phainon wouldn’t have noticed if he hadn’t been watching so closely.

A moment passed. Mydei sipped his water, then asked, casually, “You always this charming, or is it a special occasion?”

Phainon gave a crooked grin. “Depends. You always this smug, or is it genetic?”

Mydei tipped his head, considering. “Bit of both.”

Phainon chuckled, despite himself.

It should’ve stopped there—but the weird current between them didn’t let up. Something about the soft lighting made the sharp edges between them dull just enough to invite curiosity in.

“So,” Phainon said, leaning forward on his forearms. “Since we’re apparently trapped here ‘til our organs show up on tiny plates, might as well make conversation.”

Mydei quirked a brow, amused. “You’re doing a stellar job of it.”

“Yeah, well,” Phainon drawled, a hint of charm slipping in like second nature, “if I don’t flirt with my enemies a little, I get rusty.”

The words left his mouth before he could stop them, and to his surprise— no, horror—it actually landed.

Mydei’s lashes lowered just a fraction, his gaze a glint of something unreadable in the dim light. “Is that what this is?” he murmured, tone mild but edged.

Phainon grinned wider, tapping the table. “Wouldn’t you like to know.”

Another pause, a hair longer than necessary. Then Mydei leaned back, that same faint smirk still tugging at his mouth.

“Alright then, country boy,” he said. “What’s the worst date you’ve ever had?”

Phainon blinked. “What?”

“You heard me. You’re so full of talk—let’s hear it.”

Phainon huffed a laugh, rubbing a hand over his jaw. “Fine. There was this one girl back home, real sweet, but we went to this late-night diner and she, uh… tried to convince me to join her in stealing a bus.”

Mydei’s brow lifted. “A bus.”

“Full-sized,” Phainon confirmed. “Like, transport-children-to-school kind. Her plan was to drive it into a cornfield and ‘see what happens.’”

Mydei laughed—actually laughed, rich and low. Phainon tried not to visibly preen.

“What about you?” Phainon asked, grinning now. “Gotta be a few skeletons in your walk-in closet.”

Mydei swirled his water, thinking. “One guy took me to this pop-up sushi place in an alley. Swore it was ‘an underground gem.’ Turned out it was literally underground—as in, basement of a vape shop. I left halfway through when he started a monologue about how monogamy was a capitalist construct.”

The sound Phainon accidentally made was loud enough to turn a server’s head.

And just like that, the air between them shifted. Not soft, not easy—but something that wasn’t pure antagonism. A truce under dim lighting and linen tablecloths.

Phainon pointed a finger at him, grinning. “See? You’re not as soulless as you look.”

Mydei rolled his eyes. “Don’t get sentimental.”

Phainon’s grin only widened.

By the time their food arrived, the conversation had mellowed into something sharp-edged but weirdly easy. The plates, when they landed, looked more like works of art than anything meant to be eaten.

A server set a gleaming dish in front of Mydei—some immaculate arrangement of the seared lamb mentioned before, delicate foam, and edible flowers that Phainon didn’t even pretend to recognize. The only thing he did clock was Mydei’s faint, satisfied hum as he eyed it.

“Special’s good,” Mydei said absently, already reaching for his utensils.

Phainon’s stomach was halfway to his knees when a second plate arrived— not quite as pretentious but still leagues beyond what his budget could’ve swallowed. He blinked up to see Hyacine standing there, a tiny, knowing smile on her face as she set it down.

“Compliments of the chef,” she said sweetly, eyes flicking toward Mydei, who was too busy dissecting a flower petal to pay attention.

Phainon’s brows lifted.

She leaned in just enough, whispering, “Don’t worry. I made sure you’ll walk out of here solvent.”

Before he could answer, she dropped a dessert plate at the far end of the table—a ridiculous, towering confection of spun sugar and something chocolate and gold-dusted.

Mydei glanced up, genuinely surprised. “I didn’t order this.”

Hyacine gave him a breezy smile. “Chef insisted. Said you’re a favorite.”

Phainon bit the inside of his cheek to keep from smiling. He already knew the man had a sweet tooth the size of a planet. Of course he wasn’t gonna turn it down.

Mydei, trying and failing to look unaffected, gave a casual nod and turned back to his plate.

As soon as his attention dropped, Hyacine subtly slid Phainon’s bill portion out from under the folded leather check holder and tucked it into her apron. No ceremony, no fuss.

Phainon caught it.

Their eyes met.

She mouthed: You owe me.

Phainon pressed a hand to his heart in silent gratitude.

Mydei, oblivious, murmured something appreciative about the citrus notes in his sauce.

Phainon just grabbed his glass and muttered to himself, “Fuckin’ city,” before taking a long drink.

By the time their plates were cleared and dessert reduced to a smear of chocolate and sugar crystals, the stress in Phainon’s shoulders had finally, blessedly, started to unknot. The food had been good—annoyingly so. And somehow the conversation, which had started sharp-edged and defensive, had settled into something easier. Not friendly, exactly, but tolerable.

The bill had come and gone without incident, Hyacine’s discreet miracle work keeping his soul firmly inside his body. And now, walking toward the front with that full, content kind of exhaustion in his bones, Phainon found himself glancing sidelong at Mydei’s hand as it lifted to adjust his cuff.

The bronze signet ring caught the warm lobby light, a simple thing, worn smooth at the edges.

“Nice ring,” Phainon muttered, the words slipping out before he’d really thought about them. “I had a friend back home who gave me something kinda like it, once. Not as clean-looking, though. Hers was this janky little thing—scratched all to hell. I wore it for, like… five years straight.” He gave a quick, sheepish huff of a laugh. “Haven’t thought about it in ages.”

The memory caught him sideways. Cyrene’s crooked grin, the way she used to tease him for getting attached to dumb little things. The nights out under busted streetlights, talking about what they’d do once they got out of their nowhere town. He didn’t realize how much he missed her face in person until just now, saying it out loud.

He shrugged it off. “Yours looks good, though. Suits you.”

For a second, there was no reply.

Phainon didn’t notice the way Mydei’s gaze dropped to his own hand, the ghost of something unreadable in his expression.

A soft, almost distracted “Huh.”

That was it.

The host was already holding the door open for them, the city’s chill night air pressing in. Phainon moved to get the door first on instinct—some stupid remnant of old manners his mama would’ve scolded him for forgetting—but Mydei was quicker.

He held the heavy glass open, the faintest flicker of a smirk tugging at his mouth.

Phainon glared, mostly at himself, and stepped out into the city’s glow. The quiet, half-formed warmth of that conversation still lingered in the air between them, unspoken, unresolved, but not unpleasant.

Neither of them mentioned it.

The night went on.

Outside, the city was damp and cool, the pavement still gleaming from an earlier drizzle. The air smelled like rain-soaked concrete and exhaust, heavy with that electric, just-about-to-storm tang. Phainon stretched his arms over his head, shoulders cracking audibly as he exhaled a long breath.

“Well,” he started, dragging the word out, hands dropping to his pockets, “guess I’ll call it here. Try my luck with whatever’s still open past midnight. Appreciate the… uh—” he gestured vaguely back toward the building, “—accidental five-star experience.”

Mydei, who was half-checking his phone, hummed absently. “You getting a ride?”

Phainon snorted. “What, you think I can’t handle a little rain?”

Mydei slid him a look. A very specific kind of side-eye—equal parts dry amusement and deadpan judgment. “That’s not what I asked.”

Phainon ignored it with the dedication of a man who’d spent his entire life dodging better advice. “I’ll walk.”

“The city’s not that safe,” Mydei said mildly, already pulling his phone back out and thumbing the screen.

“C’mon, I’m not gonna—”

But Mydei wasn’t listening. Or rather, he was, but only enough to swat a hand in Phainon’s direction as if brushing away a persistent bug. “It won’t take long. Stay there. I’ll wait with you till it comes.”

Phainon groaned, head tipping back toward the sky. “You don’t have to—”

“I’m not doing it for you,” Mydei replied, already typing. “I’m doing it because I’m not in the mood to hear about a dumbass getting stabbed two blocks from my dinner spot.”

Phainon grumbled something unintelligible, mostly to save face, but stayed put.

Mydei slipped his phone back into his pocket, posture unaffected as he leaned a shoulder against the wall nearby. Not leaving. Not making it a thing. Just… existing beside him for a while.

Neither of them spoke for a bit. The distant hum of traffic filled the space instead, and it wasn’t awful.

It was kind of nice actually.

Eventually, the car pulled up with a soft sweep of headlights across the damp street, tires hissing against wet pavement. Mydei straightened from where he’d been leaning against the wall, gesturing lazily toward the backseat.

“Your chariot,” he said, voice still that infuriatingly mild register, like none of this had been weird at all.

Phainon moved toward it, one hand on the door handle—and then hesitated. Some stupid part of him, probably the part raised by soft-spoken aunts and his grandmother’s relentless superstitions, tugged at his ribs.

Before his better judgment could stop him, Phainon dug into the front pocket of his beat-up bag and fished out a small, flattened something between the pages of a folded scrap of notebook paper. He unfolded it, a little crumpled from the night but still intact—a small, pressed wildflower, some hardy little thing with faded purple petals and stubborn edges.

“Hey—” Phainon called, and Mydei turned, brows lifting faintly.

Wordlessly, Phainon held it out, not quite meeting his eyes.

Mydei’s gaze flicked down, brow arching higher in surprise as he took it between two fingers, careful not to crush the fragile thing.

“It’s, uh…” Phainon cleared his throat, scratching the back of his neck. “A thing we do back home. For luck. Or, y’know, whatever.”

Mydei glanced between the flower and Phainon. “You just… carry this around?”

“Don’t read into it,” Phainon grumbled, already pulling open the car door.

Mydei didn’t reply right away, just let the silence settle like a warm thing between them. He turned the little paper between his fingers once, then tucked it into his pants pockets with a soft, contemplative sound.

Phainon coughed. “Anyway. See ya.”

And with that, he ducked into the car, slamming the door shut with a finality that belied the stupid, anxious flutter in his chest.

Through the dark tint of the car window, Phainon found his gaze pulling back toward the curb before he could stop himself.

Mydei still stood there, one hand perched on his hip, the other slipping into the pocket of his coat. The streetlight caught on the fine angles of his face, painting him in soft gold and shadow. The faint, amused curve to his lips was the kind of expression you couldn’t tell if it was for you, or for some private joke you weren’t in on—and it made something in Phainon’s throat catch.

Damn it.

He’d known the guy was good-looking. Annoyingly, objectively beautiful in that untouchable way some people carried without trying. But right then —the glow on his skin, hair catching in the night breeze, that small, crooked smile—it hit different. Like something out of an old song you never admitted you liked.

Phainon let himself stare for half a breath too long.

Then Mydei’s gaze flicked up—sharp, catching, dead-on.

They locked eyes.

And to Phainon’s utter horror, Mydei lifted his hand in a lazy, two-fingered wave, something almost teasing in the angle of his wrist. Casual. Like they weren’t two strangers who’d just spent a night toeing the line between biting remarks and weirdly easy company.

It might’ve killed him a little.

Heart stumbling in his chest, Phainon jerked his eyes away, shoving his elbow against the door and fixing his attention firmly on the passing city lights. His ears burned. He absolutely wasn’t blushing. It was the heat from the car vents. Probably.

The driver, an older guy with a thick Brooklyn accent and a mustache that looked like it could win awards, gave a knowing hum.

“That your situationship?” he asked, steering them through the slick streets with one hand. “Reminds me of my Jerry. Back in ’90… met him at a bar, told myself I hated him, wound up married six years later.”

Phainon groaned, scrubbing a hand down his face. “Oh god.”

But he was too polite—too country-raised, too damn Midwestern nice—to interrupt as the guy launched into a rambling, half-laughed story about Jerry and a broken jukebox.

Outside the window, the city kept moving. Neon bleeding into misty dark, shop signs flickering, the distant sound of a train rattling overhead.

And through it all, Phainon kept thinking about the way that pressed flower had looked in Mydei’s hand. Simple. Small. Out of place in a place like that —but held carefully, like it mattered.

He didn’t know what that meant.

Didn’t know if it meant anything.

But the thought followed him all the same as the car carried him deeper into the city night.

Chapter End Notes
