chapters.title: Chapter 3: Bar Fight Etiquette 101
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Phainon covers a shift at Cipher’s, charms old ladies (again), referees an impromptu okra-eating contest, and punches a guy so hard the bar goes silent. Mydei watches, unimpressed but secretly touched. Cipher regrets leaving him in charge for five minutes. A good time was had by all.

Chapter Notes

Heyy, finally done with chapter 3😍 Speaking of, sorry guys there might be some delayed chapters because I’m trying to finish a few more fanfics before Myphai week, so until that I’m probably gonna go incognito for a bit save for a detective au ff (Yeah I caved and decided to do that) and another Flame Reaver/Phainon/Mydei one💔

Phainon thought he knew the kind of bar he was walking into.

The sort of joint with a flickering neon sign advertising beer no one drank on purpose, duct-taped stools, and a jukebox older than God that only played sad country ballads. The kind of place Hyacine usually called in favors for—somewhere you kept your coat in the car and your expectations even lower.

But this wasn’t that.

Warm, amber light spilled from inside, catching on exposed brick walls and polished oak counters worn smooth by years of elbows and spilled drinks. Bottles lined the shelves behind the bar, their glass catching the glow like stained glass in a Sunday chapel. The air carried a mix of wood polish, orange peel, and fryer oil in a way that wasn’t unpleasant—like a family gathering that overstayed its welcome.

Framed photographs of dusty back roads hung crooked on the walls, nestled between vintage tins and old neon beer signs, one of them advertising a Peoria uncle’s ill-fated brewing venture. Over the bar, a chalkboard menu listed cocktails with names like Mamaw’s Peach Cobbler Old Fashioned and Hot Buttered Rum Punch. Beneath that, a line of snack specials written in hurried chalk: Collard Green Bites, Fried Pickle Spears, Buttermilk Pie.

It wasn’t home, not exactly.

But it was close enough to fool him for a minute.

He let his gaze drift, catching brass plaques bolted to the walls: Don’t let your mouth write a check your ass can’t cash. Another read: If you don’t want to be gossiped about, don’t sit in that corner booth.

A couple of regulars sat at the far end of the bar, nursing drinks and swapping stories about somebody’s disastrous second wedding. The low hum of conversation blended with the clink of glass and the soft shuffle of chairs.

Behind the bar, Cipher was holding court, laughing at something a stocky old man in a Cubs cap had said. She moved like she owned the place— which, to be fair, she did. Sleeves rolled, a towel slung over one shoulder, hair pulled back in a loose knot. There was an ease to her, the kind of confidence that came from years of knowing every face in the room and which stories were worth hearing twice.

It wasn’t until her gaze slid toward the door that she spotted him.

Her grin came quick and sharp.

“Well, look at you.”

Phainon arched a brow, the corner of his mouth tugging up as he crossed the room.

“Thought you’d be too big city now to sling drinks,” Cipher teased, her Southern drawl pulling at the words like warm taffy.

He snorted. “You know damn well I still got that bartending license. It was either that or learn to butcher hogs for the family BBQ.”

Cipher let out a low, easy laugh. “Still got it, huh?”

“Got my bartender’s license before my driver’s,” he shot back, grinning.

They shared a look—one of those small, knowing things that only folks from the same nowhere could get away with—before Cipher reached under the bar and tossed him a folded work shirt.

“Change’s in the back,” she said, jerking her chin toward a hallway near the kitchen. “Beer taps haven’t changed. Tabs run through the register now, but don’t let the old-timers give you grief about cash.”

She turned to grab a bottle off the shelf, then paused, as if something just crossed her mind.

“Oh—someone’s supposed to drop by in about an hour. Got business with me. If they show up before I’m out here, tell ’em to hang tight.”

Phainon gave a lazy two-fingered salute. “Yes, ma’am.”

Cipher smirked, then turned back to her conversation without missing a beat.

The back room was a narrow little thing—not much more than a hallway with a coat rack, a busted record player leaning against the wall, and a shelf stacked with extra menus and backup liquor. The air was thick with the scent of fryer oil and old whiskey, with the floor creaking.

Phainon leaned back against the wall, rubbing a hand down his face.

He wasn’t supposed to be here tonight.

Hell, two days ago he’d been halfway settled into the kind of quiet evening that involved takeout and a bad crime doc when his phone lit up with Hyacine’s name. She’d opened with “Hey, you remember that favor you owe me?” and it’d been downhill from there.

Apparently, Cipher needed an extra set of hands. One of her bartenders called out last minute, and Hyacine, ever the meditator, cashed in that debt.

He’d been expecting a hole-in-the-wall in some back alley on the South Side. A place where Cipher would’ve been running a side hustle, maybe pickpocketing wallets off tourists too drunk to notice. Not this.

He shook his head, a crooked smile tugging at the corner of his mouth.

In Hyacine’s exact words: “Don’t underestimate her, Phainon. Girl’s versatile.”

And apparently, she wasn’t wrong.

Phainon blew out a slow breath, feeling the weight of it leave his chest as he started to dress. The kind of heaviness that came from showing up to things you hadn’t planned for but knowing you’d do it anyway. That old, stubborn sense of duty his grandma always said would get him killed one day.

He glanced down at his hand, flexed it once, then grabbed a rag off the shelf to wipe the dust off his palms. No sense hiding back here all night. He hadn’t come this far to sulk by the mop buckets.

Time to earn his keep.

Pushing off the wall, Phainon rolled his shoulders and stepped back through the door, the sounds of the bar folding around him like a well-worn jacket.

A few hours later, the place had settled into a kind of easy hum.

Cipher had taken off about an hour back, leaving Phainon to run the bar solo. A couple of the regulars had clocked him as new, but so long as their drinks stayed full and poured right, no one much cared. The crowd was a comfortable mix—neighborhood folks easing into the tail end of their workday, a pair of college kids nursing a single whiskey between them, an older couple slow-dancing to a Merle Haggard song bleeding out from the jukebox in the corner.

Phainon moved through it all like he’d been here for years.

It wasn’t hard.

He still remembered how it went—the rhythm of a bar, the shorthand language of bottle clinks and raised brows. How to pace the pour when a story got good, how to cut someone off without making a scene, how to listen without really needing to answer.

He tossed a bar towel over his shoulder, wiped down the counter, and slid a refill in front of a stout woman in a Bears hoodie who’d been holding court at the far end all night.

“You keep this up,” she said, giving him an appraising look, “and I’m gonna set you up with my niece. Girl needs a man with marriage hands.”

Phainon huffed a laugh. “Marriage hands, huh?”

“Yeah,” she grinned, jabbing a finger at him. “You know—strong, steady, good for fixing screen doors and carrying in the groceries. Not those flimsy city-boy hands that drop a damn casserole dish soon as it comes outta the oven.”

“Well, hell,” Phainon said, smiling as he topped off her glass. “Guess I better start working on my casserole technique.”

A few of the other patrons chuckled, the easy kind of bar laughter that didn’t ask too much of anyone. The kind born from shared space, good drinks, and just enough distance from whatever waited outside.

“Just sayin’,” the woman added with a wink, raising her glass to him. “Wouldn’t be the worst mistake she ever made.”

Phainon leaned an elbow on the bar, smirking. “I’ll take that as high praise.”

The woman laughed again, turning back to her conversation, and Phainon moved down the counter to grab a fresh stack of coasters. The night was easy now—steady enough to stay busy, quiet enough not to feel like a chore.

He liked it.

More than he figured he would.

And for a few long, untroubled minutes, it was just him, the bar, and the warm buzz of voices carrying over from table to table.

Which was, of course, exactly when the door swung open and trouble walked in.

Phainon wiped down the bar one more time out of habit, the clock overhead ticking steadily toward ten. He threw a glance at it, brow ticking up.

Right. Cipher’s business person.

He craned his neck, looking for Cipher—no sign of her. Probably in the back, taking inventory or cussing out a busted ice machine.

With a quiet sigh, he rounded the bar, weaving past a table of rowdy regulars who were deep into arguing about which of them could still outrun a cop at their age.

“Hey, barkeep!” one of them called. “Tell this fool I got more miles in these legs than he ever did.”

Phainon grinned without breaking stride. “Buddy, I’ve seen fresher knees on a seventy-year-old bowling league. But you’re all right.”

Laughter followed him as he made his way toward the door.

A figure had just stepped in, silhouetted against the amber glow from the streetlamps outside. The bell over the door gave a soft clang.

Phainon moved into place, throwing on his easy charm without thinking. “Evenin’. Welcome to Cipher’s. What can I—”

He cut off mid-sentence.

His eyes finally settled on the person in front of him.

Tall. Sharp-cut frame. Well dressed. And those damn eyes again—gold, steady, and far too familiar.

Phainon’s stomach did a little annoyed flip.

“…You’ve gotta be kidding me,” he muttered, rubbing a hand down his face.

Mydei raised a brow, equally unamused. “You work here now?”

“No—I mean, yes—what the hell are you even doing here?” Phainon shot back, voice pitching up as the reality of it sank in. He pinched the bridge of his nose, already feeling a headache spark behind his eyes. “You don’t even drink.”

“I have business with the owner,” Mydei replied evenly, glancing past him toward the back.

That snagged Phainon for a second. “You know Cipher?”

“I’m surprised you know her,” Mydei countered.

A sharp, narrow silence stretched between them.

Phainon huffed a dry laugh, shaking his head. “God, Chicago’s small.”

Neither one moved.

Then, with a long-suffering sigh, Phainon gestured toward the bar. “Whatever. Sit down. She’s not out yet.”

Mydei gave him a look—something halfway between reluctant tolerance and resigned amusement—before crossing the room and dropping onto the barstool.

Phainon circled back behind the counter, grabbing a clean glass a little harder than necessary. The faint clink of it against the polished oak made a couple of nearby heads glance up, then shrug.

The world around them kept on in its lazy, amber-lit rhythm. A blues track hummed low from the phonograph. The old casserole lady down the bar was working through another whiskey, regaling anyone within earshot about her glory days in roller derby. Two regulars bickered over who still had better hair.

Phainon kept his eyes firmly on the glass, tossing a rag over his shoulder and muttering, “Could’ve gone my whole damn life without seeing your smug face again.”

Mydei didn’t rise to it. Just let out a quiet exhale and leaned his forearms on the counter.

Phainon glanced up to fire off another jab—and that’s when he caught it.

The faint slump to Mydei’s posture. The weary drag of his hand down his face. Eyes not sharp and hunting for an opening like usual, but duller, weighed down.

Well, damn.

Phainon scowled at himself, annoyed for noticing. Annoyed for caring. He tried to shake it off, reached for a bottle to polish for the sake of doing something with his hands.

He didn’t last thirty seconds.

“…Fine,” Phainon grumbled, slumping an elbow on the bar and squinting at him. “What do you even want?”

Mydei blinked, as if he hadn’t expected the offer. “Water.”

Phainon let out a dry, unimpressed snort. “Christ, you’re worse than a Baptist mom on poker night.”

He turned, grabbed a glass, then paused—something gnawing at the edge of him. He sighed.

“You know what? Screw it.” He leaned in a little, voice dropping just enough to sound like a confession he was already regretting. “I’ll make you something off-menu. What’ll it be?”

Mydei hesitated. A tiny crease formed between his brows. “Wait… seriously?”

“Yeah, I’m feeling reckless,” Phainon muttered. “Don’t let it go to your head.”

“I don’t wanna be a hassle.”

“Buddy, this whole interaction’s already a hassle. Might as well get a drink outta it.”

A longer pause this time. Then, reluctantly:

“…Pomegranate juice.”

Phainon smirked, already reaching for the juice bottle. “Yeah. You strike me as the broody antioxidant type.”

He poured it, expecting that to be the end of it—but then Mydei cleared his throat.

“With milk.”

Phainon blinked. Actually stopped mid-pour.

“…Come again?”

Mydei, suddenly defensive, cheeks just a shade redder than usual. “I like the color.”

Phainon stared a second longer—then laughed, a low, surprised thing that cracked through the crust of his snark. “Jesus. You’re a cartoon character.”

He shook his head, grabbing the milk carton. “Coming right up, sweetheart.”

The second the words left his mouth, a sharp whistle cut through the din of the bar.

“Well, damn,” the casserole lady drawled from down the counter, elbowing her friend. “Now we know why he’s not marrying my niece, Bonnie.”

“Sugar,” Bonnie snorted, grinning, “I’d trade him a whole casserole for that smile.”

Phainon coughed into his fist, the tips of his ears warming. Mydei looked between them, confused. “What…?”

“Don’t worry about it,” Phainon muttered, giving the glass a final swirl before sliding it across the bar.

He watched Mydei eye the drink like it might bite him.

“Try it, drama queen,” Phainon teased, though it came out softer than before.

And maybe it was the lighting, or the fact that Mydei’s lashes were stupidly long for a guy, but for a second Phainon caught himself thinking: damn, he’s kinda cute when he’s not being an insufferable asshole.

He shoved the thought aside with a mental curse and grabbed a new towel.

“Drink your weird-ass milk juice,” he grumbled. “I got better things to do than babysit you.”

But even as he turned away, his gaze flicked back once, just to see if Mydei would actually drink it.

He did.

Not even a flinch. Took a sip like it was the most normal thing in the world. And for reasons Phainon didn’t particularly care to examine, that loosened something sharp in his chest.

He grabbed a rag, wiping down a section of the counter that didn’t need it, when a familiar gravelly voice called out down the bar.

“Well, well, look at lover boy over there.”

Phainon shot a glare toward the far corner where two of the bar’s usual fixtures, Nikos and Theo, sat nursing whiskey and soda. Both well past retirement, both hell-bent on giving him grief since he clocked in.

“Mind your business, old man,” Phainon fired back, not bothering to hide the smirk tugging at his mouth.

Theo snorted, leaning in with a conspiratorial stage-whisper to Nikos. “Kid’s got it bad.”

“Poor thing,” Nikos wheezed, shaking his head like a disappointed uncle. “Boy needs hobbies.”

“I have hobbies,” Phainon shot back, grabbing a handful of coasters to stack just for something to do.

“Yeah, chasing off coyotes and breaking city boys’ hearts apparently,” Nikos chuckled, clinking his glass against Theo’s.

Phainon rolled his eyes so hard it hurt. “God, you two are a menace.”

“Go on,” Theo waved a hand, grinning. “We’ll hold down the fort.”

“Like hell you will,” Phainon muttered under his breath, but his feet were already carrying him toward the end of the bar where Mydei sat, half-slouched on the stool, nursing that bizarre drink.

He made a show of casually dropping a coaster in front of him, leaning an elbow on the bar like he hadn’t just been publicly heckled by geriatrics.

“So,” Phainon started, aiming for offhand and not quite landing it. “What’re your hobbies?”

Mydei raised a brow, a slow blink like he couldn’t believe that was the line Phainon went with.

Phainon scowled. “Relax. Not tryna pick you up, princess. Just—” he waved a vague hand, “conversation. It’s a bar. People do that here.”

A beat passed. The corners of Mydei’s mouth twitched like he might smile, but he was too tired to commit to it.

“You first,” Mydei said.

Phainon perked up a little, grateful for the redirect. “Alright. Uh… fishing, when I can find a decent lake. Building stuff sometimes—tables, cabinets, fixed my grandma’s porch swing last fall. I’m a menace at a grill, too. Those hobbies.”

He shrugged, smiling.

“Call it a rural upbringing clause.”

Mydei snorted softly, looking back at his drink. “Figures.”

He let the silence sit for a moment, then quietly offered, “Reading. Sketching. Hiking if I can get out of the city.”

Phainon hummed, a half-smile curling his mouth. “Didn’t peg you for the tree-hugging type.”

Mydei’s gaze flicked up, a spark of amusement there now. “Also boxing.”

Phainon nearly dropped the rag he’d been fiddling with. He barked out a laugh, leaning his weight against the bar. “Seriously?”

“Good for stress,” Mydei deadpanned, lips quirking at the edges.

Phainon grinned, that crooked thing that made the older ladies coo at him and annoyed every one of his cousins back home. “Yeah, remind me to stay on your good side.”

“You’re not there yet,” Mydei shot back, but it lacked heat. If anything, the air between them felt less tense now.

Phainon tapped a knuckle against the counter. “Noted.”

A beat. Mydei took another sip of his ridiculous drink.

“Y’know,” Phainon said, dropping his voice just a notch, “for a guy who’s allegedly a massive pain in my ass, you’re not bad company tonight.”

Mydei smirked, this time letting it show. “It’s the milk.”

Phainon laughed, leaning back to glance toward Nikos and Theo, who were pretending not to watch but doing a piss-poor job of it. He flipped them off without turning his head.

Then back to Mydei, eyes catching on gold for a second too long before he cleared his throat.

“You’re exhausting,” Phainon muttered.

“Likewise,” Mydei murmured.

And neither of them moved.

Phainon tapped his knuckles against the counter again, glancing at Mydei like he was sizing him up for a second.

“Come to think of it,” he started, head cocking to the side, “what do you even do for work? I mean—technically this is my job for the night, tragic as it is. You know mine. What about you?”

Mydei looked like he might actually answer, one hand turning his glass absently on the bar.

But before he could open his mouth, a sharp clatter sounded from across the room—the telltale scrape of a stool toppling over, a voice rising a little too loud, too slurred.

Phainon sighed, already pushing off the bar. “Sorry. Looks like I gotta go cut someone off before Theo starts swinging a cane at ‘em.”

He pointed a finger at Mydei as he backed away. “Hold that thought, angel.”

And then he was gone, moving through the hum of the bar with that easy confidence again—the regulars parting just enough for him to slip through, already calling out, “Alright, who’s being a dumbass?”

Leaving Mydei behind, alone with his strange drink and whatever answer he’d been about to give.

The bar had settled into that golden stretch of night—the kind where conversation blurred into laughter, glasses clinked steady, and even the neon signs seemed to glow a little warmer.

At one battered corner table, two regulars were deep in a challenge. One, stocky with a mop of dark curls, was waving a pickled okra spear like a weapon. The other, lean and sharp-faced, lounged in his seat with the smugness of a man convinced he’d already won.

“I’m tellin’ you, Petros,” the curly-haired one slurred, “five, no problem. I won’t even blink.”

Petros scoffed, raising his glass. “Manos, you made a face last week when the souvlaki was too peppery.”

A ripple of laughter circled the table. Someone clapped Manos on the shoulder, nearly knocking him over.

“All right, all right,” Phainon called from behind the bar, grabbing the mason jar of Cipher’s infamous pickled okra. “Five apiece, no water, no grimaces, and loser picks up a round for these freeloaders.”

The bar whooped in approval.

“Hope your stomach’s stronger than your hairline,” someone teased, earning a roar of laughter.

Phainon chuckled. “Easy, Nico. One more shot and you’ll be singing love songs to the fruit machine again.”

The jar thunked onto the table. “On my count, lads.”

The first okra went down easy, though Petros twitched just enough for someone to shout, “That’s a face!”

“Wasn’t,” he grunted, reaching for another.

Phainon leaned against the bar, watching them, the pulse of the room threading through him.

And then he let his gaze drift back to the counter.

There was Mydei.

Same spot, elbow propped on the worn oak, eyes half-lidded as he watched the commotion. The faintest trace of a smile ghosted his lips. Not a full one, not the one Phainon was used to. This one was entertained, less guarded.

It made Phainon want to stroll over and say something dumb, maybe needle him about being too chicken to join in, see if he could coax that smile out just a little more.

He was halfway through setting down a glass when a flicker of movement caught his eye.

A young man had slipped up beside Mydei. Could’ve passed for any other night’s stray patron—late twenties, dark hair mussed like it hadn’t seen a comb all week, jacket slung carelessly over his shoulder. But there was something off in the angle of his lean, the too-familiar ease with which he planted a hand on the counter.

Phainon’s pulse tapped a little faster.

It wasn’t anything obvious. No raised voices or threats.

But he saw the way Mydei’s posture stiffened, how his fingers curled slightly against the wood. How his eyes, a breath quicker than before, flicked toward the door.

A low hum settled in Phainon’s chest.

The okra contest carried on behind him—Manos gagging theatrically on his third spear as the crowd erupted—but the sound dulled, distant.

Phainon didn’t move yet, he just watched

Trouble had a look, and it rarely announced itself. It slid in sideways, polite and quiet, like a wolf trying on a lamb’s grin.

And something about this one smelled like teeth.

He clocked the exchange without meaning to. The guy was too familiar for someone who hadn’t been invited. He said something, lost under the sound of the bar, but the tone carried enough to make Phainon’s gut tighten.

Mydei didn’t so much as blink. He tilted his head slightly, expression unreadable but edged sharp, like a warning dressed up as disinterest. Whatever he said back was cold and clipped, but it landed. You didn’t need to hear the words to feel the way the air shifted around them.

The other man chuckled, a dry, humorless sound, like someone trying to needle a reaction.

Phainon’s fingers twitched against the bar. He started to move—half a step, instinct tugging at him—then stopped himself.

He knew Mydei.

Knew the man would probably be more pissed if he jumped in like some well-meaning fool. Mydei wasn’t one to need saving, and he sure as hell didn’t like an audience.

Still, it sat wrong.

Across the room, the pickled okra contest reached its inevitable conclusion. One of them threw his hands up in triumph while the other gagged dramatically into a napkin. The crowd broke into cheers and jeers, and someone called for another round like it was the Fourth of July.

Phainon forced a smile and turned to pour, but his eyes flicked back toward the bar every other heartbeat. Not interfering. Just… keeping an eye on things.

It started small.

A hand on Mydei’s shoulder. Phainon caught it mid-pour, brow ticking up. Mydei didn’t flinch, but his jaw tightened—a warning if you knew how to see it.

The guy leaned in, saying something else. Phainon couldn’t catch the words, but he didn’t need to. The tone was easy to recognize.

Near the end of the bar, one of the old regulars gave a short snort, not bothering to turn his head. “That one’s askin’ for it.”

Phainon set the bottle down, wiping his hands on a rag. For a second, he tried to talk himself out of it. Mydei wasn’t the type to take charity, and from the look of it, he wasn’t even rattled. If anything, he looked annoyed.

Their eyes met, just a quick glance—I had it handled—and Phainon answered it by moving anyway.

He came around the bar, voice sharp and easy. “Hey. You bothering my customer?”

The guy glanced over his shoulder, smirking like he thought he was funny. “Didn’t know you hired bodyguards.”

Phainon kept walking, stopping just beside them, his grin all teeth. “Didn’t know you were this desperate for company.”

The guy puffed up, straightening like he meant to start something. Mydei didn’t say a word, leaning back slightly with a look that said this isn’t worth my time.

Phainon met Mydei’s eyes again—this time a flat don’t intervene—and ignored it.

“You’re done,” Phainon said, calm as anything. “Walk.”

The bar had quieted just a notch, enough to feel the tension gathering.

The guy’s laugh came rough, sharp around the edges, like a nail dragged down glass. He started to step past, but couldn’t help himself—leaned in, breath close enough that Mydei tilted his head back a fraction, the barest sign of distance.

And then the words, pitched low, just for him.

“Bet you look a lot less mean when someone’s got their hands on you.”

A smirk, all teeth and cheap bravado.

The room didn’t catch it. No one at the tables noticed. But Phainon did.

He wasn’t even sure what told him first—maybe the faint twitch in Mydei’s jaw, or the way his fingers stayed wrapped around his glass, a little too tight, like the grip alone was keeping him from saying something sharp enough to cut. His expression didn’t crack, didn’t so much as twitch. But there was something cold and ancient in the way his gaze slid past the man, like he wasn’t worth even the flicker of acknowledgement.

Bigger man. Always had been.

But Phainon could feel it. The air stretched thin.

He spoke, voice level, the smile on his face the same sharp-edged thing he gave drunk creeps he was about to throw out.

“You need to leave.”

The guy snorted, playing the aggrieved innocent. Hands up, palms out. “Easy, bartender. Just saying hey.”

Phainon didn’t blink.

The man turned, heading for the door—but made sure to clip Mydei’s shoulder as he passed. Deliberate. Petty. Meant to be small enough to excuse, but sharp enough to sting.

And for the first time all night, Mydei’s mask faltered.

Not a flinch. Just a stiffening of his shoulders, a muscle jumping in his jaw. A glint of something ugly in those eyes.

Phainon didn’t need a second invitation.

The second Mydei’s shoulder tensed, Phainon moved.

Didn’t think.

His body just went—vaulting the bar like his grandmother had called his full damn name from the church steps and he knew better than to keep her waiting.

The room barely had time to register it.

The drunk turned, smug still curling his lip, starting to say something —“What, you gonna—”

Crack.

One clean, farm-raised haymaker. The kind born from hauling livestock gates and splitting cordwood.

Phainon’s fist collided with the man’s jaw so hard the sound snapped through the bar like a starter’s pistol. A sharp, vicious noise that silenced every voice, every clink of glass. Even the radio felt quieter.

The guy staggered back a step, surprise blooming across his face—for a single, stupid second—before his legs went out and he hit the floor like a sack of wet feed.

Dead weight. Out cold.

The silence after stretched long.

No one moved. No one breathed.

Not the old men in the corner, not the casserole ladiy halfway through a gossip, not the two okra competitors mid-chew.

And then—a voice, rough and pleased from the back.

“’Bout damn time.”

It broke the spell. A few snorts of laughter, muttered agreements. Nobody moved to help the prick on the floor.

Phainon flexed his hand, blood already welling up in split knuckles, and finally exhaled.

Only then did he look to Mydei.

Still at the bar. Glass in hand. Those sharp golden eyes wide—not scared, never that, just… caught off-guard. Like the last person in the room who expected that out of him.

For once, Mydei had nothing to say.

Phainon huffed a humorless snort, shaking out his hand.

“Should’ve done it two minutes ago,” he muttered, already turning toward the back to fetch ice.

Mydei shifted, like he might reach out—maybe to stop him, maybe to say something—but it was right then that Cipher burst through the back door with her usual flair.

“I’m back~ Hope you didn’t miss me too—”

She caught sight of Mydei first, halfway into a grin, then her eyes dropped to the crumpled body on the floor.

“Holy shit.”

Everyone stayed quiet, watching her.

Phainon, already behind the counter again, wrapping a clean towel around his knuckles, didn’t even glance up. “Handled it.”

Cipher’s gaze bounced from the knocked-out guy to Phainon, to Mydei, then back again. Her brow twitched.

Before she could ask, one of the men in the corner grunted, “Fool was gettin’ too handsy. Had it comin’.”

Another chimed in, “Guy was askin’ for it.”

Cipher let out a long, bone-deep sigh, scrubbing a hand over her face. “Knew I shouldn’t’ve let you near whiskey drinkers.”

Phainon shrugged, still tying off the towel around his split knuckles.

“You know what,” she muttered, waving it off. “Fine. I’ll deal with the rest of your shift. Go get that cleaned up before you bleed on my floor.”

She jerked her chin at the bouncer loitering by the jukebox. “Get this idiot outta here.”

The guy grunted and moved toward the dead weight on the ground.

A few murmurs floated up around the room. A lady whispered, “Didn’t think that one had it in him.”

Another one snorted. “Guess the quiet ones’ll do you in every time.”

As Phainon headed for the back, passing by a cluster of curious stares, he muttered just loud enough to be heard, “Surprise.”

The door swung shut behind him.

The muffled hum of the bar dropped away, replaced by the quiet drip of a leaky faucet and the sharp, metallic tang of blood on his knuckles.

He twisted the tap, cold water gushing out with a groan. The sting hit as soon as his skin touched it, but he let it wash over him, streaks of red swirling down the drain. He watched it go, jaw tight.

Did he regret it? Not one bit.

Causing Cipher a headache, though—yeah, that part gnawed at him. She ran a tight ship, and he wasn’t the type to leave a mess for someone else to clean up. He’d make it up to her. Another shift favor, a case of that weird cherry brandy she liked, hell, fixing that janky stool by the window she kept swearing she’d get to.

He flexed his hand under the water, watching blood mix with bruising already rising under the skin. A familiar ache. One he hadn’t felt in a while.

It pulled a memory up with it—Cyrene, back when they were kids. She used to get it bad from some little assholes in their neighborhood. Mean for no reason, the way kids could be. Phainon never even thought about it. He just started walking her everywhere, posted up by her side like a second shadow. The first time someone got brave and tried something with him around, he broke a kid’s nose before he knew he was moving.

That had been the end of that.

He reached for the medkit, the latch sticking like always. Popped it open with a thumb and grabbed a wad of gauze. The antiseptic stung like hell, but whatever. He’d taken worse.

This wasn’t the same though. Mydei wasn’t some kid who needed watching. Hell, if Phainon hadn’t stepped in, he half-wondered if Mydei would’ve handled it himself, maybe worse.

And yet, the look—that flicker, barely there—had hit something in him. Something ugly. He didn’t like seeing it. Not on Mydei. Not on anyone.

Phainon worked the gauze around his knuckles, flexed his fingers, winced. Should’ve hit the bastard harder.

He shut the kit, leaning against the counter for a second. The ache in his hand, the leftover pulse of adrenaline in his veins—it all left him restless.

But yeah—he’d square things with Cipher later.

For now, he needed air.

The back door groaned as Phainon shoved it open with his shoulder, the heavy night air rushing to meet him. Cool, a little damp, carrying the distant hum of traffic and the faint sour tang of garbage from the next alley over. But it was better than inside—quieter.

He let the door swing shut behind him with a dull thud and leaned his weight against the brick wall, tipping his head back to look at the sky. City stars—faint, blurred out by light pollution, but there if you knew where to look. He filled his lungs, the tension slowly uncoiling from his shoulders. His hand throbbed under the makeshift wrap, a dull, steady reminder of his temper.

A muscle jumped in his jaw.

He let out a breath.

The silence didn’t last long.

Footsteps. Light, even ones, shoes scuffing faintly against the cracked concrete. Phainon didn’t open his eyes, figured it was Cipher, maybe sending one of the bouncers to scold him or check he wasn’t bleeding out.

But then the scent hit him—clean, sharp, a little expensive. Sandalwood and something crisp, like bergamot.

He cracked one eye open.

Beige.

Of course.

Mydei stepped into the alley like he belonged there, hands in his pocket, eyes catching on Phainon with that same unreadable calm he wore like armor.

Phainon let his head thunk lightly against the brick behind him.

“Well,” he muttered, “figured you’d be halfway home by now.”

Mydei leaned against the opposite wall, a lazy sort of posture that still felt deliberate. “Didn’t feel like it.”

Phainon huffed a breath, something between a laugh and a sigh. “You alright?”

Mydei’s brow ticked up, like the question surprised him. “You should be asking yourself that.”

Phainon shrugged, glancing down at his hand, flexing stiff fingers against the bloodied towel. “I’ve been through worse.”

A beat passed. Mydei didn’t leave. Didn’t crack a joke or throw an insult. Just stood there, watching him like he was trying to puzzle out how someone so aggravating could also be so goddamn reckless.

“You didn’t have to do that,” Mydei said, careful.

Phainon gave a crooked smile. “Yeah, I know. I wanted to.”

Mydei sighed, rubbing a hand over his face. “You’re an idiot.”

“Getting that a lot tonight.”

“You could’ve waited. Cipher’s place is neutral. Deal with it outside the line.”

Phainon blinked, then squinted at him. “Wait… that’s what you were gonna —?”

“Handle it quietly with no witnesses, no trouble for Cipher.” Mydei’s tone was flat, but there was the faintest twitch of something amused in his expression. “Now you went and made it a thing.”

“Oh,” Phainon muttered, sheepish. “Guess I stepped on your moment, huh?”

Mydei didn’t answer. Just crossed the space between them in a few steps, stopping close enough to grab Phainon’s wrist and pry the towel loose. His fingers were cool, careful in a way that caught Phainon off guard.

“Dumbass,” Mydei muttered, inspecting the raw knuckles. “Messy punch. Bet your hand hurts worse than his face.”

“Hey, worked, didn’t it?”

Mydei rolled his eyes but didn’t let go. “Next time, keep your thumb outside your fist.”

Phainon smirked, leaning a little into the contact without thinking. “Look at you, giving me lessons now.”

“Somebody has to.”

Mydei let go of his hand, stepping back like nothing’d happened. The air felt heavier for it.

“Get that cleaned properly,” Mydei murmured, already tucking his hands back into his pockets.

“Yeah, yeah,” Phainon grumbled, managing a lopsided grin. “Next time, maybe carry some pepper spray on you.”

Mydei snorted, eyes catching on his like he wanted to say something else— didn’t. The two of them lingered there a beat longer than necessary, the distance between them thinning in the quiet, something unspoken but not uncomfortable hanging in the air.

Then—

“Oi, lover boy,” Cipher’s voice cracked sharp from the doorway. “If you’re done brooding in my alley, get your ass back inside.”

Phainon groaned, letting his head thump back against the wall. “Gods, kill me.”

Mydei chuckled under his breath, a rare, quiet thing, and with that, the moment scattered like dust.

They headed back in, no words needed.

And that was that.
