Phainon stepped off the crowded bus and into a neighborhood that made his skin itch.

Everything here gleamed. The streets were spotless, the storefront windows polished to a shine so sharp it caught the last scraps of sunlight like cut glass. Even the trees looked like they’d been handpicked, shipped in, and arranged just so—branches manicured within an inch of their lives, leaves the same shade of green. He could practically hear the maintenance budget bleeding out for them.

The borrowed blazer hung heavy on his shoulders. Caelus was shorter by a couple inches, but he preferred oversized, and so the sleeves kept sliding down to swallow half his hands. Phainon tugged at the lapels and muttered, mostly to himself.

“Alright. Let’s get this over with.”

Ahead, the building rose up like something out of an architectural digest spread—all glass, pale stone, and sharp, modernist edges. Warm light spilled out through tall windows, amber and inviting, while the low pulse of music drifted past the automatic doors. It barely carried over the steady hiss of traffic and the occasional slap of a car door closing.

Valets in tailored uniforms moved like clockwork along the curb, ushering guests into black sedans, murmuring into earpieces, vanishing through side entrances. Somewhere inside, laughter broke through the hum of conversation, a bright splash of sound quickly swallowed by the night.

Phainon stayed where he was for a beat longer than he should have. Hands in his pockets, shoulders hunched against the lake breeze that always came creeping up in the evenings, no matter how hot the day had been. The sun had already started to dip, but in this part of the city, it didn’t matter. The streets never really went dark. Every window reflected the next, coins flashing under streetlights, the skyline turning to a mosaic of artificial gold.

He exhaled through his nose.

God, I hate these things.

He wasn’t supposed to be here. Not really. The invitation—if you could call it that—had been for department heads, project leads, and “key integration personnel.” A mixer. A networking event. A thin excuse to drink wine, feign goodwill, and let Castrum Kremnos plant their flag before the merger officially landed. A show of force dressed up as team-building.

And Phainon? He worked spreadsheets. That was it. His face wasn’t on any company-wide memo. No one sent him priority emails or looped him into project calls. He was a warm body in a cubicle, one desk in a sea of them.

But the email had been clear: attendance strongly encouraged. And Phainon… well. He needed this job. Desperately. Cyrene’s tuition wasn’t going to pay itself, and there weren’t a lot of openings back in Missouri for a kid who could juggle financial reports faster than most people could tie their shoes.

So here he was. In a neighborhood his bank account resented, wearing a jacket that didn’t fit, after twelve hours of back-to-back outages, three passive-aggressive Procurement tickets, and one HR training video that somehow managed to make the word synergy sound obscene.

Another breath, heavier this time.

It was going to be a long night.

A car door thunked shut nearby, crisp in the evening air. A man in a suit— phone pressed to his ear—brushed past without so much as a glance, deep in conversation, laughing at something Phainon didn’t catch.

Everyone here had a place to be. A person to meet. A conversation to start. None of it involved the guy in the too-big blazer loitering at the curb.

He rolled his shoulders. Adjusted the jacket again. His feet ached. He smelled like the bus. But there was whiskey inside, and he could fake a smile for a couple hours.

Time to earn that tuition.

Phainon made himself move, crossing the pavement toward the doors.

Just inside the doors, a check-in podium stood like a customs station for the terminally overdressed. A young woman in a fitted black suit manned it, tablet in hand, her expression the kind of professionally polite that suggested she, too, was counting the hours until this was over.

Her eyes lifted as Phainon approached, flicking over the too-large blazer, the creased collar of his shirt, and the faint sheen of sweat still clinging to his skin from the bus ride. If she had an opinion about any of it, she kept it to herself. Maybe one eyebrow ticked upward, just a fraction, but the polite smile stayed in place.

“Name and department?” she asked, already tapping at the screen.

Phainon tugged at the front of his jacket, though it didn’t help. His voice came out low, rough around the edges.

“Phainon. Okhema Tech.”

Her fingers moved quickly, scrolling through the list. She repeated his name under her breath, a faint note of skepticism in it, like she wasn’t sure she’d heard it right. Then, after a beat, she found it. A small nod.

“You’re all set. Enjoy your evening.”

He didn’t bother with a reply. Just gave a tired, half-hearted smile and kept moving.

The space beyond the checkpoint opened up like the lobby of some luxury hotel, cavernous and overdesigned, every surface engineered to impress. Marble floors gleamed under the steady glow of amber lighting. Classical music drifted through the air, all strings and soft percussion—the kind of piece you wouldn’t be able to name, but would instantly recognize as old. It sounded like movies about estate disputes and legal battles.

Catering staff in uniforms wove through the room, balancing trays of delicate, abstract hors d’oeuvres that looked like they’d been assembled with tweezers. No one actually seemed to be eating them. They were props. Texture for the room.

It wasn’t hard to tell the Okhema staff from the Kremnos suits. Okhema people gathered along the perimeter, clustered near exits, walls, and conveniently placed potted plants. You could spot them by the way their eyes kept scanning the room, looking for allies, escape routes, or reasons to pretend they were checking a message. Most of them had the uneasy, braced-for-impact posture of people uncertain whether they were at a celebration or a culling.

The Kremnos crowd, on the other hand, moved like apex predators. Tailored suits, practiced smiles, and the kind of laughter that always landed half a decibel too loud. Groups shifted through the room in practiced orbits, speaking the language of ownership without having to say it out loud.

Phainon sighed quietly, stepping further in. He recognized a handful of faces—a few people from his floor, a couple of managers he vaguely remembered from company-wide emails—but none he was in any hurry to talk to. Nobody looked his way. Which was fine. Preferable, really.

A tray passed by, carrying tiny, symmetrical creations balanced on crackers and what looked like edible flowers. Phainon gave it a wide berth. The day he voluntarily ate something that cost more than his lunch was the day he tendered his resignation.

His eyes swept the room and landed on the bar.

It stretched along the far wall, all backlit gold and glass shelves stacked with bottles so spotless they practically sparkled. If there was one thing this city consistently got right, it was a good bar, even in places like this.

Well. When in Chicago.

He made his way through the crowd, weaving between clusters of Kremnos execs and a pair of Okhema engineers pretending to be deeply invested in the health of a decorative ficus. The music and chatter rolled around him in waves, all carefully modulated with the perfected the art of sounding affable while measuring social capital.

At the bar, a lean, nice-looking bartender greeted him with a small, professional nod.

“What can I get you?”

“Whiskey,” Phainon said, resting both hands on the bar’s edge. “Neat.”

The bartender didn’t ask which kind. He reached for a bottle with a label Phainon didn’t bother trying to read. The glass landed in front of him a moment later, the liquid catching the light like old brass.

Phainon knocked it back in one go. It hit hard, warmth unspooling in his chest and stomach, a steady burn that chased away the lingering edge of exhaustion. He set the glass down a little too firmly, earning a brief flick of a glance from the bartender.

“Another?” the man asked, already reaching for the bottle.

Phainon hesitated for half a second, then gave a nod.

“Better make it a double.”

He wasn’t sure how long he’d need to last here, but he already knew he was going to need it.

The second glass went down slower. Not by much. Phainon let the burn linger a little longer this time, rolling over his tongue before he tipped the last of it back. The glass made a soft clink as he set it down, and the bartender—ever watchful—reached for the bottle again.

Phainon waved him off with a small shake of his head.

He let out a breath through his nose, leaned forward onto the bar, and rested his forearms against the cool wood. His head dipped, forehead brushing the backs of his crossed arms. Eyes closed.

It wasn’t so bad, really.

Nobody was bothering him. He wasn’t expected to make conversation. There was decent liquor in his system and a seat with his name on it. For a guy who’d spent hours wrangling spreadsheets and rebooting servers that had no business still being in production, this counted as peace.

If his hometown friends could see him now—hair mussed, jacket borrowed and a size too big, hiding out in a high-rise ballroom while a string quartet murdered something in C minor—they’d have a field day.

He let the sound of the room dull around him. It was easy enough to tune out when you tried.

And then—

“Hey.”

The voice was soft. Close enough to his ear that it cut through the fog and made him jolt upright, heart giving a hard, startled thud against his ribs. He twisted in his seat, scowl already forming, some half-baked You shouldn’t sneak up on people like that on the tip of his tongue.

Until he saw her.

“Castorice,” he blinked, tension bleeding from his shoulders like a slow release valve. A sincere smile tugged at his mouth. “Well, hell. Didn’t expect to see you tonight.”

She gave a sheepish little smile, one corner of her mouth pulling higher than the other as if not sure whether to apologize. Her hands fidgeted with the sleeves of her blouse for a second before she slid onto the stool beside him.

“I was lurking,” she admitted. “Figured I should act social before someone from HR notices.”

Phainon huffed a tired, appreciative laugh. “Same here.”

They both fell quiet for a moment. The music shifted—something slower now, more somber.

Castorice leaned in a touch, lowering her voice. “Truth is, I was avoiding Caenis.”

That earned a wince from Phainon. “Yeah. Fair call.”

“Did you see her today?” Castorice asked, eyes flicking across the room like Caenis might materialize at any moment.

“I did,” Phainon muttered. “Made eye contact once. Think my soul tried to leave my body.”

That got a real laugh out of her, small, but there.

They lapsed into another easy silence, watching the room move around them. The catering staff, the clink of glass, the gentle glow of the backlit shelves behind the bar. Phainon caught himself studying the shine of a decanter and let his gaze drift.

“I wish Aglaea was here,” he said, quiet, almost to himself.

Castorice’s smile softened. “Yeah. Me too.”

Aglaea wasn’t the kind of person to show up at these things. She didn’t need to. Her presence was reserved for boardrooms and final calls, not glass-walled mixers with $30 crackers. But she’d taken care of them, both of them, in her way. Remembered names. Pulled strings when it counted.

Phainon turned his glass between his hands, watching the last of the amber liquid catch the light. “Figures. We get left with Caenis.”

“She’s on a warpath,” Castorice murmured, her gaze drifting toward a cluster of people at the far side of the room. “Has been for weeks.”

Phainon nodded grimly. Everyone at Okhema knew what that meant. Caenis, Regional Director and head of the Chicago branch, wasn’t the kind of woman to take losing ground lightly. Not after years spent trying to claw her way into the upper circle—buying favors, making noise, staking claims. And now, with Kremnos moving in, whatever power she had left was hanging by threads.

“Can’t blame her,” Phainon admitted. “I mean, losing half your control overnight? And now you’ve got these people rolling in like they already own the place. I’d be ready to bite throats too.”

“Yeah, well,” Castorice sighed, “she’s mostly biting middle management.”

“Story of corporate America,” Phainon muttered.

The bartender slid another drink toward him, unasked. Castorice reached for it before Phainon could, curling her fingers around the glass like it was a life preserver.

“God, please,” she whispered before taking a careful sip.

Phainon watched her with a smile, lifting his own drink in a half-hearted toast. “To mutual suffering.”

She clinked her glass to his.

A little island of quiet in a place built to be loud.

The din of the mixer had dulled some—or maybe it only felt that way with Castorice settled on the stool beside him. Phainon caught the way her hands stayed folded in her lap, her posture a touch too careful for an off-the-clock evening. Like she was waiting for someone to tell her she wasn’t supposed to be here.

He gave her a small nudge with his elbow. “How’s Pollux been? Haven’t crossed paths with her in a while.”

Castorice blinked, surprised by the question, though a pleased kind of surprise. Her face softened. “She’s good. Busy, as always. But she likes it.”

She hesitated, then let out a soft chuckle, glancing down at her drink. “Actually, she called me this morning. Said she’s got a client’s family insisting on a full Renaissance-themed wake this weekend. Velvet doublets, lute music, the whole thing.”

Phainon’s brow lifted. “You’re serious?”

“Unfortunately.” Castorice’s smile turned faintly exasperated. “She’s been trying to track down a harpist on short notice. And apparently three separate people have asked if they can bring a falcon.”

That earned a laugh from him. “People, man. That’s… I mean, part of me wants to call that ridiculous, but honestly? Kind of admire the commitment.”

“She said if one more person mentions birds of prey, she’s handing them the keys and walking out.”

Phainon grinned, shaking his head. “I don’t know how she does it. I get squeamish just swapping out the toner cartridge. Can’t imagine dealing with…” he gestured vaguely, “…all that.” Bodies.

Castorice’s smile gentled, and she let out a soft breath, tucking a loose strand of hair behind her ear. “Most people get weird about it. Either grossed out or… I don’t know, morbidly fascinated. But she’s always been like that. Wants to help. Says grief’s easier to carry when someone actually sees you.”

Phainon nodded, the words settling in.

“Sounds like good work to me,” he said quietly.

Castorice looked down, tracing the rim of her glass with a fingertip. “Yeah. It is. I just…” She hesitated. “Sometimes I worry she takes on too much. It wears on her. But she says it’s worth it, so.”

Phainon gave a small nod. “The world could use a few more like that.”

She glanced up then, and for a moment their eyes met.

Castorice offered a genuine smile and took a sip of her drink.

Phainon finished off the last of his whiskey. His gaze drifted absently over the crowd. Same faces. Same suits and easy, hollow laughs. He was about to turn back to Castorice when—

A flicker of blonde cut through the crowd.

Something about it hit sharp and sudden, a clean, involuntary jolt. Phainon’s throat caught on the last of his drink, the liquor burning the wrong way.

He coughed, nearly choking, glass clinking against the bar as his fingers twitched. His heart gave a sharp, unwelcome skip.

No. Way.

Phainon hadn’t meant to stare.

One moment, he was idly scanning the crowd, half-listening to the music, and the next—there he was.

Leaning casually against one of those marble-topped cocktail tables, water glass in hand, hair catching the light like it had been arranged that way on purpose. It wasn’t perfect, though. Slicked back, sure, but just a little messy near the crown, almost purposeful. The suit was tailored, somehow managing to look effortless in a room full of people trying far too hard.

And he was smiling.

Not the self-satisfied smirk Phainon had expected, either. This was easier. Unpolished. Whatever some man beside him had said made him laugh, his head tipping slightly, teeth flashing before he caught himself and settled back into something softer. He held the glass loosely in his fingers, completely at ease in a room that made Phainon feel like he’d come in through the freight elevator.

The sinking feeling in his stomach arrived right on cue.

He didn’t even realize how long he’d been looking until Castorice shifted beside him, following his gaze.

“…What are you—?”

Phainon winced and reached out, guiding her gently down behind the oversized floral arrangement on the bar. “Don’t look.”

Castorice blinked at him, puzzled but compliant, lowering her voice. “Why? Who is it?”

“Just—hang on.” He peered out again, careful. Castorice hesitated, then angled her head to get a better look. A flicker of recognition crossed her face, brows drawing together.

“I’ve seen him online before. That’s Kremnos’s—”

“—damn coffee thief,” Phainon finished, his voice sharp with the kind of bitterness usually reserved for tax audits.

Castorice turned to him, confusion giving way to reluctant amusement. “Wait. That’s the one you’re always complaining about? The guy who keeps taking your orders?”

“Yes,” Phainon muttered, slumping forward against the bar like he could disappear into it. “That’s him. I knew it. Of course he works for Kremnos. He looks like the kind of guy who gets a VP title just for having a family trust.”

He let out a quiet groan, scrubbing a hand over his face. “I swear, it’s like the city’s conspiring against me. First at the café, then at Cipher’s place, now here? There’s three million people in this city, Castorice.”

She watched him for a moment, something flickering behind her calm expression.

“You sure you’re not exaggerating?” she asked, brow lifted.

Phainon opened his mouth, a protest half-formed, but the words stalled.

“He’s…rude,” he managed, gesturing vaguely toward the far side of the room. “One of those people who acts like the whole world’s his living room. And look at him.” He shook his head, the irritation prickling under his skin. “I mean, come on. Nobody should be allowed to have a face like that and still make it worse by knowing it.”

He hesitated, his gaze drifting back.

“His figure too,” Phainon muttered, almost to himself. “Tall, narrow waist, broad-shouldered, but not in a loud way. Carries it well. And then there’s those eyes…”

He trailed off, frowning at his own words.

Castorice’s lips twitched.

“Phainon,” she said, eyes glinting with amusement.

“What?”

“You realize you’re describing someone you’d swipe right on so fast you’d sprain your wrist.”

He shot her a scowl, warmth creeping onto his face. “I hate him.”

She took a sip from her glass, her smirk barely contained. “Sure you do.”

“It’s not personal,” Phainon muttered. “I don’t care who people are. But it’s the principle of the thing. Who drinks someone else’s Americano with oat milk three times and has the nerve to act like I’m the problem for not grabbing it faster?”

Castorice made a sympathetic noise, though the corner of her mouth quirked up again.

“Sounds exhausting.”

“Oh, he’s a menace,” Phainon grumbled, peeking over the flowers once more.

Mydei—still standing by that table—was leaning back now as someone in a navy tie showed him something in a small leather notebook. Whatever it was, it pulled another unguarded smile from him.

And worse than that, people gravitated to him. Faces turned his way, conversations tilted to include him. He had that easy, magnetic pull, like a natural center of gravity in a room full of artificial ones.

Phainon’s stomach tightened in a way he pointedly refused to examine.

“You’re staring again,” Castorice murmured.

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He made a face, knocking back the last of his drink. “Not my type,” he added, a little too fast.

Castorice bit her lip, fighting a grin, eyes glinting behind the rim of her glass.

Phainon was just about to tell her to wipe that look off her face when the room shifted. It was subtle at first—a ripple through the crowd as conversations stuttered, laughter stalled, and heads turned toward the broad staircase at the far side of the floor.

A voice cut through, bright and sharp as glass.

“Ladies and gentlemen.”

Phainon winced. He didn’t need to look to know.

Caenis.

There she stood, a step above the floor like a queen surveying lesser kingdoms. Her dress was a charcoal gray, cut to intimidate rather than flatter, and her silver hair was pinned back with the kind of precision that suggested weapons training. She held a champagne flute like it might double as a blade.

“If I could have your attention for a moment.”

The Kremnos people turned toward her politely. The Okhema employees stiffened in place, every one of them clocking the social temperature drop like deer catching a distant scent. Phainon felt his jaw tighten reflexively. He wasn’t even doing anything, and still half-expected to get written up for whatever reason.

Caenis smiled—or showed teeth. It was a fine line.

“I’d like to propose a toast,” she went on, voice polished to a dangerous shine. “To new partnerships, shared innovation, and the opportunities ahead as our two companies integrate.”

She said it like a battlefield report.

Servers slipped through the crowd with silver trays, tall, narrow flutes catching the light. Phainon grabbed one without hesitation—a muscle memory from years of office parties where the drinks were the only thing worth showing up for.

Beside him, Castorice reached for one too, then hesitated with a faint grimace.

“Hang on,” she murmured, nodding toward a passing tray carrying something non-alcoholic.

Phainon tipped his glass toward her. “Godspeed.”

She disappeared into the moving current of people, a soft flicker of lavender in a sea of black and navy.

Caenis was still talking. Legacy, market synergy, shared values. Phainon’s mind bailed at synergy, his stomach lurching in protest. He gave the champagne a slow swirl, watching the bubbles race to the surface like tiny, doomed escape attempts.

He was halfway through debating whether to bother drinking it when Castorice reappeared, eyeing him skeptically.

“Phainon…” she said, eyeing the flute in his hand, “you know whiskey and champagne don’t mix.”

He shrugged. “Neither do Okhema and Kremnos.”

Castorice made a face, because it wasn’t wrong.

“Be careful,” she said, softer now.

Before he could answer, someone behind her called her name—one of the HR reps, mouthing an apologetic sorry like it mattered.

Castorice sighed, tilting her head toward the sound. “Back in a minute.”

Phainon lifted his glass in a lazy salute. “I’ll be here.”

She smiled, then slipped back into the crowd.

Eventually, Caenis’s voice fading back into the background hum. Phainon glanced down at the champagne in his hand.

He lifted it to eye level.

You know what?

Tipped the glass slightly.

I’m drinking until I tolerate these people… or forget them.

And downed it in one go.

He coughed once, snorted a laugh at himself, and reached for the whiskey he’d left abandoned nearby.

The night, he decided, still had room to get worse.

And for now, that felt fine.

Phainon had lost track of how long it had been since Castorice vanished into the crowd again, or how many flutes of champagne he’d pilfered off passing trays. The buzz had settled in comfortably, a warmth in his chest, a pleasant hum behind his eyes.

He stood, stretching a little, scanning the room for another drink and maybe a friendly face. A tray passed by and he reached for it—and missed.

“Shit—”

The tray wobbled. The server’s eyes went wide.

Phainon caught it just in time, steadying the glasses with a half-apologetic gesture. “Easy, bud. My bad. I owe you one.”

The server gave him a tight, grateful nod and hurried off. Phainon chuckled under his breath, turned—and nearly walked straight into someone.

He stumbled a step back. “Oh—sorry, ma’am. Didn’t see you there.”

The woman he’d almost bowled over regarded him with a cool, unreadable look. Pale eyes, the color of golden frost under glass. Not young, though it was hard to tell exactly how old. The kind of face ruthless genetics preserved.

Her dress was deep red, clean lines and fitter, a signet ring on one hand. Hair nearly white-blonde, swept back like it had taken hours to style.

An elegant brow arched.

“Ma’am?” she repeated, voice smooth as polished glass. There was the faintest glint of humor in it. “How old do you think I am?”

Phainon, buzzed but not a complete fool, gave a grin. “Couldn’t say, ma’am. My mama taught me better than to guess. ‘Ma’am’s just good manners where I come from. I call my niece ma’am when she’s got a butter knife.”

A flicker of something—amusement, maybe—tugged at the corner of her mouth.

Before either of them could say more, Castorice’s voice cut in, a little breathless as she hurried up.

“There you are—sorry, they needed me for—”

She stopped mid-sentence, her expression freezing.

Phainon glanced back at her, still grinning. “You missed it. I was about to charm this nice lady here—”

Castorice’s face drained of color. She flicked her gaze from the woman to Phainon. “Hi,” she said, brittle, dipping her head in a polite nod. “So sorry to interrupt. They just—uh, needed me for something. Everything’s fine now.”

Phainon frowned, caught off guard by the sudden shift in her tone.

“What?”

Castorice slid up beside him, her elbow nudging his ribs, and leaned in close enough he could feel her breath against his ear.

“That’s Gorgo,” she murmured.

He blinked.

“The who?”

“The Gorgo. Chairwoman. Castrum Kremnos.”

Phainon felt the blood drain from his face so fast it left his ears ringing.

“Oh,” he said faintly.

Castorice pasted on a professional smile, directing it toward Gorgo like a peace offering.

“Wonderful celebration you’re hosting, ma’am, right Phainon?”

She elbowed Phainon again, harder this time.

He cleared his throat, his earlier bravado shriveling under the weight of the realization.

“Right. Uh. Yep. Real… festive. Big fan of… uh. Mergers.”

The words came out like a man digging his own grave with a dessert spoon.

Gorgo studied him, head tilted slightly, those pale eyes sharp and assessing. He had the distinct, certain feeling he was being filed, categorized, and judged in the space of a heartbeat.

And then—the smallest twitch of her mouth when she heard Castorice.

“Phainon, is it?”

He swallowed.

“Yes, ma’am.”

She made a quiet, thoughtful sound, almost to herself.

Castorice looked like she might faint.

“Well, we should probably—” she started, grabbing for Phainon’s sleeve.

But Gorgo lifted a hand, a small, absent gesture that stopped them cold.

“You and I,” she started. “We’ll have to catch up. I hear,” and here her voice dipped, more to herself than to them, “something about coffee?”

Phainon’s stomach sank somewhere near his knees.

Gorgo took another unhurried sip, gave him one final glance, then turned and walked away, her heels clicking against the marble like distant hammer strikes.

Phainon let out a slow, shaky breath.

“Castorice.”

She was already halfway to moving again. “Yeah?”

“I’m so, so fired.”

Castorice gave him a helpless look, sympathy clear in her expression, then muttered something about good luck before vanishing into the crowd.

Phainon took a steadying breath, ducked around a cluster of people, and picked up his pace.

“Hey—uh, ma’am,” he called softly as he caught up.

Gorgo didn’t stop right away. She slowed, then glanced over her shoulder, one brow lifting in faint, almost lazy curiosity.

He hesitated, then managed an apologetic smile. “Didn’t mean to be a pain earlier. Figured since I already made an ass of myself, might as well finish the job proper.”

That earned him a long look. But instead of the cool dismissal he half-expected, she turned to face him fully.

“You’ve got nerve.”

“Blame the champagne,” he shrugged. “Or my mother. Could go either way.”

A small sound escaped her, somewhere between a scoff and a laugh. But she stayed.

Gorgo studied him a moment longer, then asked, casual in tone, precise in intent:

“Where are you from?”

Phainon blinked at the bluntness. “Missouri. Farm town. Middle of nowhere.”

She gave a slight nod, filing it away. “And what do you do?”

“Numbers,” he said simply. “Finance division. Okhema.”

Her brow lifted, just a fraction. “And how did you land that?”

He huffed a laugh. “Honestly? Dumb luck. I was new in town, ran into Aglaea at this old diner a couple years back. Didn’t know who she was. She liked my attitude. Gave me a job.”

Both her brows rose this time, though she made no comment. Aglaea. That, he could tell, had landed somewhere important.

She took a slow sip from her glass, eyes never leaving him.

“And Chicago?”

His grin softened, a little sheepish. “Seemed like the kind of place you could either make something of yourself, or fall on your face so hard it left a crater. Figured either way, it’d be a story worth telling.”

The honesty of it hung there for a beat.

It disarmed her more than she expected.

“And why this work?” she asked, voice a touch quieter now, though still edged with a kind of test.

Phainon thought about hedging. Didn’t.

“I’m good at it,” he said. “Numbers make sense when people don’t. Guess that’s reason enough.”

A flicker of interest sharpened her gaze.

“And this room?” she asked, gesturing subtly to the expanse of  people’s. “What’s your read?”

He hesitated. Not out of fear—more a quiet calculation. How much would get him fired, and how much was worth saying anyway.

“Too many people here think ambition makes cruelty clever,” he said after a moment. “Ambition’s fine. Necessary, even. But there’s a difference between being sharp and being a prick about it.”

He scratched the back of his neck. “World could use more people who don’t treat empathy like a weakness.”

For a quiet second, she didn’t answer.

Then, in a rare and unsettlingly moment, the hard line of her mouth sharpened.

She tipped her glass toward him. “You might survive here.”

Phainon raised his empty glass in return. “Wouldn’t bet on it.”

That earned a sharp, almost surprised breath of amusement from her. He still couldn’t tell whether she was entertained, impressed, or just enjoying the novelty of someone not breaking into a sweat under her gaze.

He cocked his head, testing the waters between them.

“Tell me,” he said, “is it always this much of a circus?”

A wry glint in her eye now.

“This is a quiet night.”

He groaned. “Christ.”

And for the first time, her smile reached the edges of her eyes.

For a few minutes, the conversation lingered there—a strange, easy sort of detente. The wheeling and dealing of the room carried on beyond their little corner, but it felt distant. A background hum neither of them particularly cared to join.

Then, her gaze flicked past him. Something shifted in her posture.

Phainon caught the change, followed her line of sight.

Across the room, Mydei stood half-turned, deep in conversation with one of the old guard from the Okhema board. The warm overhead light caught the angles of his face, the way he moved with grace.

Then Mydei’s gaze lifted.

Their eyes met.

A jolt—sharp, immediate. Like grabbing a live wire.

Phainon’s stomach did an undignified somersault.

Mydei’s expression flickered, something too fast to name. Surprise, maybe. Or irritation. Then his gaze dropped to Gorgo standing beside him.

The shift in his face was immediate. His mouth tightened. Eyes narrowing, calculating.

And then, without a word, Mydei started toward them.

A slow, deliberate pace.

Phainon felt his pulse kick up.

“Oh, for the love of—”

Gorgo smiled.

Phainon braced.

What the hell did he want now?

And then—

“Everything alright?” Mydei asked, his voice threaded through with a polite neutrality that didn’t fool Phainon for a second.

Gorgo smiled, an elegant tilt of her head. “Of course. Why wouldn’t it be?”

Mydei’s expression didn’t shift, but Phainon caught the faint narrowing of his eyes. There was something underneath it, a quiet what the hell are you doing that.

“I wasn’t aware you were taking meetings tonight,” Mydei said lightly.

“Who said this was a meeting?” Gorgo countered. “I’m perfectly capable of having a conversation without an agenda.”

Mydei didn’t argue, though it was clear from his posture that he didn’t buy it. His gaze flicked once more to Phainon, and though his face remained polite, there was a weight to it.

Before Phainon could excuse himself, Gorgo glanced at the time on her watch. “Well,” she murmured, “I should be getting on.”

She took a step past Mydei, paused, and with a small, conspiratorial smile, murmured just for him, “I do like him, though.”

If Mydei’s eyes twitched at that, it was barely perceptible.

And then she was gone, heels clicking against the marble as she disappeared into the crowd.

The silence that settled in her wake was immediate.

Mydei turned back to him, gaze cool. “It’s you.”

Phainon, already knowing this was a terrible idea, grabbed a passing glass of something pale and sparkling, downing it in one go before answering.

“Who else?”

Mydei’s brow lifted, a fraction. The way his gaze lingered, the slight crease between his brows—a flicker of something like concern, showed before disappearing. He adjusted his cuff, looking the other man over like a puzzle piece that didn’t belong on his board.

“You work for Kremnos, then?” Phainon asked, managing to keep his tone casual, if a little tight.

“And you,” Mydei replied, “at Okhema.”

Phainon gave a humorless smile. “Lucky us.”

They stood there for a moment, neither willing to back down just yet.

“Are you following me?” Mydei asked idly, though there was a pointed edge to it.

Phainon snorted. “I should be the one asking you that.”

“Sure,” Mydei said mildly, though the glint in his eyes suggested he didn’t believe it for a second.

Another beat. A flicker of mutual irritation softened, just barely, into something that wasn’t quite hostility.

“I’m sure you have better people to talk to,” Mydei said finally.

Phainon raised a brow. “Same.”

A mutual, noncommittal sound passed between them—a clipped, amused huff on one side, a humorless grunt on the other. And then, without ceremony, they both turned and walked in opposite directions.

Phainon didn’t look back.

He cut through the throng of guests, eyes scanning for Castorice again. He spotted her a few feet away, caught in awkward conversation with a man who looked like he hadn’t noticed her discomfort or didn’t care to. She stood rigid, polite smile stretched too thin.

Without breaking stride, Phainon reached her, gently but firmly taking her by the arm.

“Let’s go,” he muttered.

The man started to protest, but Phainon shot him a look that made it clear he was done with pleasantries. “Move.”

It worked. The man’s mouth closed. He stepped aside.

Phainon steered Castorice away from the cluster of people and didn’t let go until they’d put several bodies between themselves and the rest of the room.

“Thanks,” Castorice said, blinking up at him, clearly surprised by the abrupt shift in his mood. “You okay?”

He ran a hand through his hair. “Define okay.”

She sighed, a little relieved. “Well, good news is we’ve got about an hour left before it’s socially acceptable to leave.”

“Fantastic,” Phainon muttered. “What now?”

Castorice gave him a sidelong look. “What do you think?”

“No,” she said preemptively, seeing the glint in his eye.

He raised a brow. “Got a better idea?”

She opened her mouth, hesitated, then grimaced. “Bar it is… again.”

“Thought so.”

It wasn’t like this was new.

Phainon and Castorice had a long, reliable history of nights like this— usually ending with one of them half-carrying the other out of some bar, navigating streets and subway stops by sheer muscle memory. It wasn’t something they planned so much as a system that had evolved naturally over time. Whoever sobered up first took the other home, no questions asked. Castorice, more often than not, was the lightweight. Not tonight.

Somewhere along the way, Phainon had passed the event horizon of drunk. He couldn’t remember how much he had. What he did remember was leaning heavily against Castorice now, head lolling a little toward her shoulder, content. She’d just finished saying something—something completely idiotic, though in the moment it had struck him as the most incisive wit imaginable.

“—and then I told him, buddy,” Castorice was crowing, brandishing her glass as she spoke, “if you’re gonna try flirting with me, at least learn what a P/E ratio is first.”

Phainon let out a laugh so loud it startled the people nearest them, nearly doubling over where he sat. “No. No, you didn’t.”

“Dead serious.”

“Genius,” he slurred, pointing a finger at her like she’d just delivered the greatest punchline in modern history. “That’s—you should be giving seminars, Cast.”

She giggled, cheeks flushed but still solidly in control of her faculties. “You’re a mess.”

“I’m peak performance,” Phainon declared, lifting his empty glass in a grand, sloppy toast before realizing it was long since drained.

It might’ve gone on like that—harmlessly drunk, good-naturedly obnoxious, the two of them in their own little orbit—if not for the abrupt vibration of Castorice’s phone against her palm.

She frowned, glanced down at the screen. A number she didn’t recognize. “Hold on,” she murmured, moving to answer.

Phainon didn’t pay it any mind at first. He was still riding the high of their ridiculous joke, snickering to himself. But something about Castorice’s posture changed. The slouch of tipsy comfort vanished, her shoulders going rigid. The color drained from her face by degrees, and her voice dropped to a hush.

He blinked, trying to focus.

“Hey,” he slurred, reaching out to nudge her arm, “you good?”

She didn’t answer at first, murmuring something low into the phone he couldn’t catch. Then, all at once, she stiffened, setting her drink aside with a carelessness that sent it sloshing dangerously close to the rim.

Phainon’s heart sank. “Castorice?”

She ended the call with a sharp exhale, scrubbing a hand over her face. “Shit.”

That cut through the fog. Castorice didn’t swear usually.

“What happened?”

“Family emergency,” she blurted, already fumbling for her bag. “I gotta go.”

“Oh… hell,” Phainon muttered. “Yeah, go. It’s fine.”

She hovered, biting her lip, eyes darting between him and the door, clearly torn. Her face said she didn’t want to leave him here, but whatever was happening on her end sounded serious.

Phainon, still too drunk for subtlety but a decent enough person underneath it, patted her shoulder. “Cas. Go,” he said gently. “I’m a grown man. I can handle myself.”

She hesitated a second longer, then scanned the room—looking for something, or someone. And when her gaze finally snagged on a particular figure, Phainon followed it lazily, not immediately making the connection.

Tall. Good looking. Talking to someone.

Mydeimos.

And his stomach dropped like a stone.

“Oh, fuck me,” Phainon groaned, slouching lower in his chair, but it was too late. Castorice was already cutting a path through the crowd, zeroed in.

“Wait—waitwaitwait,” Phainon hissed, scrambling upright and nearly overbalancing in the process.

But there was no stopping her now.

He watched, stomach churning, as Castorice caught Mydei’s attention with a polite tap to the arm. The look on Mydei’s face shifted in an instant, from vague surprise to practiced neutrality. He glanced at her, likely expecting some routine, polite party small talk.

“I’m sorry,” Castorice began, her voice urgent. “I—I need a favor.”

Even from a distance, Phainon could see the flicker of confusion cross Mydei’s face. He said something in return, but whatever it was, Castorice was already gesturing for him to step aside with her.

Phainon’s skin prickled. He didn’t have to hear the words to fill in the blanks.

He watched the exact moment she told him. Watched as Mydei’s face slipped from polite indulgence to flat skepticism.

Then came the name. Aglaea.

Whatever Castorice said about her made Mydei hesitate, just for a fraction of a second. His jaw tightened. The polite mask slipped back into place, but there was a hardness to it now.

“Why would I?” Phainon could almost hear it from here.

A fair question.

And it might’ve ended there—should’ve, really—if not for the universe’s reliably bad timing. A guest, some overly friendly party kid Phainon only vaguely remembered seeing earlier, sidled up beside him. Laid a hand on his arm and leaned in a little too close.

“Hey, cutie.”

Phainon blinked, bleary and confused. He offered them a sunny smile. “Howdy,” he drawled, because manners were manners.

He didn’t catch Castorice’s expression of horror, nor the near-imperceptible shift in the room’s temperature.

But he felt it, a second later. He turned just in time to catch the darkening of Mydei’s gaze, the flicker of something unreadable beneath it.

Castorice gestured subtly toward the scene, her expression desperate, a silent see what I mean?

Mydei sighed, long and bone-deep, the sound of a man whose night had just taken a nosedive.

“Fine,” he muttered, already pulling his phone from his pocket. “What’s his address?”

And just like that, it was done.

Phainon stared, dazed, as the pieces fell into place around him. He barely had time to register Castorice’s quick approach, the press of her lips to his cheek.

“Good luck,” she whispered, and then she was gone, disappearing toward the door without another word.

He watched her leave, some distant, disbelieving part of him still hoping this was a stress-induced hallucination. But when he turned, Mydei was already there, looming at his side like some elegantly dressed harbinger of doom.

Phainon groaned softly, dragging a hand down his face.

What a day.

And so it ended like this.

Phainon, too drunk to protest properly being half-dragged across the flagstone drive by none other than Mydeimos. The cool night air hit them like a slap. Somewhere down the street, the faint sounds of traffic murmured. A breeze tugged at the edges of Phainon’s jacket, and he shivered, though not enough to regain full sense.

He followed.

Docilely.

Well—mostly.

“Mydei,” Phainon chirped after a moment, stumbling a half-step to the side. He caught himself against the shorter man’s shoulder. “If you’re kidnapping me, you better at least feed me something.”

Mydei’s jaw twitched, a muscle feathering tight along the side of his face. He let out a steady exhale through his nose as if calming himself. “It’s not a kidnapping,” he muttered, pulling his keys from his pocket with a flick of his wrist. “Shut up.”

Phainon snorted, one of those loose, breathy laughs that came from deep in his chest. “Coulda fooled me,” he said, grinning like a drunk idiot.

They made it about three more steps before a voice called out behind them.

“Hey—hold up!”

Phainon squinted over his shoulder. A tall figure jogged toward them, hair a little wind-tossed, face familiar in that vague way most party acquaintances were. Took Phainon a second to place him—the guy from earlier, with the little leather book.

The man reached them, slightly out of breath but still smiling like they were all old friends. “Hey. Can you drop me too? Perdikkas ditched me.”

Mydei turned, fixing him with a flat, unimpressed stare that could’ve soured milk. “No.”

The guy’s grin only widened. His gaze shifted to Phainon, visibly noting the half-collapsed state of him slumped against Mydei’s side.

“Oh hey,” the man greeted cheerfully. “You okay, man?”

Phainon beamed, his cheeks flushed a rosy pink and his eyes just a touch too glassy. “Never better,” he declared, sounding so chipper it might’ve been believable if he hadn’t looked like someone midway through losing a drinking contest with gravity.

Mydei sighed, thoroughly exhausted.

He was just about to shut the whole thing down when Phainon leaned in again without warning, his nose brushing lightly against the side of Mydei’s neck. It was so casual, so absentminded, that for a second Mydei’s brain failed to compute what was happening.

“You smell good,” Phainon mumbled, voice low and entirely pleased, as if imparting a particularly valuable secret.

Mydei went stock-still.

The man standing in front of them blinked, then his face split into a delighted, shit-eating grin. “Oooooh,” he drawled, practically vibrating with amusement.

Mydei’s expression darkened. His glare alone could’ve taken down a small government.

“Out, Ptolemy,” he said, voice lethal.

Ptolemy threw up his hands in mock surrender, the picture of easy, unbothered energy. “Alright, alright—toodles!” He gave them both a lazy wink, spun on his heel, and strolled back toward the building without a care in the world.

Phainon sighed, still half-clinging to Mydei like an affectionate, slightly inebriated barn cat. There was a content little hum from his throat, his head lolling briefly against the man’s shoulder again like it was a perfectly acceptable place to take a nap.

Mydei stood there for a long, resigned moment, lips pressed into a line, before gently prying him off and steering them both toward the sleek black car idling at the curb. It was a gorgeous machine, all polished curves and chrome, the kind of car that practically broadcast its sticker price without needing to.

Phainon blinked blearily at it, lips parting in appreciation. “Nice car,” he mumbled, half to himself.

“Get in.”

There wasn’t a trace of warmth in it.

“Okay,” Phainon agreed easily, reaching for the handle.

His balance betrayed him immediately. His fingers missed the door entirely and he swayed forward, almost faceplanting into the pavement.

Mydei caught him without looking, one hand closing around his arm with the reflexes of someone who’d spent far too long managing other people’s disasters.

“Jesus Christ,” he muttered, hauling him upright.

Phainon, rather than steadying himself, took the opportunity to latch on again, leaning against Mydei with a pleased little hum. His head tipped toward him, resting against his shoulder in a way that felt entirely unearned.

“You’re warm,” Phainon noted, as though it were a rare, fascinating discovery.

Mydei’s sigh was long, and somehow managed to convey both deep weariness and a distant sort of patience. The tips of his ears, however, betrayed him—flushed a shade darker than the rest of him, though he pretended not to notice.

“If you throw up in this car,” Mydei said darkly, fishing for the keys again, “I’m mailing you the cleaning bill.”

Phainon grinned, a lazy, sun-soaked thing. “You’d have to get my address for that.”

“Unfortunately,” Mydei muttered as he unlocked the car, “I have it.”

Getting Phainon into the passenger seat turned out to be a rodeo.

He wriggled, laughed, slipped half out of Mydei’s grip as the man tried to angle him inside without cracking his skull against the doorframe.

“Sit,” Mydei ground out, teeth clenched.

Phainon snorted, slumping into the seat sideways like somebody had removed all his bones. “Bossy.”

Buckling him in was worse.

Mydei leaned over, reaching for the seatbelt, and Phainon’s head immediately lolled against his shoulder, cheek pressing against the fabric of his suit with a content sigh.

“You smell nice,” Phainon mumbled.

Mydei’s breath caught. Barely a hitch, but there.

He didn’t answer. Just muttered something under his breath, wrestled Phainon upright, and reached for the buckle again.

“Sit still.”

“No.”

And then, for reasons known only to whatever stray impulse fired off in Phainon’s drunk brain, he grabbed at Mydei’s waist. Not hard. Just a rough tug, like pulling a cousin into a river.

Unfortunately for everyone, Mydei was not built for this.

He made a sharp, startled noise, braced a hand on the door, and half-fell forward, practically landing in Phainon’s lap.

“Are you—” Mydei started, disbelieving.

And before anything else could happen, Phainon’s brain coughed up a singular thought, and with zero filter, he bit him.

Right where neck met collar. Not hard, just firm enough to be unmistakable.

Mydei recoiled like he’d been electrocuted.

“Did you just fucking bite me?!”

Phainon blinked up at him, glassy-eyed and pink-cheeked. “No.”

Mydei’s stare could’ve peeled paint. His hands flexed like he was weighing the pros and cons of homicide.

For one drawn-out second, Phainon was almost sure he was about to get left on the curb.

But instead, Mydei muttered something that sounded like a curse, buckled him in with short, clipped motions, and just as he clicked the buckle home —Phainon laid a hand over his.

Mydei went completely still.

“What,” he said, low and dangerous.

Phainon squinted down at their hands. Mydei’s was long-fingered, steady, strong. For some reason, it struck him.

“You’ve got nice hands,” Phainon murmured, and this time it came out sincere.

Silence.

The air went strange. A beat too long.

Then Mydei made a noise in his throat—halfway between a scoff and a strangled laugh—yanked his hand back, and slammed the door shut hard enough to rattle the frame.

Phainon slumped sideways in the seat, humming to himself.

Nice car.

Nice hands.

Nice neck.

Weird night.

Phainon let his head rest against the window, cheek pressed to the cool glass. Outside, the city slipped by in blurs of sodium light, streetlamps streaking past like slow-moving stars. He watched them, unfocused, the steady rhythm of it pulling at something in the back of his mind.

“Y’know…” he said eventually. “you’re not bad company.”

Silence.

Not unexpected.

Mydei didn’t respond, eyes fixed on the road ahead.

Figures.

They drove like that for a while. The city easing by around them. Phainon counted traffic lights in his head—three green, two red, one yellow. Pointless, but it kept his hands still.

After a while, he sighed, shifting in his seat. “No talking, huh?”

Nothing.

“Right.” Phainon straightened a little, wincing as the car hit a shallow pothole. “Fine. I’ll talk.”

And without waiting for permission, he did.

“I got three older cousins,” he began. “Bunch of stubborn idiots. Used to run around raising hell back home. Haven’t seen ‘em in a couple years. Miss them sometimes, though I’d probably punch them if I did.”

He risked a glance at Mydei. Nothing.

Unfazed, Phainon kept going. “My dad’s got hands like catcher’s mitts. Worked his whole life, tough as hell. But he’s soft, underneath. Pretends he’s not, but you can tell. And my mom’s sharp. Real sharp. She’s got this way of smiling at you until you realize you’re wrong about whatever dumb thing you thought you knew. Doesn’t even have to say anything. It’s kind of terrifying.”

The faintest snort, so quiet it barely registered.

But it was there.

Phainon beamed to himself. “See? Got a reaction.”

Mydei didn’t look over, but there was the barest flicker at the corner of his mouth. “Don’t get ahead of yourself,” he muttered.

Phainon hummed, leaning his head back against the seat. He was quiet for a moment, then added, “Could tell you about my first week here.”

This time, a slight tilt of Mydei’s head. Subtle. But present.

Phainon took it as permission. “Got lost in the L station trying to switch trains. Swore I was gonna end up in Milwaukee. Called my mom half in tears ‘cause I got stuck in this weird underground mall. Couldn’t find an exit for, like, an hour and a half. Bought four packs of discount socks just to feel like I accomplished something.”

A long beat.

And then—the faintest exhale. Barely a sound, but it was closer to a laugh than anything else.

Phainon turned his head, smiling. “Rude.”

“Don’t bite me again and maybe I’ll be nicer.”

Phainon chuckled before turning just enough to watch Mydei. “You probably already know my family owns a farm.”

A noncommittal sound from the driver’s side.

“It’s nice, most of the time. Good to help out, keep your hands busy. But when I didn’t wanna be bothered, I’d head out into the wheat fields. Just lay there, staring up at the sky. Could lose whole afternoons like that.”

His voice had settled, softer now.

A small, almost absent smile tugged at his mouth. “Course, Snowy always found me, no matter how quiet I was. Oh, that’s our fluffy white puppy. He’s always got a smile on his face, like this!”

Phainon tilted his head slightly, mimicking it—eyes bright, mouth crooked in a loose, open smile that caught in the dashboard light.

And something in Mydei’s chest went tight.

He gripped the wheel a little harder, jaw flexing as he pulled his gaze hard back to the road.

“Don’t do that,” he muttered.

Phainon blinked. “Do what?”

“Nothing.”

A soft laugh. Phainon let his head fall back against the headrest.

“Snowy’s a good dog,” he murmured.

Mydei said nothing.

After a while, without looking over, he spoke.

“Cyrene’d probably like you.”

Mydei’s brow edged up, a flick of curiosity in his voice. “Who’s that?”

“My best friend,” Phainon said, a fondness threading through the words. “We grew up together. She’s smart as hell, real good at reading people. Nicest person I’ve ever met also.”

There was an easy warmth in the way he said it, like the thought alone steadied something in him.

“She’s the reason I never took up boxing, actually,” Phainon added, glancing over. “I thought about joining this local club back home—figured it’d toughen me up, keep me out of trouble. But then Cyrene needed help with school, and math was always my thing. So, tutoring it was.”

He shrugged, like it wasn’t a story worth much, though his voice softened at the edges. “Guess I figured if one of us had a shot at getting out of there, it oughta count.”

Mydei’s hand flexed lightly on the wheel. He didn’t look over, but his voice cut through the quiet.

“I could teach you.”

Phainon blinked, sitting up a bit. “What, boxing?”

“I said what I said.”

A slow, amused grin spread across Phainon’s face. “Yeah? You any good?”

“You couldn’t keep up.”

That pulled a real laugh from Phainon, easy and bright in the dark. “Bet I could. Might surprise you.”

For the first time all night, the faintest smirk tugged at Mydei’s mouth, sharp and involuntary. “I’ll give you my number when I drop you off. Set a date.”

Phainon let out a soft, pleased whoop. “Look at that. We’re basically friends now.”

“Let’s not get ahead of ourselves.”

But the tease in Mydei’s voice undercut the words, a note lighter than before.

He was about to continue but then—casual but curious, “What about you? Got family?”

Mydei hesitated, his jaw working for a moment like he wasn’t sure if he’d answer.

Eventually, he did. “My mother. Taught me how to cook.”

Phainon perked up a little, turning toward him. “Yeah? Are you any good?”

“I am.”

“Damn,” Phainon whistled. “I only know how to keep myself alive. Scrambled eggs, boxed pasta. That’s about it. Bet it’s nice, knowing how to actually put a real meal together.”

Mydei’s gaze stayed forward, but his voice softened, almost despite himself. “I could show you sometime.”

Phainon blinked, a small, surprised smile creeping in. “Man,” he said, shaking his head with amusement, “you’re just full of surprises tonight.”

Mydei slightly chuckled that. The city slid past them in long, quiet streaks of light.

And for the first time all night, the silence between them felt easy.

At some point, Phainon went quiet. His head rested against the window, eyes half-lidded as the city slipped by in smudged streaks of color. Everything felt softened at the edges—the warmth of the car, the hush of the road, the way the world outside blurred like an old lullaby you could almost remember.

Then—the car slowed, the engine easing into a low idle before cutting off with a quiet shudder.

A soft metallic click as the keys turned.

“We’re here.”

Phainon blinked, the sound tugging him from the comfortable fog. He lifted his head, squinting out at the familiar sprawl of the apartment complex lit by buzzing porch lamps. “Already?” He rubbed at his face. “Man, you drive fast.”

“I drive like a sane person,” Mydei muttered. “You just wouldn’t shut up.”

Phainon snorted, a rough laugh catching in his throat. “Touché.”

Mydei reached out, palm open. “Phone.”

Phainon blinked at him, sluggish. “What?”

“Your phone,” Mydei repeated, the kind of patience usually reserved for dealing with confused pets and small children.

Still a little slow on the uptake, Phainon fished the device from his pocket and handed it over. Mydei unlocked it with a few deft taps, scrolling through something.

It took a second, but then Phainon squinted. “Wait—hang on. What’re you doing?”

Mydei shot him a flat, unimpressed look. “Relax.”

A few seconds later, he passed it back. “There.”

Phainon glanced down. A new contact. Just Mydei, clean and unembellished. His stomach gave a ridiculous, unhelpful flip at the sight of it.

“Oh,” he said, playing it off with a half-smile. “Yeah… yeah, cool.”

Mydei leaned back against the headrest, one hand scrubbing over his face, the faintest trace of a laugh in his exhale. “You owe me one.”

Phainon grinned, leaning an elbow on the door. “What, you want a goodnight kiss or something?”

The effect was immediate. Mydei’s eyes widened like he’d just been blindsided by a glass door, and for a heartbeat he seemed to short-circuit. “You—” he started, then cut himself off with a sharp breath, shaking his head. “You’re an idiot.”

A beat passed.

Then, a little quieter, not quite grudging, “You want me to walk you up?”

Phainon snorted, unbuckling his seatbelt with a soft click. “I’m six-one, man. Nobody’s messing with me.”

He paused, thoughtful. “Well… maybe Lygus. He’s weird.”

Mydei frowned. “Who the hell is Lygus?”

“Neighbor. Guy stares at me every time I leave my place, but I swear I’ve never actually seen him in the building.” Phainon shrugged like it wasn’t worth worrying about, though the corner of Mydei’s eye twitched.

Before he could say whatever cutting remark was already loaded in his brain, Phainon cracked the door open. Cool night air spilled into the car, brushing against warm skin and the scent of leather seats. He lingered a second, half-turning.

“Hey,” he said, voice softer now. “Thanks for the ride.”

There was something in the way he said it—a note of quiet sincerity that caught Mydei a little off guard. His shoulders stiffened before he could help it.

Phainon either didn’t notice or chose not to, slipping out of the car with a thud of the door. The gravel lot crunched under his boots as he headed for the stairwell, keys jingling faintly in his hand.

At the door, he fumbled with the lock for a moment before glancing back.

The car was still there. Headlights on, engine idling, Mydei’s silhouette faintly visible behind the wheel.

Waiting.

Phainon’s chest went a little warm. He huffed a soft, crooked smile to himself and finally slipped inside.
