Chapter Summary

Phainon takes time off work, gets punched (romantically), eats a lunch he didn’t pack, almost decides to kiss a man before getting interrupted, and ends the day narrowly avoiding unemployment via divine CEO intervention. Ice cream is acquired. Feelings are caught. Caenis leaves spiritually bruised.

Chapter Notes

Late again sorry :’)

It was, by all accounts, a beautiful morning in Chicago.

That rare kind of bright that made even the L look gentler than usual. Sunlight spilled in through the windows, laying long slats across rumpled suits, scuffed sneakers, the glossy edge of a thermos tucked into someone’s side pocket. The train hummed steady beneath it all, wheels grinding along the curve of the track.

The car smelled like coffee and warm metal. Someone behind him was eating dry cereal out of a plastic container. There was a faint beat leaking from a teenager’s headphones a few seats down, something tinny and fast. It was quiet otherwise—weekday quiet, tired quiet. The kind of calm that only really existed between rush hours.

And it would’ve been perfect. A normal Tuesday, even.

Except, of course, for Phainon.

He sat hunched near the back of the car, legs crossed, elbows resting on his knee, one hand gripping the strap of his old gym bag like it might try and run off if he let go. The canvas had long since lost whatever structure it used to have—slumped now between his boots, frayed at the zipper, stained at the corners. His hoodie was zipped halfway, sleeves pushed to the elbows. A soft navy blue, or used to be. There was a splotch of faded bleach right over the stomach, round and blotchy like a sad little ghost.

He looked fine. Like any other guy on his way to the gym. Normal.

Except his phone screen had just lit up for the fifth time in three minutes. 10:07 AM.

He locked it. Unlocked it. Still 10:07.

He sighed. Pinched the bridge of his nose.

“Lord,” he murmured to himself, not quite under his breath.

He’d been holding it together all morning—barely, but still. Playing it cool. Doing his best to pretend this was just a regular day. Because technically, it was. Technically.

But Phainon had a problem. And it wasn’t one of those little ones, like rent being late or his water pressure being weak. No, this one was personal. Embarrassing, even. Possibly criminal, depending how you looked at it.

Because recently—very recently—he had bitten someone.

Bitten. Like full teeth. Like a drunk raccoon.

And not just anyone, either.

No. He’d bitten Mydei.

Phainon groaned quietly and dropped his head into the crook of his elbow. Stayed there, breathing against the fabric of his sleeve, stewing in his shame.

Mydei, with the marble face and voice like a locked door. Mydei, who smelled like dry cedar and pomegranate and always looked like he’d stepped out of a magazine called “I’m Better Than You.” Mydei, who, by some miracle of the divine, hadn’t ghosted him entirely. Or sued. Or called animal control.

“Did I actually—?” Phainon whispered, eyes fixed on the grimy floor. “No. Nooo.”

But the memory was there. Clear as day.

“He let me?” He frowned. “He didn’t stop me?”

A pause.

“Lord above, I’m a feral dog.”

The man sitting next to him adjusted his briefcase and leaned slightly to the side.

Phainon didn’t notice. Or didn’t care.

“If my mama were here,” he muttered, low and distant, “she’d whoop me back to last Sunday and call the church to get me re-baptized.”

He ran a hand down his face. Slumped even further down the seat, spine curved like a melting popsicle stick.

Another sigh.

Because really, what was he supposed to think? He hadn’t seen Mydei since that night—hadn’t even heard his voice. Just silence. And in that silence, Phainon had gone through every possible emotional reaction a man could fit into a two-day period. Regret. Horror. Denial. Grief. Hope. And now, this. The anxious purgatory of not knowing what the hell came next.

He didn’t think Mydei was the forgiving type. Didn’t strike him as someone who let things slide. Especially not accidental bite marks.

But then.

There’d been a text.

[Tomorrow. 10AM. Wear proper gear.]

That was it.

Phainon had stared at it for a long time. Double-checked the contact. Read it three more times just to be sure it wasn’t some weird dream artifact his brain had cooked up to make him feel worse.

But it had been real. Still was. Sitting there on his lockscreen, plain as day.

And now, here he was. On the train. On the way.

To meet the guy he’d bitten. To box. Probably.

He wasn’t even sure if it was a setup. Maybe Mydei was just luring him into some private ring so he could get even. Or maybe—worse—he was serious. About the boxing lesson. About the promise he’d made that night. The one Phainon could barely remember between all the noise and the way he’d pressed his cheek against Mydei’s shoulder like a fool.

“He’s really gonna teach me?” he mumbled now, dazed. “Off a promise to a drunken guy?”

Then, quieter.

“Nah. But then again…”

He glanced down at the screen. At the text.

“…He texted me.”

And yeah. There it was. That dumb flutter in his chest again. That spark of something he didn’t wanna name. Something warm. Bright. A little shy.

He sat up a little straighter before he could stop himself. Then immediately caught his own reflection in the window and forced his shoulders back down.

He didn’t like the guy. Not really. Not like that. Mostly. But maybe, deep down, he wanted to be liked. And to like him too. Just a little. Just enough.

Not that it mattered. He’d keep it normal. Keep it cool. No touching. No biting. No nothing.

Just two guys. Boxing. Sweatin’. Making physical contact in a closed, humid space.

He paused. Closed his eyes.

“Just a normal boxing lesson,” he muttered. “Totally not weird.”

A second later—

“…Real tight. Real close—alright cowboy, let’s not pass out on public transit.”

He gave the side of his head a firm little nudge against the window. Cold glass. Metal rattle. A deep, full breath.

Outside, the skyline dipped as the train curved north.

And Phainon couldn’t wait for his stop.

By the time Phainon stepped off the train, the morning had grown into itself —full and golden, just shy of noon heat. Sunlight bounced off windshields and glass windows, and the sidewalk shimmered faintly with that almost-summer glow.

He tugged his gym bag higher on his shoulder, adjusted the strap twice, and stood still for a moment on the corner. Let the day settle around him.

The gym was only a few blocks out, and he’d left early on purpose—half out of nerves, half out of that irritatingly earnest impulse to never be late, especially when someone was doing him a favor. So he strolled. Humming something tuneless under his breath, just enough to keep himself from overthinking again.

The neighborhood was nice. Fancy in a not-unpleasant way. Modest brownstones pressed shoulder to shoulder with minimalist storefronts, their windows displaying candles and tiny succulents in handmade clay pots.

Phainon passed a juice bar with its menu scrawled in pastel cursive on the window: 7-Day Cellular Reset. He gave it a once-over. Beside it, a café had half a dozen tiny tables lined up along the curb, each one perfectly spaced and cutesy. A green smoothie sat sweating on the farthest edge—abandoned or forgotten, hard to say.

He slowed as he passed it, squinting into the cup.

“…Is it still a smoothie if it’s got kale in it?” he asked quietly, side-eying it.

Half a block later, he stopped again—this time beside another storefront with shelves stacked full of tiny succulents in ceramic pots the size of shot glasses. One had a handwritten tag looped around the base: $34.

“Y’all are outta your minds,” he murmured, not unkindly, and moved on.

Every block had something else to look at, like a boutique with pyramid displays of hand-poured candles or a bookstore that only sold zines and hand-stitched journals. Phainon didn’t try to catalog it all. He just let it wash over him, steady and strange in its own beautiful way.

Phainon pulled out his phone again just to double-check the number. He glanced around, frowning faintly, not seeing anything that screamed gym. He took another few steps, peering up at the signage.

Then he spotted it.

Tucked snugly between a sleek vegan café and a co-working space that looked like it came with its own NFT consultant, was a set of understated frosted glass doors with no sign above them. Only a small plaque beside the handle read:

MEMBERS ONLY.

Phainon came to a full stop, tilted his head.

Let out a low whistle. “Well,” he said, under his breath, “this ain’t no Planet Fitness.”

The doors didn’t budge. No bell. No buzz. He shifted his bag, thumbed the edge of his hoodie sleeve. Stared at the glass like it might blink first.

Then, steadying himself, he rolled his shoulders back.

And reached for the handle.

The moment Phainon stepped inside, the noise of the street folded neatly behind him like someone had closed a book. The lobby smelled faintly of eucalyptus and something even softer under it—linen, maybe. Whatever it was, it had clearly been picked out of a catalog with names like Awaken or Serenity.

The lighting was low and warm, diffused across pale oak floors and sleek metal trim. No front-facing dumbbells or treadmill lineups were in sight. Just clean open space, high ceilings, and a few leather benches arranged meticulously. Across from them, a pane of glass revealed a studio where a man in athletic shorts was stretching deep into a split.

Phainon blinked. Then politely looked away.

At the front desk, a woman scrolled through a tablet with one manicured finger. Her blonde hair was clipped up behind her head, and a pair of thin reading glasses sat perched in her hair like a decoration. She looked up just long enough to let him know she’d seen him.

“Hey, uh—morning,” Phainon said, his voice polite. “I think I’m on the list? I’ve got a session. Someone’s supposed to be showin’ me around.”

Her eyes flicked back down to the tablet, scrolling with quiet confidence. “You’re here for a private?”

“Yess’m,” he said automatically, then caught himself. “Yeah. Private. Name’s Phainon. P-H-A—I mean. I’m with Mydeimos.”

That seemed to help. She tapped once, then nodded without looking up. “He’s in Studio Three.”

Phainon gave a quick smile, then paused mid-step when she didn’t elaborate. He hovered awkwardly for half a second before she added, calm as anything, “Down the hallway to your right. You’ll need the code he sent. Studio doors don’t open without it.”

“Oh. Right. Yeah. Got it.” He dug his phone out again. The text was still there, tucked between two weather alerts and a work reminder he’d ignored this morning:

[Use this to get in.]

Then a random string of numbers.

“Appreciate it,” he said as he moved past the desk, thumb already hovering over his screen.

Beyond the lobby, the hallway stretched out clean and hushed. He only heard the muffled sounds drifting from behind closed doors—sharp exhalations, the steady pop of padwork, and the hiss of someone counting in sets of four.

He passed a vending wall stocked with pre-chilled eucalyptus towels and vacuum-sealed protein bars labeled nootropic-enhanced. One of the protein drinks had a name he couldn’t pronounce. Another had no name at all—just a logo shaped like a water droplet trapped in a triangle.

He gave it a vaguely respectful nod and kept walking.

A man came around the corner wearing a fitted set of matching slate-gray gear, everything tone-matched from shirt to shoes. His eyes scanned Phainon briefly—hoodie, frayed sleeve, gym bag slung low. Then lower, down to his boots.

Phainon didn’t break stride.

But as he passed, he murmured without turning, “You got a retail tag hanging off your sleeve, brother.”

The man faltered mid-step behind him. Phainon kept walking, the corner of his mouth twitching once, then smoothing again.

He tapped his fingers lightly against his thigh, scanning the hallway.

“Studio Three…” he said under his breath, half to himself.

Studio One came first. Then Studio Two—door closed, a faint rhythmic thump behind it. And just past it, tucked to the right in a corner that might’ve been missed if you weren’t looking, sat a door marked with a simple, elegant plaque:

STUDIO 3

The same muted tones and a soft black keypad mounted to the wall beside it, waiting.

Phainon exhaled, pulled up the text again, and carefully tapped in the numbers.

3-3-5-0-0-3-3-6.

The keypad beeped. A small green light blinked once. The lock gave a soft mechanical click.

He stood there for a second longer, hand still resting against the handle. His shoulders had crept up again without asking, half-tense like he didn’t know if he was about to enter a sparring ring or an interview.

He rolled his neck once. Flexed his hand around the strap of his bag.

Then he pushed the door open and stepped inside.

The door clicked shut behind Phainon, sealing the studio into quiet.

The air inside was calmer somehow, padded floors dulling each step, the walls insulated just enough to hush the distant rhythm of the rest of the gym. He moved in slowly, taking in the room—mirrored panels lining one side, a rack of gear stacked neatly in the corner, and the soft ambient thud of someone hitting pads two rooms over.

Near the far wall, seated on a low bench and lacing up his shoes, was Mydei.

He was bent forward, sleeves cut high, the matte wraps already on his hands. The compression tank clung to him in a way that made it impossible not to notice how compact he was—muscle over lines, frame efficient without being bulky. The red ink on his forearm caught the overhead lights, sharpened into crisp brushstroke arcs that looked almost ceremonial in this lighting.

Phainon blinked. Then again.

And then smiled like someone who’d just found something rare on a high shelf.

“Well, damn,” he called out lightly. “Don’t you look good.”

Mydei didn’t glance up. “You’re late.”

Phainon stepped fully in. “I’m three minutes early.”

“You should’ve been five.”

“Alright then, Captain Punctual,” he muttered, setting his bag by the wall.

That earned him a glance—a brow raised like Phainon had just asked if stretching was optional. Then, without a word, Mydei picked up a pair of gloves from beside him and lobbed them across the room.

They hit Phainon’s chest with a soft thump. He caught them a beat later.

“Boot camp rules already?” he said, adjusting his grip.

“No talking. Wrap up.”

Phainon lifted one glove and held it between two fingers. “Over or under?”

Mydei sighed. He stood and crossed the mat in three steps, stopping in front of him like he’d decided doing it himself was faster than explaining.

“Hold still,” he said, pulling a wrap loose from the roll.

“I am holding still,” Phainon replied, eyes amused. “I’m being a model of pliability.”

“You’re still talking.”

“Now that’s just unfair.”

The wrap slid across Phainon’s knuckles, pulled snug with an even pressure that spoke of repetition. The fabric whispered with each pass—over the knuckles, across the palm, back again.

Phainon watched his hands more than the wrap itself.

“You always do this for your clients?” Phainon asked, voice light, but curious. “Wrap them up yourself, all gentle-like?”

Mydei’s glance was brief. “Only the ones who can’t follow directions.”

“Lucky me,” Phainon said, not bothering to hide the smile.

He looked down again, watching as Mydei guided the wrap across his hand.

“You always this good with your hands?” Phainon asked quieter.

Mydei didn’t look up. But the corners of his mouth twitched. “You’re not the first person to ask me that.”

Phainon huffed a laugh. “Guess I walked right into that one.”

“You think?”

He finished the final loop and tucked the edge into place, thumb pressing it down smooth. Then he stepped back—not far, but enough to give Phainon space to flex his fingers.

“There,” Mydei said. “Passable.”

Phainon held one hand up, admiring it like he was judging craftmanship. “You always tie up your enemies this gentle?”

“I thought we weren’t enemies anymore.”

That made him pause, just a fraction too long.

“…We’re not,” Phainon said, and it came out softer than he meant it.

So he added, quickly, “But I’m still suspicious. You look like a man who owns at least one decorative sword.”

Mydei blinked once. “Only one?”

“See? That’s exactly what I mean. That’s a red flag.”

Mydei tilted his head, nodding toward the mat. “Then by all means. Punch it out of me.”

Phainon gave a short laugh and moved to the center. “You sure you’re ready for that?”

“I was born ready.”

“Of course, angel.”

“I don’t hear you denying it.”

Phainon bounced lightly on the tip of his feet, rolling one shoulder back, grin starting to creep. “You like a challenge, huh?”

“I like shutting people up.”

“Oh honey,” Phainon drawled, hands lifting. “You really don’t wanna open that door.”

And this time, Mydei smiled.

Just enough.

Mydei tipped his chin toward the heavy bag, arms crossed. “Let’s see what you’ve got.”

Phainon exhaled, rolling out his shoulders like that might somehow shake the nerves loose. “You’re not gonna be impressed, city boy.”

“I don’t impress easy.”

Then, after a beat—almost offhand:

“But I’m watching.”

And Phainon really wished he hadn’t said it like that.

To be fair, Phainon hadn’t expected to be great.

He wasn’t waiting for a movie moment. No underdog montage, no sudden unlock of hidden muscle memory. He knew he was rusty—okay, maybe worse than rusty. His fists had weight but no discipline. Like someone handed a sledgehammer to a kid and said go nuts.

Still, he hadn’t thought he was this bad.

“Too much shoulder,” Mydei said again, voice calm and frustratingly consistent. “You’re loading your whole upper body before the punch. That’s a tell.”

Phainon grunted, shoulders rising and falling with uneven breath. “You could just say I suck.”

“You suck.”

Phainon snorted. “God, finally. Affirmation.”

The last half hour had been a blur of warm-up drills, footwork, and corrections. They’d skipped past anything flashy—Mydei had insisted on basics: stance, breath, movement. And when Phainon fumbled, which he had, repeatedly, Mydei didn’t scold—he simply noted. Adjusted. Watched.

“Your stance is too wide again,” Mydei added. “You’re losing power in the follow-through.”

Phainon shifted, dragging his foot in without much grace. “Guess muscle memory don’t count for much when all the muscle’s in the wrong place.”

“You’ve got power,” Mydei said, stepping forward. “But power without control gets you winded and hit.”

He crouched slightly and rapped two knuckles lightly against Phainon’s back foot. “Bring this in. You want tension through the hips, not your knees.”

Phainon did as told, watching him. “How do you even know all this?”

“I told you I trained,” Mydei replied. “And I read.”

“Of course you do,” Phainon muttered, shifting his balance as Mydei hovered close again.

“Ball of your foot. Push from the ground. Tight core, loose shoulders.” He spoke as he moved—light contact here and there to guide alignment. A tap to Phainon’s hip. A brush behind his elbow. “Throw a jab, slow.”

Phainon tried—right form, wrong rhythm.

“Breathe out on impact,” Mydei said. “You’ll gas out otherwise.”

Phainon tried again, exhaling on the punch this time. It felt weird. But Mydei watched, quiet, arms crossed.

“Again.”

He did it again.

And again.

And then once more.

After the fourth repetition, Mydei nodded. “That’s the start of a good habit.”

Phainon swiped his forearm across his brow. “You’re actually pretty patient. Beginners always get this treatment?”

“No.”

That caught him off guard—enough to glance over.

“You’re listening,” Mydei said, like it was an explanation and a surprise all at once.

“I mean… yeah,” Phainon said. “You didn’t have to do this. Most people don’t help unless they’re getting something back.” He shrugged, then winced at the pull on his shoulder. “So. Y’know. I appreciate it.”

And besides, when else was someone like him gonna get a one-on-one boxing lesson from someone who actually knows what they’re doing?

Mydei stilled slightly.

Something flickered across his face subtly—like the sincerity had caught him off guard.

He looked away, hand flexing once where it rested on his arm. “You’re sweating on my floor,” he said flatly. “Try not to make a puddle.”

Phainon smiled, shoulders easing back into his usual rhythm. “Awww, so you’re the type to get all soft when people say thank you.”

“I get irritated when they stop punching.”

“That so?” Phainon flexed his fingers, settling back into stance. “You ready for me to knock the bag off the chain?”

“You’re still leading with your shoulder,” Mydei said without missing a beat.

Phainon groaned. “You’re relentless.”

“I’m efficient.”

“Same thing.”

He lined up for another set—form tighter now, breath steadier. Mydei stood a few paces off, arms folded again, watching like a quiet metronome.

Jab.

Cross.

Jab. Step.

Cross. Reset.

Each hit sounded cleaner now. Less splash, more snap. He was trying his best to apply Mydei’s instructions into it.

And after a string of half-decent hits, he heard it:

“Better.”

Just that.

Phainon almost ruined the next punch out of pure surprise.

He straightened slowly, sweat glinting off his jaw, then glanced over. “So,” he said, trying to play it casual. “We moving on to the pads, coach?”

Mydei’s gaze flicked toward the wall where the mitts hung. A slow nod.

“If you think you’re ready.”

Phainon smirked. “Only one way to find out.”

The pads hit back.

Not literally, but Mydei could feel every blow thunder through his forearms. Phainon wasn’t polished—not by a long shot—but there was force behind every strike. Enough to jolt his elbows and pull a wince out of him when a hook slipped too far inside.

Mydei winced as the angle jarred his wrist. “Jesus. You trying to crack bone?”

Phainon laughed. “Where were you when I was breaking noses at thirteen?”

“Hopefully nowhere near Missouri.”

“‘Bout three hours south of St. Louis, actually,” Phainon fired back, curls sweat-damp and clinging to his forehead. His collar was stretched, shirt plastered to his back, and still he stayed light on his feet, bouncing in rhythm. No real finesse yet, but there was something laser-focused in his eyes. He was listening. Trying.

Mydei raised the left mitt, angled off-center. “Jab. Let it land before the cross. Don’t rush.”

Phainon obeyed without comment, landing a fast, precise punch.

Another. Then a cross. He missed the alignment and rotated off-balance.

“Again,” Mydei said. “Tighter core this time. You’re twisting from your waist.”

Phainon nodded once, shook out his arms, and tried again.

Better. Still clumsy, but centered now.

“Where’d you learn this anyway?” Mydei asked, adjusting his footing to shift the pad angle for a lead hook.

“Hm?” Phainon didn’t quite catch it, shoulders still working. He threw another combo before registering the question. “Oh. Myself, I guess. I wouldn’t call it learning. More like… had to.”

Mydei didn’t push, just gave a nod and repositioned his stance. “Someone picked on you?”

Phainon’s next hit struck clean. He reset, then shrugged with one shoulder as he circled around. “Not me. I mean, look at me.” He paused long enough to adjust his footing before adding, “It was Cyrene. Real small, scrappy thing. Smart. Got picked on for it. I got tired of watching it happen, so I started getting in the way.”

Mydei paused. Blinked.

“You started boxing to take hits for someone else.”

Phainon grinned. “More or less.”

“…So you’re a brawler.”

“Born and raised.”

Mydei shook his head, muttering something under his breath that might’ve been unbelievable. Still, he lifted the mitts again, a new glint in his eye. “Alright, brawler. Try this—one-two-slip-hook. And keep your damn chin tucked.”

Phainon gave a sharp nod, lips pressed tight in focus.

Mydei adjusted the mitts higher, watching him carefully.

“You’ve got power,” he said at last. “But you can’t just throw punches and hope they land. That hook earlier nearly over-rotated your front knee. If I were an opponent and not holding mitts—”

“You’d be on the floor?” Phainon teased, ducking under the pads with a quick slip.

Then he quickly added, “What about you? What got you into boxing?”

The question came just as he pivoted and faked low. Mydei’s stance was mid-shift when Phainon ducked inside with a soft laugh and clipped the edge of the mitt—

The angle hit just right. Mydei stumbled. Only a half step, but it was enough.

Phainon’s face lit up like Christmas in July. “Yes.”

Mydei blinked, stunned. “…You little sh—”

He cut himself off, closed his eyes, and exhaled through his nose like a man choosing peace.

“Don’t gloat.”

“Who’s gloating?” Phainon beamed, extending a hand, cocky as hell. “C’mon, you didn’t answer me.”

Mydei glanced down at the offered hand like it was bait—then took it anyway, grip firm and warm even as he grumbled under his breath.

“My parents hired a trainer,” he admitted. “Wanted me to be able to defend myself. In case something… ever came up.”

Phainon hummed as he helped him up, stepping back again as Mydei reset. “Smart. Big city like this… I’d imagine there’s a lotta folks who think they’ve got the right to get their hands on someone else.”

He said it lightly—but the words turned over in his mouth afterward, just a little heavier.

His eyes flicked toward Mydei. Watched the way his shoulders rolled back into stance.

Something in Phainon clenched—sour and unfamiliar at the sudden thought of Mydei getting hurt.

He looked away.

“So…” he drawled, “no praise for flooring your coach?”

“You cheated,” Mydei said flatly, still adjusting the mitts. “Absolutely not.”

“Excuses, excuses,” Phainon sang.

Mydei gave him a look. The kind of long, soul-deep stare that could flatten a less shameless man. It only made Phainon smile harder.

“You’re impossible.”

“And yet,” Phainon said brightly, “here you are.”

Mydei didn’t dignify that with a reply.

But as he lowered the mitts, Phainon caught it. Barely.

His lips pressed together in what was definitely meant to be irritation— except it crept just a little too close to a pout. The kind you’d never catch him admitting to, not even under oath.

Cute.

He’d never admit it—not in this life, or the next—but Phainon was absolutely going to remember that look. And chase it again.

Mydei stepped closer, close enough that Phainon felt it first in the shift of the air between them. His stance barely changed, but it still managed to feel like a push.

“Keep your guard up,” Mydei said. “I’m testing your shell—if I get in clean, that’s a point lost.”

Phainon nodded, adjusting without thinking. He pulled his gloves in tighter, forearms tucked in, elbows angled down. “You mean like this?”

“Almost,” Mydei said. Then, “Not quite.”

He stepped in with purpose, and they moved together—Mydei subtly guiding him with one hand at the small of his back until Phainon’s shoulders adjusted. The tension along the line made his spine straighten on instinct.

Tap. Tap.

Left rib, right rib.

Phainon twitched both times.

“Too stiff,” Mydei said. “Too reactive. Settle into it.”

“Easy for you to say,” Phainon muttered, shifting his weight. “Isn’t your sides getting flicked like that.”

“Don’t flinch.”

And then Mydei didn’t wait—he just reached out, took Phainon’s glove by the wrist, and shifted it across his torso.

It was all instructional. Just one guy correcting another guy’s form.

But they were chest-to-chest now. And when Mydei adjusted his footing to square them up, his thigh bumped lightly against Phainon’s knee, his hand sliding down from glove to forearm effortlessly.

“You’re tense,” Mydei said, glancing down, then up. “Relax your back foot. Rotate from the core.”

“Sure,” Phainon said, though his voice came out thinner than he meant. “Real relaxed here.”

He didn’t know what registered first—the heat of Mydei’s palm at his side, or the way Mydei braced one arm just above his shoulder, pressing in close without crowding. A fraction too near.

And Phainon, loud as he was, didn’t move.

Because Mydei hadn’t asked.

Then the hand at his hip shifted again. Thumb to waistband. A soft pressure.

Adjusting stance, yeah. Just more form-checking. That’s all.

But—

Right there.

A curve of muscle through his shirt. The sharp line of a collarbone, faint but obvious where the collar dipped wide. Not overly bulked out, but carved in.

And strong.

Really strong.

Phainon blinked hard. What the—?

That shouldn’t be catching his eye. That shouldn’t even be on the radar. He wasn’t—

No. Nope.

This was not the time to suddenly realize that Mydei—sugary coffee drinker, probably never touched a tractor in his life—was, objectively, more than capable of manhandling a guy like Phainon into proper form.

Which he was currently doing.

Casually.

With one hand.

How in the hell was that allowed?

Phainon could take a hit. He’d scrapped behind bleachers and rolled down hills and hauled livestock with a bum wrist. He was solid—nobody moved him unless he let them.

And yet here he was. Being shifted. Guided. Set like a damn prop.

And he felt it.

Felt it in the buzz under his ribs, in the brief flex at his core when Mydei’s hand skimmed down to correct his hip angle again. Felt it in the quiet voice in the back of his head whispering something ridiculous like: okay, cool, yeah, maybe you’re into this now, congrats.

Internally: blank panic.

Externally: still.

Too still.

Mydei said something—probably another cue about stance—but it passed through Phainon’s brain like water through a sieve.

Since when do people born in a skyline end up this built? This steady?

He’d figured Mydei for the sharp-tongued type—quick with a jab, but more bark than brawn. The kind of guy who leaned on attitude, not muscle. Not someone who could square up and make it stick.

It didn’t add up.

And yet, here they were. Him, pinned by eye contact and a single hand on his hip. Mydei, cool as ever, still adjusting his posture like this wasn’t illegal levels of close.

Okay, Phainon thought, mouth dry. Okay cool great awesome I think I just developed a kink. Excellent. Love that for me.

He went a little red.

Then very red.

Then snapped upright so fast he nearly clocked Mydei with his own glove.

“So!” he chirped, far too brightly. “How’m I doing now, coach? Still pivoting like a deer on moonshine, or am I up to a mildly sober elk?”

He facepalmed internally. How’m? Sober elk???

Mydei, halfway through re-strapping the mitts, paused.

He looked up.

“…Are you okay?”

“Peachy.” Phainon nodded fast. Too fast. “Better than peachy. Plum good, even.”

Mydei squinted. “Did you hit your head.”

“Not that I noticed. Unless this is one of those shady tactics where you elbowed me when I wasn’t looking.”

“I would’ve aimed higher.”

“See? Shady.”

A long, flat stare.

Phainon grinned, all teeth.

“Alright,” Mydei muttered. “Get back in stance.”

Phainon bounced back like an overexcited retriever who knew he’d done something wrong but didn’t want to admit it.

Because yeah—he felt weirdly guilty.

He wasn’t supposed to be noticing things. Not like that. Not here. Mydei was just trying to help. Just being professional. And Phainon—

Mydei stepped back, arms lowering as he studied Phainon—eyes too wide, stance too springy for someone who’d just been drilled. Too much energy. Not enough guard.

Then, without a word, he stripped off the pads and tossed them aside with a lazy flick of the wrist. “Wanna spar?”

Phainon blinked. “Wait—seriously?”

Mydei’s mouth ticked, just slightly. “Might be the only way to get you to focus.”

Phainon lit up, grinning as he pointed a gloved finger toward him. “You’re feeling real confident for someone about to eat canvas.”

“Keep talking,” Mydei said, already turning. “I’ll knock the vowels outta that accent.”

Phainon laughed, quick on his heels. “Good luck. Dad raised me too damn proud to quit on a consonant.”

The rules were simple.

Thirty percent strength, nothing stupid.

Phainon stretched his arms, beaming. Mydei just rolled his shoulders. His stance was economical—tight guard, chin tucked, elbows in. He tilted his head slightly.

Phainon mirrored him, looser, more relaxed.

They started slow. Footwork first. Just the shuffle and slide of sneakers on canvas. Mydei circled tight, forcing Phainon to pivot, to follow—testing his balance. His gaze swept sharp over Phainon’s form, calculating.

Phainon adjusted quickly. Saw the look, narrowed his eyes, and drew his guard up. “That all you got?”

Mydei didn’t answer.

He just hit.

It was fast—more a flick than a punch, snapping clean toward Phainon’s lead shoulder. Phainon blocked, stumbled a half-step, and caught himself with a grunt.

They reset. Circled again. The rhythm building, small and tense.

Phainon fainted a hook and chuckled when Mydei didn’t bite. “Am I making you show off?”

“Focus.”

Then Mydei tested him again—a lead punch, low cross toward the ribs. Not hard, but precise. Phainon caught one, missed the other.

“Shit—”

“Eyes up. You’re telegraphing with your weight.”

“Bossy today,” Phainon muttered.

He launched a quick combo—two light jabs and a hook that just skimmed Mydei’s shoulder. “Gotcha!”

Mydei didn’t flinch. He dipped his frame low, pivoted his hips, and drove a tight counter into Phainon’s ribs. Not hard—but a compact shot that knocked the air out of him.

“So did I,” Mydei said.

Phainon wheezed. “Damn. Okay.”

Their movement quickened. Phainon’s footwork started to clean up, weight moving more naturally across the his feet. Mydei adjusted his rhythm in response, his body angling closed, forcing tighter turns. A new layer of sweat bloomed across their skin.

Mydei pressed in with more hits and Phainon blocked most of them, though one clipped his side again. He circled, breathing hard, and caught Mydei off-guard with a low body feint and tight inside hook.

Mydei ducked, caught it with a tucked elbow, and came back in close.

Too close.

They bumped. Glove to glove, shoulder to chest. Neither backed off.

“Y’know,” Phainon said, “for thirty percent, you hit like you holdin’ a grudge.”

“Move your damn feet.”

They collided again on the next turn. Mydei’s hand came up to adjust Phainon’s elbow—again—and Phainon found himself swallowing hard.

The rhythm was starting to fray.

Phainon slipped in confidently, launched a cross—and then his back foot slid out from under him.

Sweat. Canvas. Bad luck.

“Fu—”

He pitched forward, flailing for balance—and reflexively grabbed the closest thing to him.

Which happened to be Mydei’s arm.

Who was not expecting to be full-body yanked by a man with the center of gravity of a linebacker.

They crashed hard. A messy, tangled sprawl of limbs, gloves, and noise.

THUD.

Mydei barely caught himself, one arm braced firm above Phainon’s head. Their gloves ended up squished between them. Phainon’s knee was somewhere near Mydei’s hip. Someone’s foot might’ve been under someone’s thigh. It didn’t matter. They were close.

Close in the kind of way that made time get weird.

Phainon blinked up at him, dazed.

“…Hi,” he breathed.

Mydei blinked back. Like he was rapidly updating several mental spreadsheets.

Phainon smiled, sweat-stupid. “So. You come here often?”

A beat. Mydei made a noise—tight, like a laugh jammed between his teeth —and shoved himself up in one smooth, aggressively neutral motion.

He turned so fast Phainon didn’t catch his face. But his ears?

Yeah. Red.

Phainon sat up a second later, slower, rubbing at the back of his neck. “You okay? That was kinda a trust fall, but like, with malice.”

No answer.

Just the echo of their breath. The soft pad of Mydei’s footsteps. The thump of a glove hitting the bench.

Phainon exhaled, still smiling faintly—right up until—

His stomach let out a full-bodied, open-mouth scream. Like it had been personally wronged.

“…Oh, come on.”

Mydei turned. Slowly. With the full weight of judgment on his face.

“…You didn’t eat?”

Phainon paused. “I—uh. I don’t usually do breakfast?”

That wasn’t the right answer.

Mydei stared. Silent.

“…Are you an idiot?”

Phainon blinked. “Wh—I mean, probably?”

Mydei dragged a hand through his hair, eyes briefly closing like someone mentally updating a file titled Stupid Things Phainon Has Done. “You can’t spar without eating.”

“I didn’t know we were gonna spar!”

“I did.”

“You escalated!”

“We’re done.”

“What—but—”

“Shower.” Mydei’s voice cut like glass. He was already stripping his gloves. “Then food.”

Phainon mumbled, “fine,” and peeled himself off the mat, stomach still muttering threats. His face was pink, his ribs ached, and his hair was sticking to the side of his head.

Mydei was already walking away. Too fast. Too rigid.

Phainon followed—warm, sore, and still deeply, deeply confused.

And maybe just a little bit smug.

Because he might’ve lost, but at least he got to watch Mydei flustered.

The showers were private. Marble-walled, echo-soft, and so spotless Phainon felt like he was gonna get fined just for tracking water on the tile. He’d whistled low under his breath the second the door swung shut behind him.

Down the row, Mydei’s stall had shut with a firm, definitive thunk.

Now, fresh out and changed into a fitted tee and the least-wrinkled pair of jeans he’d managed to fold into his bag, Phainon stretched until his spine cracked, then flopped down onto one of the wooden benches lining the back of the locker room.

Real wood, too.

He leaned forward, elbows braced on his knees, and let his head tip back with a quiet exhale. His skin still felt warm from the steam. He blinked at the ceiling. Waited.

Totally normal thoughts.

Like how nice the water pressure was. Or how the shampoo didn’t smell like pennies. Or how—

Yeah okay, he’d absolutely seen Mydei toweling off on the way out. Brief glance, totally accidental, totally unimportant. It wasn’t like his brain had short-circuited at the sight of that towel hanging too low on his hips, or the long slope of his back, or the—

Phainon groaned and dropped his face into both hands. His voice came out muffled. “Lord, take me now.”

His hands slid down to his jaw. His eyes were fixed dead ahead.

And the worst part? That bite mark. Still there, faded into the side of Mydei’s neck. That little bruise he’d left behind like a damn calling card.

What the hell was he even supposed to say? Sorry I treated your shoulder like a chew toy while you were doing me a favor? My bad, thanks for the ride dude?

Maybe it was fine. Maybe he could just pretend he hadn’t seen it. Mydei hadn’t said a word about it, after all—

“Hey.”

Phainon flinched so hard he nearly fell off the bench.

He turned fast. Mydei stood a few paces away, toweling his damp hair one last time before slinging it around his neck. He was wearing loose joggers and a soft colored crewneck. His long hair curled around his collar and temples in damp waves.

Honestly, he looked… stupidly cute. Catlike. Tired but sleek, soft-edged, domestic in a way Phainon wasn’t emotionally prepared for.

“Hey,” Phainon said back.

Mydei walked over and sat beside him. Not close, but not far either.

Phainon started to say something, then paused as Mydei bent over his bag.

He rummaged for a second. Then pulled something out—a large bento box. He didn’t look at Phainon, just held it between them for a beat.

Phainon tilted his head, brows lifting. Still smiling, faint and puppy-eyed.

A few seconds passed.

Then Mydei sighed through his nose. “…Well?” he muttered. “Are you gonna take it or not?”

Phainon blinked. “Wait—this for me?”

Mydei’s only answer was to push the box gently into his hands, then turn his face away like he hadn’t just gifted him the Holy Grail.

Phainon blinked down at it. “Uh. Thanks?”

He popped the lid.

Immediately the scent hit him—fresh and warm and herby. There were grilled chicken skewers nestled over lemon rice, roasted red peppers drizzled with olive oil, a little side of cucumber-tomato salad, and a neat container of soft, folded pita with hummus on the side. Still faintly warm. Homemade, but practical. Packed to travel. Thoughtful.

Phainon’s stomach let out a traitorous growl again.

“This smells amazing,” he murmured, wide-eyed. “Where’d you get it?”

“I made it,” Mydei said simply.

Phainon looked up, stunned. “Really?”

His face practically lit up. Like someone’d just handed him a puppy and told him it was his.

Mydei didn’t meet his eyes. Just adjusted his sleeve. “Eat.”

“Right,” Phainon said, grinning now. “Yes sir.”

He picked up a skewer and bit in. A little hum left him before he could stop it. “Oh man. That’s so good. Like, restaurant good. You sure you ain’t hiding a second job?”

Mydei gave him a side glance, dry. “I barely have time for the first.”

Phainon snorted—and paused. Then carefully shifted some of the food onto the lid and set it in Mydei’s lap.

“I’m not hungry.”

“Sure you aren’t,” Phainon said.

Mydei gave him a look that should’ve been withering. Should’ve.

Phainon met it head-on. Then leaned over, picked up a piece of pita, and held it out. Just hovering, deliberate.

Mydei squinted. “Don’t.”

Phainon tilted his head. “You sure?”

Mydei opened his mouth—to argue, probably—but in that exact second Phainon popped the bite in.

It landed. Right in his mouth.

Mydei froze.

Chewed. Slowly.

Then narrowed his eyes, murderous. “You—”

“You what?” Phainon provoked.

“That was ambush by carb.”

Phainon gave him a bright, innocent look. “Food tastes better when it’s shared.”

“That’s not how you share.”

“Mm. Sounds like someone’s scared of losing.”

Mydei stiffened like someone had struck a nerve. “Scared?”

Phainon’s smile deepened. “Bullseye.”

There was a pause. And then, flatly: “Who the hell do you think you’re talking to?”

Phainon just shrugged, lips twitching. “Guess we’ll find out.”

He popped another bite into his own mouth. “Whoever finishes their half first wins.”

“Wins what?”

Phainon beamed. “Bragging rights. Eternal glory. My undying admiration.”

Mydei narrowed his eyes. Then, without a word, picked up a skewer and started eating.

Phainon watched him.

Yeah. He’d baited him clean.

Mydei was too easy sometimes.

Internally? He was cackling.

Externally?

He offered Mydei the last piece of pita like a peace treaty.

“You’re an idiot,” Mydei muttered.

But he took it anyway.

Phainon had won their little food competition.

He’d been extremely humble about it.

Which meant, of course, that he threw both arms in the air like he’d just clinched Olympic gold, then offered Mydei a victory handshake with the kind of smirk that made it very clear he was trying not to wiggle his eyebrows.

To his credit, Mydei only rolled his eyes once before muttering, “Shut up and finish chewing.”

Phainon did—happily, hungrily, and with absolutely no further commentary except for the occasional satisfied hum.

Later, when the bento was packed away and their water bottles sat half-drained between them, Mydei checked the time. He said it casually, like it was nothing. “There’s a library a few blocks from here. I need to return something.”

Phainon looked up, eyes wide. “Wait—you can read?”

Mydei froze mid-motion like someone had just slapped the book out of his hand. He turned slowly, expression still with offense.

“I graduated top of my class,” he said, voice deadly calm. “In three languages.”

“Yeah, yeah,” Phainon waved him off. “But like—reading for fun?”

“I own a library card.”

“Oh, so you’re a nerd on purpose.”

Mydei stared at him. “Do you want to get hit again?”

“What, with a book? Go on then, Shakespeare, make it hurt.”

Mydei glared.

Phainon cracked—doubling over with laughter, nearly falling off the bench in the process.

So now they were walking.

The sidewalk shimmered faintly in the late-summer heat. Sunlight pooled gold along the edges of the road, filtered through the soft haze of trees and mid-rise buildings. A lazy breeze stirred Mydei’s hair as they turned down a quieter block—less traffic, more dog walkers. Phainon had picked up another story somewhere along the way and was mid-recital, his hands carving through the air with a kind of full-body enthusiasm that suggested he’d been waiting all day for someone to listen.

Every few steps, he drifted too close—shoulder brushing, sleeves grazing, a gesturing arm bumping Mydei’s side before flinching back with a sheepish “my bad.”

If it bothered Mydei, he didn’t show it.

They passed under a row of sycamores shedding early leaves, past a hot dog cart steaming on a corner, past a window full of handmade earrings shaped like frogs. The scent of fresh mulch and burnt sugar wafted from somewhere—maybe a food truck or someone’s backyard grill.

“So anyway,” Phainon was saying, “I dared Caelus to eat a raw egg like a shot, and he did, but then Stelle got mad ‘cause it was her egg and she wanted to throw it at a goose. Long story.”

Mydei blinked at him. “…That was the trimmed version?”

Phainon pointed a finger. “Hey. The long version involves raccoons and a porch swing. I’m doing you a kindness.”

“I’m not convinced.”

“Listen, it was a tense time. Emotions were high.”

“…Why was she throwing eggs at geese?”

“I think one hissed at her wrong. Girl’s got vendettas.”

Mydei made a quiet sound that might’ve been a laugh—just barely there.

“They’re twins,” Phainon added as they crossed at a sleepy intersection. “Caelus and Stelle. Grew up with them. Used to call them my partners in crime, but they kinda dropped the ‘partner’ part once I left town.”

He didn’t say it with any sadness—but there was something softer in the way he smiled. Something a little homesick around the corners.

“Any stories like that from when you were a kid?” he asked as they passed beneath a canopy of rustling leaves. “Y’know. Dumb stuff.”

Mydei tilted his head, thinking.

Then: “I once broke my cousin’s nose at a wedding.”

Phainon’s eyebrows flew up. “Oh.”

“It was an accident,” Mydei added. “Mostly.”

“…Mostly??”

“He tried to put cake down the back of my shirt.”

“That warrants a felony?”

“It was reflex. He learned about consequences.”

Phainon squinted at him. “You were the kid who decked grown men in dodgeball, weren’t you.”

Mydei’s silence said everything.

Up ahead, nestled between ivy-covered buildings and a crooked fence lined with overgrown basil, sat a cozy brick library with tall windows and a wooden door worn smooth by years of use. Sycamores lined the front walk. A rusted bike rack stood crooked near the curb. The sign above the door read: GARBANIPHORO LIBRARY in hand-painted letters, half-faded by sun.

Phainon slowed, eyes lighting up. “Well damn. This is cute.”

He reached for the door and swung it open with a small flourish, then stepped aside, sweeping his arm low in an exaggerated half-bow.

“After you, sire.”

Mydei raised a brow. “You’re joking.”

“Never.”

Still dry as ever, Mydei stepped past him and into the cool, quiet hush of polished wood and old paper.

Phainon followed, smile still lingering as the door clicked shut behind them.

The library looked smaller from the outside.

Red brick, ivy trailing down its edges, and an old hanging lantern above the door made it seem more like a neighborhood bookshop than anything else —something half-forgotten, wedged between a pastry café and an insurance office on a side street no one meant to walk down. You’d miss it if you weren’t looking for it. That felt intentional.

The kind of place you didn’t find unless someone told you where to look.

Inside, though, it stretched open in a way that didn’t match the modest exterior. Cool air greeted them—tinged with old wood, tea leaves, and maybe something floral tucked into a corner somewhere. Rows of narrow bookshelves unfolded ahead like ribs, vanishing beneath vaulted ceilings ribbed with beams. Dust swam through sunlight from high-set windows. Ancient ceiling fans turned in slow, creaky rhythm. Wooden ladders leaned against shelves like they’d grown roots there.

Phainon stood still for a moment, just… taking it in.

He’d expected cozy. But this wasn’t just cozy. It was lived-in. Safe in a way most places in the city weren’t.

A silver-haired woman looked up from behind a tall desk, a thick book spread open in front of her. Round glasses perched low on her nose. Her braid was streaked with gray and curled at the end. She wore a faded cardigan and a look that knew everything without asking.

She smiled.

“Well,” she said, voice soft and amused. “Look who actually brought it back on time.”

“I always do,” Mydei replied, defensive.

“Sure you do.” She glanced over at Phainon, eyes twinkling. “And what’s this? You bringing home strays now?”

Mydei said nothing. But Phainon beamed.

“Yes, ma’am. He feeds me and everything,” he said cheerfully, tipping his imaginary hat.

The woman laughed under her breath and turned back to her book.

Mydei walked toward the desk, pulling a slim volume from the crook of his arm. Phainon trailed behind a little slower, eyes skating over the tall bookshelves and faded rugs, the tucked-away nooks with mismatched chairs, the chalkboard sign above the tea cart that read No cell phones, No noise, Yes baklava.

He liked it here.

There was something gentle about the way the place breathed.

He found a narrow bench near the front and sat while Mydei returned his book. When he circled back around, he didn’t look in a rush to leave.

“I’m gonna stay a while,” Mydei said. “You don’t have to—if you’ve got things.”

Phainon blinked. “And miss you willingly interacting with printed words? Nah, I’m good.”

Mydei gave him a faintly unimpressed glance but said nothing.

They drifted in deeper together, past rows labeled “Modern Fiction” and “Translated Works,” until the shelves grew older and the wood underfoot shifted from bright pine to a darker, more honeyed oak.

Eventually, they split without needing to say anything.

Mydei peeled off toward the back corner where “History/Cultural Studies” stretched in tall, slender shelves.

Phainon meandered slower.

He paused near a squat display stand and tilted his head.

Dogs of the World.

“Well don’t mind if I do,” he murmured, flipping the cover open.

He wandered slowly as he read. It was mostly pictures—big-eyed shaggy things and majestic breeds with names he couldn’t pronounce. Somewhere in there was a Samoyed that looked like Snowy, which made him smile a little too fondly.

He was halfway through a spread on herding dogs when something in his peripheral vision tugged him sideways.

Mydei. Settled into a corner armchair beneath one of the taller lamps. Book open, legs stretched out comfortably, already deep in whatever page he’d flipped to.

Phainon wandered over. Tucked the dog book under his arm.

“Hey,” he said. “Scoot.”

Mydei didn’t look up. “Seriously?”

Phainon leaned a little closer, nudging his elbow. “The chair’s wide enough if you don’t manspread.”

“It’s not wide enough for you,” Mydei muttered. But he shifted over. Barely. Begrudgingly.

That was all the invitation Phainon needed.

He wedged himself in with a little laugh, shoulder bumping against Mydei’s. Their thighs touched. He let out a slow exhale, flipping open his book again like this was a normal, reasonable arrangement.

Mydei finally glanced sideways. Faintly long-suffering.

Phainon stifled a yawn. “Told you I was staying.”

Mydei, after the interruption, seemed content to retreat behind his book like nothing had happened.

Phainon gave it thirty seconds.

Then he bumped his shoulder. Light, at first.

“Whatcha reading?”

Nothing.

He bumped him again, a little firmer this time. “Hey. You gonna be like that?”

Still no reaction.

“Alright,” he murmured, leaning in until their arms touched fully. “Now I gotta see what’s got you so enthralled.”

He peered over the pages.

The text was dense—black ink on thin paper, written in sharp strokes. A few of the letters looked Greek. Others didn’t. It was structured but unfamiliar, like something regionally specific.

“…What’s that?”

Mydei turned the page slowly. “Kremnoan dialect.”

Phainon blinked. “Kremnoan?”

A pause. Then his face brightened in recognition. “Ohh, like your company. Castrum Kremnos. That’s where the name comes from, right?”

“Roughly,” Mydei said. “The dialect’s older than the company. Older than the state, even.”

Phainon whistled under his breath. “So you’re not just into history,” he said, leaning back a little. “You’re into your history.”

Mydei’s fingers hovered over the edge of the page.

“…Heritage,” he corrected eventually. “Not history.”

Phainon blinked again, the distinction settling around him. He tilted his head, brow furrowed.

“Huh,” he said. “That’s actually kinda— I mean. That’s cool. Like, really cool.”

He rubbed the back of his neck. “Kremnoans, huh? That’s some lineage. Weren’t they the mountain types? Spartan-adjacent? Real quiet, real tough?”

Mydei’s mouth twitched like he was trying not to smile. “Something like that.”

“Damn.” Phainon chuckled. “You don’t do anything halfway, do you.”

Something in Mydei’s tone must’ve cracked something open—because before Phainon could think twice, he was saying:

“My folks came from Arcadia,” he said. “Long time ago. It’s more sheep pastures and shepherd’s flutes than tactical warfare, but—” He shrugged. “There’s pride in it, I guess. We always said that’s where the garden gene came from. Growing things. Sticking close to the land.”

“…Arcadia,” Mydei repeated, like he was turning it over in his mouth.

“Yeah. All the old paintings make it look like some peaceful paradise— green hills, fig trees, people laying around playing music. Real life probably meant dirt and chasing goats. Still.” He smiled faintly. “There’s worse things to come from.”

Mydei glanced back down at his page—but only for a moment. “You don’t talk like someone who knows old dialects.”

“Well,” Phainon said, bumping him again, this time more affection than teasing, “I got outvoted. None of the Greek stuck past my papou’s generation. Just the food and the guilt.”

That earned him a quiet laugh.

Phainon tilted his head toward the book again. “You think you could teach me a little?”

Mydei looked over at him.

Phainon wasn’t being rude. His eyes were curious. There was no mockery, no false play at being impressed. Just a kind of eagerness that snuck under your skin.

Mydei studied him for a long moment, then shut the book halfway.

“Fine,” he said. “But don’t waste my time.”

Phainon lit up. “Yes, sir.”

They’d had too good a time in that damn library.

What started as a joke—a single word Phainon had mispronounced so badly it made Mydei pause and visibly reconsider his life—had unraveled into a full-on, half-messy, half-earnest study session tucked between the warm, worn stacks of books. The quiet was filled with whisper-fighting and muffled laughter, Phainon’s increasingly flustered “I am saying it right” clashing against Mydei’s muttered corrections and exasperated sighs that somehow carried the weight of fondness.

It was, to Phainon’s surprise, kind of magical.

The library light had shifted slowly as they spoke, the late afternoon sun slipping gold through the dusty high windows. Neither of them noticed the hour until the librarian passed by again with the gentlest throat clear in the world. They both paused then, blinking like they’d just come up for air.

Still, neither quite moved.

Eventually, Mydei closed his book—fingers lingering a beat too long on the edge of the page—and Phainon tucked his dog encyclopedia under his arm. They returned their borrowed items, waved the librarian a quiet goodbye (Mydei with a polite nod, Phainon with a bright, dimpled smile), and stepped out into the hum of a Chicago evening.

It was warm and breezy, the sky going soft at the edges.

They walked without a real destination.

“Meant to show you this earlier,” Phainon said after a few steps, tugging his phone from his pocket.

He swiped a few times, then turned the screen toward Mydei. “Here. One of the few good pics I’ve actually got.”

It was a sunlit photo, taken on a field somewhere—wild grass up to their knees. Three figures. A girl in scuffed boots, lean and smiling; a younger Phainon with an unfortunate haircut and both arms outstretched; and a blur of white fur in the middle, tongue out, tail mid-wag.

“That’s Cyrene,” Phainon said proudly, tapping the left side. “And that’s me, obviously, before I had the sense to get a proper trim. And that’s Snowy.” He zoomed in on the dog’s fuzzy face. “Tell me he ain’t the cutest damn thing you’ve ever seen.”

Mydei didn’t answer.

Phainon glanced over. “What?”

Mydei’s eyes hadn’t moved from the screen. When he spoke, his voice was quiet. “Yeah,” he said. “Cute.”

Phainon beamed. “Right?? Look at those dumb little paws. He used to sneak into the barn and try to herd the goats. No fear, all floof.”

Mydei huffed. Phainon caught it.

But then the moment slowed. They kept walking, quieter now.

Phainon hesitated. His voice dropped, not dramatic, just suddenly sincere. “Hey… thanks.”

Mydei glanced at him.

Phainon rubbed the back of his neck. “For hanging out with me today. I know I kinda… crashed your morning with the whole boxing thing. And I talk a lot. And I’m real good at making everything take three times as long.”

“You’re also terrible at pronunciation,” Mydei added helpfully.

Phainon laughed. “That too.”

A pause. Then softer: “But I had a good time. It meant a lot. So. Yeah.”

They came to a stop at the corner, waiting for the crosswalk to change. The sun had dipped lower now, turning the sidewalk golden. A light breeze blew past, brushing warm air against their arms and hair.

Mydei turned slightly to face him. His expression was strange—but he was looking.

Really looking.

And Phainon felt it—like heat humming under his skin. He stepped a little closer without meaning to.

They didn’t say anything. Didn’t have to.

And maybe, if nothing had interrupted them, one of them might have done something about it.

But—

“Oh fuck,” Phainon whispered.

He yanked Mydei back by the wrist like a man trying to dodge a sniper. “Quick—bus stop—hide—now.”

Mydei, entirely off-balance, stumbled behind him. “What the hell—?”

“It’s Caenis,” Phainon hissed, flattening himself against the side of the shelter. “Hide. Pretend to be dead. Be the wind.”

Mydei blinked. “Who the hell is Caenis?”

“My boss,” Phainon groaned. “And today, I may have taken off work to frolic through Chicago with you. And by may, I mean I did. Even though she said all hands on deck because of some big Kremnoan exec drop-in.”

“You didn’t check the calendar?”

“I don’t live by a calendar, I live by the sun and consequences—move—”

They ducked out again, zig-zagging past a man with a double stroller and around a food cart selling mango slices. Mydei’s phone nearly flew from his hand as Phainon pulled him along with purpose and the silent desperation of a hunted animal.

Which was exactly why he didn’t see the woman with the stack of cardboard boxes until she stepped right into his path.

“Oh ma’am—I am so sorry—”

The impact was light, but enough to topple the uppermost box. Phainon’s grip slipped from Mydei as he immediately dropped to a crouch.

“Lemme help—shoot, you okay?” He was already scooping up the papers scattered across the sidewalk.

The woman blinked in surprise, then smiled. “Sorry—I’m fine, don’t worry.”

“Still, I should’ve been watching where I was going—wasn’t your fault at all, ma’am, promise.” Phainon handed her the final sheet of printed graphs and smiled sheepishly.

And then he looked up.

And over the top of her shoulder—

Caenis.

Impeccable black heels. Silhouetted suit. Cold, stunning expression. Cutting across the sidewalk like a glacier in Louboutin.

Staring straight at him.

Phainon froze like a deer on an open highway.

Then he blinked fast, crammed the last binder into the woman’s stack, and patted it like it was a horse being sent off to pasture. “You have a real lovely evening now,” he said in a single breath, already turning.

He walked stiffly back to Mydei, who was waiting with his arms crossed and one unimpressed brow raised.

“Maybe she didn’t see me,” Phainon muttered.

“She looked directly at you.”

“Yeah, but like, looked, or recognized?”

“You are the only person in a three-block radius dressed like a rancher going to a PTA meeting.”

“Rude.”

And then—

click. click. click.

The sound of Caenis’s heels, echoing closer.

Phainon closed his eyes and looked up. “I once skipped Uncle Davis’s funeral to avoid a land dispute with my aunt over fifty feet of pig-barn siding,” he muttered grimly. “If the Good Lord didn’t smite me then, this might finally be it.”

Mydei side-eyed him. “What the hell is wrong with you?”

“Silence, fiend.”

Phainon didn’t want to turn.

He stood still, half a breath longer.

He exhaled, smoothed down his shirt with one palm, and finally turned.

“…Miss. Hello,” he said, forcing the corners of his mouth up into something polite.

Caenis stood before him in a tailored cream blazer and pointed heels that clicked far too quietly.

“Phainon,” she said, like she’d discovered a toy she forgot she owned. “Small city.”

“Heh,” he chuckled, a little breathless. “Real small.”

Her eyes dipped down his frame—his creased gym tee, the empty duffel bag slung over one shoulder—then flicked back up, the same smile still in place.

“You’ve been keeping busy, I see.”

Phainon shifted his weight. “Just squeezing in a little training. Trying to stay active. You know how it goes.”

“I do,” she said pleasantly. “I just didn’t expect you to.”

He faltered, smile hitching.

“But it’s good you’re getting out,” she went on. “That’s healthy. I always say a strong body helps with a clear head.” She gestured idly to his duffel. “Of course, not everyone needs a clear head at work.”

Phainon blinked. “Sorry?”

She waved it off. “Oh, don’t worry. It’s just—we’ve all been adjusting, I know. Some of us faster than others.”

He tried not to bristle. He was still smiling. Still holding the bag strap. “I really didn’t mean to miss the in-person,” he said. “Thought the exec wasn’t coming until later—guess I got the wrong message.”

Her brows rose. “Did you?”

The pause hung.

“I suppose that explains the two emails you missed. And the dashboard ticket that still hasn’t moved since last Thursday.”

He opened his mouth. Then shut it again.

Caenis just smiled, like she hadn’t said anything at all.

She tilted her head. “We’ve always appreciated your… charisma, Phainon. You’ve got a nice way of putting people at ease. People like that—until they need results.”

Phainon’s gut twisted. “I’m—sorry, I didn’t mean to let anybody down.”

“Of course not,” she replied quickly. “You wouldn’t. You just… don’t really know what’s expected of you yet.”

His mouth went dry.

“You’ve got heart,” she continued, lightly. “And that’s rare. But that’s not always enough. Not when you don’t quite have the instincts yet. Or the polish.”

It hit like a compliment. Sounded like advice.

Felt like a kick.

Phainon swallowed. “I’m trying to learn. Fast as I can.”

“I’m sure you are. But there’s learning,” she said gently, “and there’s keeping up. Most of the team doesn’t have time to hold hands. Especially with all the structural things you’ve missed—well. I know it’s a lot. You didn’t grow up with this kind of pace.”

She smiled again. No malice in sight. Just concern.

“Back home, I’m sure you did great. But here, in the real world, the market’s a little sharper. People don’t wait.”

He flinched, barely.

A quiet heat was curling up behind his ribs. Shame. And something worse.

She doesn’t know me.

But he didn’t say it. Because what would be the point?

She wouldn’t understand the hours he worked scraping paint off barns in ninety-degree heat. The time he slept on a friend’s floor to save for rent. How he patched up Cyrene’s FAFSA forms by hand and sat on hold with health insurance for three hours last week just to get an ID reissued.

How he had ambition. She just couldn’t see it past his accent.

He clenched his jaw. He was smiling. He was still smiling.

“I’m just trying to do my best,” he muttered, eyes on the sidewalk.

“And we appreciate that,” Caenis said brightly. “It’s just—if your best is what we’ve seen, then maybe we should talk about setting more realistic goals.”

Phainon didn’t respond. He couldn’t.

He was angry.

Hot with it, under the collar, in the chest. But there was nothing to do with it. Nowhere to put it. He needed this job. He needed next month’s paycheck, and the one after that. He needed the insurance, the network. He needed not to piss off a woman who could quietly get him reassigned into obscurity.

But God, it stung.

And it stung worse because Mydei was here.

Because he’d seen it.

Because Phainon was standing in front of him looking like some dumbass hayseed who didn’t know how to answer emails. Like he was soft. Small. Like a child trying to dress up for an interview he didn’t deserve.

“I’m only saying this,” Caenis said, as if wrapping a bow on it, “because I know you mean well. And I want you to grow.”

“Right,” Phainon muttered. “Thanks.”

She adjusted the strap on her purse, preparing to pivot with some final, gracious remark—and then:

“Is there a problem?”

The voice was a blade.

Phainon blinked. His head turned slowly.

Mydei had stepped forward—shoulders set, back straight, expression unreadable.

Like stone. Or something sharper.

Phainon immediately waved him off. “No—no, he’s fine, really, just a little workplace talk—”

Caenis turned, irritated, already gearing up to dismiss the interruption.

“Excuse me, this is a private—”

Then saw his face.

And stopped.

Her gaze swept over him—once, carefully, like she was trying to make sense of him.

Recognition hit like a slap. Her mouth parted.

She blinked.

Phainon looked between them, confused. “Uh… what’s going on?”

Mydei didn’t respond. Didn’t glance at him. His gaze stayed on Caenis, slow and level and glacial.

Caenis gathered herself in a blink too fast. Her voice jumped half an octave. “Oh—I didn’t realize you two were—”

“Acquainted?” Phainon filled in, sheepishly and slightly red. “He’s the one who brought me here, actually. Great spot.”

Caenis turned back to Mydei with something very close to disbelief flashing behind her eyes.

He didn’t look away. His silence crackled like frost.

Then he spoke.

Absolutely unsympathetic.

“I believe your schedule is full. Don’t waste your time here.”

That was all.

Phainon gawked. “Whoa—hey, y’all, it’s not a—”

Caenis’s breath hitched. Her mouth opened—closed again.

She tried a laugh.

It came out brittle.

“Of course,” she said, voice thinner than before. “You’re absolutely right. Just passing through.”

She took a step back. Adjusted her bag. Nodded too quickly. Her smile still hadn’t fully recovered.

Then she turned. Heels clicking, strides too fast to seem casual.

Phainon stared after her, dumbstruck.

A long silence followed.

He looked over at Mydei.

“…What the hell was that?”

Phainon was still watching Caenis disappear down the block when he realized—

Mydei still hadn’t moved.

He turned, slowly. “Seriously. What was—”

“Is she always like that?”

The question came even. But sharp enough to cut.

Phainon blinked. “Caenis?”

Mydei didn’t answer. Just waited.

“…Yeah,” Phainon said finally, rubbing at the back of his neck. “I mean. Kinda. Not all the time. She’s just—real polished. Real… driven. That’s just how she is with me, I guess.”

Mydei’s eyes narrowed, just slightly.

Phainon caught the shift and veered fast. “Uh—anyway. Thanks. Back there.”

“Don’t mention it.”

“No, but—seriously.” He glanced over. “What even was that?”

“You ask too many questions.”

Phainon snorted. “You say that like you’re not used to it by now.”

Something in Mydei’s mouth twitched. Not a smile, not quite. But the edge of something softer.

Still, the tension hadn’t left his shoulders.

Phainon studied him a second.

Mydei wasn’t just annoyed.

He was angry.

Still coiled up under the surface, too careful, too still. And not for his own sake.

He was angry… for him?

That realization landed suddenly, somewhere between Phainon’s ribs.

He cleared his throat. Lightened his voice. “Wanna get ice cream?”

Mydei blinked. “…It’s sixty-five degrees.”

Phainon coughed. “So that’s not a no.”

There was a pause. Then:

“…Lead the way.”

Phainon smiled—this time, for real.

He nudged Mydei’s shoulder as they fell into step, the two of them blending back into the late-afternoon flow. The sky had started to stretch golden, clouds streaked like soft brushstrokes across the rooftops. Downtown shimmered ahead, glass and steel catching the sun.

They walked in rhythm. Close, but not touching.

Until—somewhere between one step and the next—Phainon’s pinky brushed against Mydei’s.

And Mydei’s curled back.

No words. Just the quiet press of skin. Gentle. Intentional.

They kept walking.

Phainon didn’t say anything about it. He just smiled—and didn’t move his hand.

chapters.title: Chapter 6: The CEO of My Heart (Unfortunately)
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Phainon starts his evening dodging calls, ends it dodging (unsuccessfully) emotional trauma. Somewhere in between, there’s Caelus being Caelus, mutual trauma dumping, Aglaea running a corporate sermon, and the soul-crushing realization that the guy he just kissed is actually the CEO everyone’s been waiting for.

What a night.

Chapter Notes

Finally back to this!!!

Nothing about today felt special at first.

Phainon sat in his recliner, half-awake, staring at a muted Cubs game limping through another loss on his beat-up TV. The Red Line rattled past his window, steady as a heartbeat. His fridge hummed along, its door a scrapbook of his whole damn life—crooked pizza coupons, a church festival calendar with Snowy stealing a bratwurst in the photo, a second-grade Polaroid of Cyrene throwing a peace sign, and the old cow magnet still holding up his bills like it was pulling duty.

His phone buzzed, loudspeaker crackling, and then—

HOOOOOOONK!

Phainon flinched.

“If I get T-boned by a Ford F-150 mid-call,” Stelle bellowed, Kansas wind and road noise roaring around her, “you’re putting flowers on my grave at Arrowhead and reading my eulogy on the fifty-yard line!”

“Jesus Christ, Stelle.” He dragged a hand down his face. “Focus on the damn road before you distract yourself into a casket.”

A softer laugh cut through the chaos. “Don’t worry,” Cyrene said from her dorm room, her mic catching faint pop music—one of those bright, overproduced choruses Phainon couldn’t name if his life depended on it. He remembered Caelus mentioning Cyrene’s roommate once, March, said she was always singing. Seemed true if the background noise was something to go by. “I’ll write the eulogy,” Cyrene teased. “Phainon would just cry through it.”

“I ain’t crying through nothing,” he muttered, sinking deeper into the recliner. “Anyway. Cubs lost again.”

“Again?” Cyrene perked up.

“Fifth in a row,” Phainon said, reaching for the Coke can on his coffee table.

“Tragic,” Stelle’s voice shot back, flat as a cornfield. A second later: “WHO GAVE YOU A LICENSE, MA’AM?!”

The phone filled with more honking, muffled cussing, then the slam of her open window.

Phainon shook his head. “Don’t act like you care. You don’t even know what city the Cubs play in.”

“I know they’re not in Kansas,” Stelle retorted. “Can’t say that about your mystery man, though.”

Phainon narrowed his eyes, but let that one slide. “So, Cyrene. How’re classes? You sound tired.”

On the other end, he heard paper shuffle, a pen clatter. Her voice came more tired, the smile thinning. “Midterms. Two down, three to go.”

Phainon sat up a little. “That’s a hell of a week.”

“It’s fine,” she said quickly.

“You eating? Sleeping? I can come down this weekend, stock your fridge —”

“Phainon.” She laughed under her breath. “I’m okay.”

He caught the tail end of the song in her dorm, someone belting a high note, and for a moment it stung—how far away she sounded, like she was building her own life all alone while he sat uselessly in this apartment with the same rattling train outside. He chuckled once, awkward. “Sorry. Don’t mean to hover. Just… my little sister, in university.” He shook his head. “Something I never even came close to. Makes a guy proud, y’know?”

He rubbed at the back of his neck, realizing he’d gone soft. “First one of us to get out. First one to—”

“Oh my God.” Stelle’s voice cracked in, exasperated. “Sappy. He’s getting sappy.”

Phainon straightened. “Don’t you start, Miss Fancy Pants with your car payments and your GPS. Aren’t you proud too?”

“Of course I’m proud—HEY! HEY! USE YOUR BLINKER! YOU SON OF A—” Her voice cut off mid-curse, followed by another blaring horn and the sharp click of a mute button.

Silence.

Phainon raised his brows at Cyrene’s video square.

“Uh…” he ventured.

“Yeah,” Cyrene agreed. “We don’t ask.”

“Right.”

For a second it almost felt like the call would wind down. Cyrene leaned forward into her webcam, chin in her palm, eyes sly.

“So, Phainon…” she began, dragging it out. A little smile tugged at her lips. “Don’t you have anything you wanna tell us, too?”

The question landed like a weight in his chest.

He laughed, too fast, shaking his head. “N-no? What’s that supposed to mean?”

Cyrene tilted her head, the grin growing. “Mhm.”

A bead of sweat rolled down his temple. Phainon had a gut-deep certainty that whatever came next, he wasn’t gonna like it.

“So, Phainon…” Cyrene’s voice lilted in that suspicious way only little sisters could manage, each syllable dragged out like a net she was about to throw over him. Her face was propped in her palm on the video square, eyes sharp with mischief. “You been hanging out with that guy again? What’s his name—the one you kept calling your nemesis?”

Phainon made the mistake of taking a sip of water right then and nearly choked. He coughed into his sleeve, eyes narrowing. “Nemesis—what kinda—yeah, I mean… Mydeimos. But what’s he got to do with anything right now?”

Cyrene leaned back, flipping her pen between her fingers like she wasn’t watching his every twitch. “Oh, nothing. Just asking. Funny, though, you do bring him up a lot. More than anyone else lately.”

“Funny how you’re suddenly the FBI,” Phainon muttered, shifting in his recliner. “What, you keeping a case file on me now?”

“Don’t need a case file,” she said sweetly. “It’s just patterns. And the pattern is you getting all defensive every time his name comes up.”

“I don’t get defensive,” he said—way too quick. “I just don’t see why my social life’s on trial when you should be—” He caught himself just in time before saying studying, realizing he was about to veer back into midterm territory.

Grumbling, he stood and wandered toward the kitchen. The fridge gave a tired groan when he yanked it open, rummaging for a bottle of water. Cyrene leaned closer to her screen, sharp-eyed as always.

“You still have the cow magnet?” she said suddenly, laughing. “Oh my God. That thing’s ancient. I think it’s older than me.”

Phainon glanced over his shoulder, offended. “What, I ain’t supposed to keep a piece of home? That cow’s holding up my bills. She’s a working gal. Don’t disrespect her.”

Cyrene cracked up, shaking her head. “Only you would get sentimental about a fridge magnet.” She wagged her finger at the camera. “And don’t think that little detour saved you. We’re still on the subject of your nemesis.”

“You don’t let a guy breathe,” Phainon groaned, filling his glass. “It ain’t even—”

Before he could finish, Stelle’s line suddenly crackled alive again, exploding into chaos. The tinny twang of a country radio fought against honking horns, a man somewhere outside screamed “PULL UP, YOU JACKASS,” and the distinct crinkle of a fast-food bag made it clear she had somehow acquired fries mid-road rage.

Phainon and Cyrene both froze, staring at their screens in the same flat disbelief.

“…Was that a goat?” Cyrene asked finally, brow arched.

Phainon squinted at the phone like it might provide an answer. “That was definitely a goat.”

“Sorry, sorry—what’d I miss?” Stelle’s voice shouted through the yelling, totally unfazed.

Cyrene smirked, seizing her chance. “Oh, just Phainon’s little crush.”

“HEY!” He spun around so fast his water sloshed, nearly spilling down his shirt. “Not a crush—”

Stelle perked right up. “Wait—ohhh. You mean that dude he’s been ranting about unprompted? The one with the name that sounds like a Greek god? Yeah, yeah, you’re right—he never shuts up about him.”

“Bro,” she added, not missing a beat, “you sound like a middle-aged book club lady who clutches her wine glass while swooning over the mysterious man at the coffee shop.”

Cyrene gasped with glee, covering her mouth. “No, no—that’s not it. He sounds like Dad. Remember when he first started courting Mom? Same tone, same look. Down so bad.”

Phainon groaned, half-whining as he dragged a hand down his face. “He’s just a guy, alright? Just a guy. Quit making it weird.”

But both of them were already grinning at him like cats who’d cornered a mouse, and Phainon knew there was no way in hell he was escaping this conversation.

Stelle let out a sigh so dramatic it rattled through the tinny speakers. “Fine, fine, I’ll shut up about your… little situation.” She even made air quotes. “I’m done. Totally done. Dropping it. Gone, poof.”

Phainon narrowed his eyes. “Good.”

A pause. Just long enough for him to start settling into the quiet.

Then Stelle leaned in with a look that spelled doom. “But respect the hustle, though. You casually dating in the city now? What is this, like Hinge but with worse sidewalks? Swipe left, swipe right, suddenly you’re at some dive bar eating mozzarella sticks with a stranger?”

“Stelle—”

“I’m serious!” she cut in, voice going muffled as she clearly shoved another fry in her mouth. “You’ve been in Chicago for a year or two, right? You’re telling me you never tested the waters? Not even a coffee shop flirtation? The old ‘oops we both reached for the same biscotti’ move?”

Cyrene perked up, amused. “Or the grocery store cart crash. Classic.”

“Exactly,” Stelle said, clapping her hands like she’d found a partner in crime. “Or dog parks, that’s the number one hot zone. You bring Snowy to the city, boom, instant dates lined up. Dogs are like wingmen with fur. A golden retriever could probably get you engaged in three weeks flat.”

Phainon grimaced. “I am not pimping out Snowy for romance.”

“Then you’re wasting resources,” Stelle shot back.

Cyrene laughed, shaking her head. “Come on, though. You’ve never been like that, Phainon. You’ve never been the casual type. Not in high school, not in college. Not ever.”

“Damn right.” He slouched deeper into his chair, like the weight of their scrutiny alone was enough to give him back pain.

Stelle raised her brows. “So what then? You only date if you’re already planning the wedding?”

It was teasing, but Phainon answered without thinking. “…Yeah. Something like that.”

The silence hit like a cymbal crash. Even the goat in the background— mercifully—shut up.

Cyrene’s eyes widened, then started sparkling.

Stelle squinted at him like she was examining a rare bug under glass. “… Hold on. Dude. Then are you implying slash telling me you wanna marry this guy?”

“Wait—wait, wait—” Cyrene was already half doubled over, hand covering her mouth.

Phainon’s face went red so fast it was almost comical. He scrambled for words, each one worse than the last. “What—no—no, that’s not—I didn’t mean—what the hell are you even—”

“You literally just said it,” Cyrene sang, delighted.

“You did,” Stelle confirmed, calm and merciless, like a judge handing down a life sentence.
