“I did not!” Phainon barked, pointing wildly at the screen. “Nope. Absolutely not. I am not having this conversation with you two. I’m done. I’m cutting the call. Good day to you, Stelle. Good day to you, Cyrene.”

“Phainon, wait—”

But the video went black, cutting them off. Stelle’s laughter shrieked through the speakers for half a second before vanishing, replaced by the hollow silence of the empty call screen.

Phainon stared at his own reflection in the laptop’s dark screen for a beat, face still on fire.

Working at Okhema had always been bad, but lately they felt like dress rehearsals for a funeral.

By the time Phainon pushed through the glass doors of Okhema Tech, the place already carried that tired, end-of-season energy, like a school limping into finals week. The lobby was bright enough, but it all looked dulled around the edges: half-drained plants by reception, carpet showing its age, the receptionist herself flipping through a magazine without even pretending to look busy. The AC clattered overhead in that way it did when the vents hadn’t been cleaned in years, and for a second, Phainon wondered if anyone would even bother fixing it now. Why spend the money if the logo on the wall would be someone else’s in a month?

He swiped his badge, waited for the turnstile to beep, and stepped into the main floor. The atmosphere hit him right away. It wasn’t tense exactly.

More like… weirdly resigned. People still typed at their desks, still took calls, but the energy was muscle memory, not motivation. Nobody was asking if the merger was happening anymore. That question had burned out weeks ago. Now it was all: When it’s done, where do we end up? How bad is the cleanup going to be?

The conversations floating over cubicle walls sounded less like coworkers chatting and more like survivors picking over wreckage.

“When the new logos go up, I’m calling dibs on a corner desk,” someone in design announced, too loudly, like claiming imaginary territory made it real.

“Corner desk?” his neighbor scoffed. “We won’t even know where the corner is. They’ll probably gut this whole floor.”

There was laughter—dry, brittle, the kind that didn’t come from anyone’s stomach. A laugh you threw out just to prove you could still make noise.

Phainon adjusted the strap of his messenger bag higher on his shoulder, weaving his way down the aisle. He passed clusters of cubicles that looked like little stages mid–set change. Some were stripped bare, with only an unplugged monitor left behind. Others were half-packed, cardboard boxes crouched under desks, photo frames leaning awkwardly against staplers and stacks of folders, waiting for the signal to flee. A few people had carted off their things already—personal mugs, bobbleheads, novelty calendars. Desk plants had vanished overnight, leaving pale squares of dust in their place.

It was almost worse seeing the ones who stayed fully decorated, like nothing was happening. A little desperate. Like if you left your cubicle untouched, you were somehow declaring immunity.

Near the breakroom, two analysts loitered with paper cups of burnt coffee, voices pitched just high enough that everyone passing could hear.

“I heard HR already merged payroll,” one said, brows raised in mock secrecy.

“No way.”

“I swear. My buddy saw a Kremnos header on his direct deposit slip.”

The other groaned. “Fantastic. Just what I needed. At least they didn’t bounce it.”

They both chuckled, but it landed flat. Phainon slid by them, head ducked, and caught sight of Greg two desks over. Greg had stationed himself right next to their manager like a golden retriever, nodding at every bland reassurance, eager laugh perfectly timed. Meanwhile, over in QA, some guy had his sneakers up on his desk and was scrolling his phone like the end of the world had already been scheduled on his calendar.

It struck Phainon as surreal: half the floor hustling harder than ever to prove their worth, the other half already living like ghosts.

“Hey, Phainon.”

He turned. A coworker leaned on the wall of his cubicle, mug in hand, smiling like this was small talk in line at the grocery store.

“Better get used to it, huh? Won’t be long before you’ve got a new boss breathing down your neck.”

Phainon forced a smile, thin but passable. “Yeah. Can’t wait.”

The guy laughed and retreated, leaving Phainon in the fluorescent hum, staring at a row of desks that looked a little more hollow every day.

He let out a breath he hadn’t realized he was holding. He dropped his bag into his chair, spun it once by the strap, and hovered there, not quite ready to sit.

From where he stood, the office spread out in its usual little islands: cubicles walled off with thumbtacked calendars, the breakroom with its perpetually out-of-order vending machine, the long row of windows where someone’s January snowflake still clung on like it had tenure. On paper, nothing had changed. But the way people carried themselves gave the lie away.

Greg, two desks over, was still glued to their manager like he thought proximity might buy him job security. Across the aisle, sneaker-guy from QA (Phainon was pretty sure his name was Tyler, but he couldn’t swear to it) had his feet propped on his desk, scrolling his phone. Every few minutes he barked a laugh, probably at Twitter, as if to prove he didn’t give a damn. A designer shuffled past balancing a cardboard box with one arm, the plastic fern sticking out at an awkward angle. She muttered something about “just taking it home early, less to carry later,” and nobody challenged her.

Phainon finally sat, rolling his chair in slow, aimless circles until it faced his monitor. His screen glowed a stubborn blue, waiting for him to log in. He ignored it.

This was the part of a merger everyone hated—the long, stale waiting room where the magazines were out of date and nobody knew if their name would be called.

They’d already had the first wave, the so-called “preliminary trimming.” Contractors dropped. Underperforming teams dissolved with zero fanfare. A handful of unlucky people escorted out after those infamous “restructuring” emails that said absolutely nothing and everything at once. It had been ugly, sure, but manageable. Just enough cuts to make Okhema look lean and glossy in the pitch deck.

Now came the pause. That eerie calm where the axe stayed in the air, casting its shadow over everyone’s desk. The logic was cold but simple: why fire people now if the new bosses were going to reshuffle anyway? Better to wait, let Kremnos do the killing once the ink dried.

And so they all waited.

“I heard recruiters are circling again.”

“Of course they are. Sharks can smell blood in the water.”

Phainon wanted to cover his ears.

“Yeah, they told us to put the rollout on ice until ‘post-integration.’”

“Translation: don’t spend money on a project when you don’t even know if the team’s still alive.”

Everywhere Phainon looked, people were bracing in their own ways. HR meetings with no listed agenda, just the cryptic “check-in.” Managers ducking questions with the same vague optimism as weather forecasters who knew a storm was coming but couldn’t admit it. Even the vendors had gotten cagey—Phainon’s inbox had two separate “pending approval” notices on invoices that normally cleared in a day.

He rubbed the back of his neck, trying to knead out the tightness. His dad had gone through this twice, and the stories always lined up: the real cuts came after signatures hit paper. Both companies slapped their org charts down side by side, circled the overlaps, and someone started making phone calls. Sometimes the purge came quick, ripping off the bandage. Sometimes it was slower, a bleed stretched over months.

Knowing Kremnos, he had a sinking feeling it’d be the quick and brutal version.

The thought pulled at his chest, a sudden tightening that left him short of breath. For a second, he imagined himself carrying a box out to the parking lot, badge disabled, cubicle stripped like he’d never been here at all. His stomach turned over at the image, hot and sour, like he’d swallowed something wrong.

He shut his eyes, forced a long exhale through his nose. It was fine. He was fine. He would be fine. No sense spiraling over something that hadn’t even happened yet.

Stretching his arm until his elbow popped, Phainon turned deliberately back toward his screen. “Work to do,” he muttered under his breath.

For now, as long as his nameplate was still taped to this cubicle, that had to be enough.

“…and anyway, the guy just hands me a bagel like it’s reparations. I don’t even work there!”

Phainon didn’t even flinch at this point. He’d learned that if he reacted too early, Caelus only got louder. Instead, he finished typing out a note in the spreadsheet, clicked save, and then looked up—just in time to catch his best friend halfway through spinning in the spare chair like he owned the place.

Caelus had made himself right at home: hoodie half-zipped, sneakers kicked up on the edge of the desk, iced coffee sweating over a stack of expense reports that definitely weren’t waterproof. He had that look on his face again—the one that said he’d already been talking for several minutes before Phainon tuned back in.

“Are you seriously eating that in here?” Phainon asked, eyeing the bagel crumbs accumulating like snow across his desk.

“It’s a public bagel,” Caelus said, mouth full. “Found property. I’m just honoring the circle of life.”

He reached over and started rearranging the magnets on Phainon’s filing cabinet, humming tunelessly under his breath. The top one—an old Batman magnet one of his baby cousins had given him—got replaced with a wrinkled sticker that read “Gaslight, Gatekeep, Grindset.”

Phainon squinted. “Please tell me you didn’t just steal that off HR’s motivation board.”

Caelus grinned without looking up. “Relax. I’m redistributing the wealth.”

“That’s what people say before they get escorted out.”

“Then I’ll finally have a story worth telling at parties.”

Phainon tried to get back to work—he really did—but Caelus had other plans.

“Bro,” Caelus said, leaning over to peer at his monitor, “what even is that? Excel? Or Minesweeper’s emo cousin? Why’s it all green and yellow like a traffic light having a crisis?”

“It’s called conditional formatting,” Phainon said, not looking up.

“Yeah, well, your conditions look terminal.”

Phainon sighed. “Don’t you have a job or something?”

Caelus waved a hand. “I’m networking.”

“You’re literally sitting in my cubicle.”

He nodded solemnly. “Networking.”

Phainon clicked his tongue, half amused, half done. “Actually—wait.” He paused, finger hovering over the keyboard. “Where do you even work now? You’ve been ‘between gigs’ since, what, 2023?”

Caelus swiveled lazily in the chair, straw still in his mouth. “Define ‘work.’”

“Define ‘income.’”

“You’re asking a lot of personal questions for someone whose office chair squeaks like a dying possum.”

“You’re deflecting.”

“You’re projecting.”

“You’re unemployed.”

“You’re using Comic Sans in a spreadsheet.”

Phainon’s head snapped up. “It’s Calibri, you gremlin.”

Caelus held up his hands. “Sure thing, corporate boy.”

Phainon couldn’t help a small laugh slipping out—it was either that or throw his mouse. Caelus always had that effect on him: half aggravation, half comfort, like an annoying brother you still wanted around.

Caelus leaned back again, crossing his ankles. “Anyway, the grind’s the grind. Capitalism. Hustle culture. Various endeavors.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It’s a vibe,” Caelus said, dead serious.

Phainon snorted. “Yeah, a broke one.”

Caelus pointed at him. “Judgment from a man who color-codes expense sheets. Wild.”

Phainon gave up with a sigh, turning back to his monitor. The clicking of his keyboard filled the silence for all of ten seconds before Caelus broke it again.

“So,” he said casually, “you seen Twitter this morning?”

“No,” Phainon said flatly, “and I’d like to keep my blood pressure that way.”

“Too late,” Caelus replied. “Okhema’s trending again. Not for the fun kind of reasons.”

Phainon froze mid-click. “…What kind of reasons, then?”

“Layoffs. Merger talk. You know the drill. People posting those vague ‘on to new adventures!’ updates on LinkedIn.” He gestured with his straw. “Half my feed’s got the little green ‘open to work’ banner again. Feels like déjà vu, man.”

“Fantastic,” Phainon muttered, eyes glued to the spreadsheet but not seeing a thing.

“Oh, and one of my friends freelances for one of your vendors? Apparently their invoice has been ‘processing’ since mid-August.”

That earned a slow blink. “…Processing,” Phainon repeated, the word heavy in his mouth.

“Yeah. Which, like, never a good sign. But hey—accounting, am I right?” Caelus said quickly, giving his shoulder a quick pat like it might undo the damage.

“Mm.” Phainon didn’t answer, staring blankly at his screen as the hum of the office seemed to dull around him.

For once, Caelus went quiet too, spinning slowly in the chair. He gave a low whistle, like he could taste the tension in the air.

“Hey,” he said finally, softer. “You’re fine, man. Worst case, you crash on my couch again. Or we both go off-grid. Start a commune somewhere. I’ll grow basil.”

“That’s the worst case?”

“It’s all I’ve got budget for.”

Phainon huffed a laugh, rubbing at the back of his neck. “You’re supposed to be my emotional support idiot, not my bringer of doom.”

Caelus smirked. “Hey, I’m just the messenger, bud. Blame the economy.”

He drained the last of his drink, stood, and stretched with an exaggerated yawn. “Anyway, I should probably go pretend to be productive somewhere else.”

“Good idea.”

Caelus slapped his shoulder lightly as he passed. “You’ll be fine. You always are.”

“Sure,” Phainon said, tone dry but eyes soft.

Caelus grinned, already halfway down the aisle. “Don’t work too hard, Calibri!”

“Go away, Caelus.”

“Can’t. Networking.”

Phainon shook his head, fighting a smile as he turned back to his screen. The sound of his friend’s sneakers faded down the hall, leaving behind the soft buzz of lights and the faint warmth of a laugh that lingered just long enough to feel like home.

By the time the spreadsheet hit line three hundred and forty-something, Phainon had stopped pretending he cared about any of it. He’d been pretending hard, too—headphones in, brow furrowed, cursor blinking in an endless grid of numbers that had long since lost meaning.

The office around him had sunk into that weird pre-lunch limbo where everyone’s soul quietly left their body. Someone was muttering about pivot tables. Someone else had been “in a meeting” since eleven and never returned. And somewhere, somehow, someone had again committed the sin of microwaving fish.

He tried to focus, really he did, but the cursor blinked like it was judging him. His brain buzzed like an unplugged outlet. Eventually he just leaned back, stretched, and let out a groan that came from deep in his soul. His spine popped audibly.

“Man, that was your spine,” Caelus said from the other chair—yes, he was back, spinning lazily in a stolen swivel like a gremlin who’d claimed it by squatter’s rights.

“Yeah,” Phainon muttered, rubbing his neck. “And that was my will to live.”

Caelus lifted his empty coffee cup in solemn salute. “May it rest.”

The clock above them dragged itself toward noon. The hum of the office printer faltered like even it was losing motivation.

“Lunch hour,” Phainon said under his breath.

“Deli time?” Caelus perked up.

“That was the plan.”

“Good, because I’m starving. And my bank account needs the five-dollar sandwich therapy.”

Phainon pushed away from his desk, stretching until his joints cracked again. His head still felt foggy, though—like he’d been running on low battery all morning. Then it hit him.

He hadn’t even had coffee.

Not a drop. Not even the burnt communal sludge by the copier.

It was, frankly, a moral failure.

He looked down at his empty mug and sighed. “You know what? Screw the sandwich. I’m getting caffeine first.”

Caelus blinked. “Now?”

“Now.”

“It’s noon.”

“And?”

“I just thought we were going to the deli.”

“We were,” Phainon said, shrugging on his jacket. “But I changed my mind. You’re on your own, partner.”

Caelus narrowed his eyes, feigning betrayal. “Unbelievable. You’re ditching protein for bean juice?”

“Character development,” Phainon said, patting his shoulder as he walked past.

“Consider buying me lunch to make up for it,” Caelus called, standing to follow anyway. “Where you headed? Jefferson?”

“Yeah. Coffee’s actually drinkable there. Less burnt, more… spiritual awakening in a cup.”

Caelus fell into step beside him as they made their way out. “Guess I’ll walk with you part of the way. Moral support.”

“Because the sidewalk’s dangerous.”

“Exactly. Full of rogue pigeons and misplaced ambition.”

And that’s how they ended up here after 5 minutes of walking.

The air hit like relief—crisp, bright, and smelling faintly of street food and overwatered planters. The lunch crowd moved in lazy herds: students, office workers, construction guys in orange vests. Conversations overlapped, traffic hissed, a bus sighed as it stopped at the light.

“Wait you were serious about getting coffee now?” Caelus said, incredulous as they weaved around a delivery bike.

Phainon laughed. “Of course I am. What’s the problem?”

“No problem,” Caelus said, dodging another pedestrian. “Just thought you were joking while we were doing the deli run. Some of us still believe in lunch.”

“Then again, you’re welcome to go without me.”

“Oh, I am,” Caelus said, grinning. “But I’m still walking with you, because apparently we’re heading in the same direction, and I enjoy annoying you.”

“Touching.”

“Truly. It’s the foundation of our friendship.”

They passed a guy arguing with his AirPods, a dog tied to a meter post eyeing the world like it owed him money, and a group of interns laughing too loud about something none of them found that funny. How interesting.

“So,” Caelus said after a beat, “you ever think about quitting?”

Phainon snorted. “Every day.”

“No, I mean actually quitting. Like, full-send. Disappear into the woods. Start a podcast. Grow a beard.”

“You wouldn’t last three hours without a phone charger.”

“I’d adapt.”

“You’d cry.”

“Incorrect. I’d hotspot off yours.”

Phainon gave him a look. “Touch grass.”

“I am. I’m literally walking next to grass.”

“That’s a weed, man.”

“Still counts.”

They reached the corner where their paths split—deli one way, coffee shop the other. The smell of toasted bread floated through the air, mocking him.

“Well,” Caelus said, slowing. “Guess this is goodbye, traitor.”

“How sad,” Phainon said. “Try not to miss me.”

“Oh, I will. Every carb-filled second.”

“Good luck with your bagel, philosopher.”

“Good luck with your bean juice, coward.”

Phainon laughed and gave his shoulder a friendly shove. “Later.”

“Later, man.”

The crowd swallowed Caelus’s voice as Phainon turned down his street. His phone buzzed in his hand—a cheerful little notification: Order ready for pickup.

Two reasons he’d come here today.

One, obviously, coffee. It wasn’t Anaxa-level perfection, but it was close. Smooth, strong, overpriced—the holy trinity.

And two…

His lips curved as he thumbed open his messages.

Phainon: [I’m here! Don’t see you though??]

The typing bubble appeared almost instantly.

Bastard❤️:

[I’m in the corner booth.]

Phainon hummed under his breath, smile growing as he pushed open the café door. The bell chimed softly, letting in a rush of espresso and cinnamon. Indie music murmured from the speakers, and sunlight streamed through the front window in perfect golden slants that made the whole place feel like a warm pocket of peace.

The barista—a tired guy with a buzzcut and three piercings—was already sliding a cup across the counter.

“Phainon?”

“That’s me,” he said, picking it up. “Mobile order.”

“Triple-shot oat latte, right?”

“Yeah.” He took a cautious sip, then smiled. “Perfect. Just shy of a spiritual awakening.”

The barista laughed. “Glad to hear it.”

“Have a good one.”

“You too, man.”

Coffee in hand, Phainon turned—and his grin broke wider, unstoppable.

Because there, tucked in the corner booth, sat Mydei—half-lit by the window, scrolling idly through his phone with one hand, the other resting next to a half-eaten cinnamon roll. Sugar clung to his sleeve; sunlight caught in his hair.

He looked up at just the right moment, met Phainon’s gaze, and smiled.

And that was enough to make the whole day start over.

For a second, Phainon just stood there. The sight hit him harder than it should’ve, this stupid mix of warmth and nerves bubbling up in his chest. He told himself it was just the caffeine he hadn’t had yet. Definitely that.

He took a quiet breath, let the flutter settle, and forced himself to move. Just coffee, just lunch, just Mydei. Totally normal.

His cheeks already hurt from smiling by the time he reached the booth. He slid into the seat across from Mydei, the leather squeaking under him. Mydei didn’t even look up again until Phainon’s knee accidentally bumped the table. Then those golden eyes lifted, assessing him like he was some minor inconvenience delivered by fate itself.

For a beat, neither of them spoke. The café hum filled the space between them—the low chatter, the hiss of the espresso machine, some indie song too mellow for its own good.

Phainon’s lips tilted into a smirk.

“So,” he said, resting his chin on his hand, “you finally figured out how to order without scaring the barista? I’m honestly surprised you haven’t stolen my order yet.”

That earned him a visible twitch at the corner of Mydei’s eye. Beautiful.

“Not my fault,” Mydei said flatly, “that they spelled your name ‘Faynon’ again. Maybe if you tipped more than spare change and rural charm.”

Phainon snorted. “Rural charm’s priceless, thank you very much.”

“You’d think that,” Mydei said, stirring his coffee. “The barista didn’t.”

“That’s fine. He can spell my name wrong as long as he makes my coffee right.”

“Did he?”

Phainon laughed under his breath, leaning back. “Good to see you too, city boy.”

“Mm. Pity’s mutual,” Mydei said, but the edge in his tone was softened by the faintest ghost of a smile—quick, reluctant, almost hidden behind his cup as he took another sip.

Phainon caught it anyway. He always did.

He lifted his own cup in reply, tapping the lid lightly against Mydei’s mug. “Guess we’re even then.”

The sound of the soft clink seemed to hang there a moment too long, the noise of the café blurring around them.

“This place,” he said, swirling his drink once before taking a slow sip. “You ever notice how every café in this neighborhood looks like a Wes Anderson set? Pastel walls, mismatched chairs, one decorative typewriter in the corner. Like if I sit still too long, some guy in a corduroy blazer’s gonna start monologuing about ennui.”

Across from him, Mydei’s mouth curved—just barely. “Says the guy drinking what can only be described as mud in a mason jar.”

Phainon’s face bloomed instantly. “That’s blue-collar authenticity, thank you. I’m supporting small business and my caffeine addiction at the same time.”

“You’re supporting your stomach ulcers.”

“Worth it.”

Mydei made a low, skeptical noise. “You’d think someone born in the Midwest would know what real coffee tastes like by now.”

“Oh, I know,” Phainon said, gesturing with his cup. “I just also know fancy espresso doesn’t hold a candle to whatever sludge my aunt brewed in a cornfield at six a.m.”

“That wasn’t coffee,” Mydei said dryly. “That was a cry for help.”

Phainon laughed—a real one, sudden and bright, startling the barista who was restocking sugar packets nearby. “Yeah, well, it got the job done. Unlike certain people who think caffeine is a personality trait.”

“Correction,” Mydei said, lifting his cup with slow precision, “I think good taste is a personality trait.”

“Right. That why you ordered something with enough foam and sugar to drown a cat?”

Mydei took a long, deliberate sip. His eyes cut toward the window, where the glass caught his reflection—tired, maybe, or just far away. When he turned back, the distance had vanished, replaced by that same cool, wry steadiness Phainon knew too well.

Phainon tilted his head. “You know,” he said lightly, “this reminds me of the time you tried to poison me.”

Mydei blinked. “Excuse me?”

“Oh, don’t act innocent. The cinnamon incident. Last year.”

A sound escaped Mydei—half groan, half laugh. “That wasn’t poisoning. That was strategic sabotage. You stole my caramel macchiato first.”

“It was labeled in Latin! How was I supposed to know it was yours?” Phainon shot back. “Who even does that? I swear Anaxa can barely stand humanity as a concept, and you made him write Vita est brevis, caffeina est vita on your cup.”

“I don’t know,” Mydei said, fighting a smile. “Maybe because normal people don’t drink whatever you call that.”

“He would’ve spit in it, you know,” Phainon said. “You’re lucky he didn’t.”

Mydei’s brows lifted. “He wouldn’t.”

“He would.”

“Worked for me,” Mydei muttered. “You spent the rest of the week glaring at me from across the shop like some gargoyle.”

“I was plotting your demise.”

“Sure. Except your ‘demise’ involved ordering cinnamon in everything just to prove a point.”

Phainon’s smile widened. “Yeah, until you accidentally swapped our drinks and doomed yourself.”

That earned a hand to Mydei’s face, muffling another reluctant laugh. “You laughed for twenty minutes with those old ladies in that book club.”

“You sneezed for thirty.”

For a moment, they were both laughing—the sound light and unguarded. Phainon felt something in his chest loosen, a warmth spreading there that wasn’t just from the coffee.

“See?” he said when their laughter tapered off. “You missed me.”

“I missed peace and quiet.”

“Same thing,” Phainon said, leaning back with mock satisfaction.

Mydei’s gaze lingered on him, steady but unreadable. There was a flicker— something shadowed and quick—that crossed his face before he smoothed it out again.

Then he smiled, faint but real, lowering his eyes to his phone. “You’re still terrible at coffee, by the way.”

“Yeah,” Phainon said, soft enough that the words barely bridged the space between them. “But I’ve got good company, so I’ll survive.”

Mydei’s thumb stilled on the screen. Just for a second, his expression went still, the air between them tightening. Then the noise of a passing bus broke the spell, and he gave a small nod, back to composed.

“Next time,” Phainon said, clearing his throat lightly, “I’m ordering for both of us. We’re not repeating that incident.”

“You couldn’t handle it.”

“Oh, I could.” Phainon’s grin turned crooked. “I’d even spell your name right this time.”

“Good luck.”

“I’ll guess. Starts with B-A-S-T-A-R-D, right?”

Mydei’s eyes lifted, that spark back just long enough to hide the weariness underneath. “Careful, angel,” he murmured. “I still know where you buy your coffee.”

Phainon laughed, but something about the look Mydei gave him—half-smile, half-silence—lingered long after.

“You know,” he said after a moment, shifting the conversation, “I kinda miss open skies. Back home, you could see forever. No buildings, no noise. Just sky and maybe a hawk.”

Mydei made a quiet sound—half a hum, half an acknowledgment—but didn’t look up.

“Here it’s different,” Phainon went on. “Every time I look up, there’s a billboard or ten miles of glass in the way. I keep saying I’ll find a place to watch the sunset, but—” he shrugged, “—somehow there’s always something else to do. Work, groceries, traffic. Life, I guess.”

When he looked up, expecting a jab about him sounding like somebody’s grandpa, Mydei wasn’t smirking. His gaze had drifted somewhere past Phainon’s shoulder, eyes unfocused, thumb tapping an uneven rhythm against his mug.

Phainon hesitated, a faint crease forming between his brows. “You good? You’re usually giving me hell by now.”

“Yeah.” Mydei’s reply came quick, too even. “Just tired. You talk too much.”

Phainon arched a brow, leaning back a little. The tease hit its mark but lacked its usual spark. “Uh-huh,” he said, unconvinced but letting it slide. Mydei’s tells were quiet ones—small, sharp flickers that disappeared if you stared too long.

The silence lingered for a beat before Mydei cleared his throat softly, like changing stations.

“You ever walk around this part of the city?” he asked, tone more casual now. “There’s a view by the river. Less noise. Better air.”

Phainon gasped. “You? Voluntarily touching grass? Who are you and what have you done with Mydei?”

Mydei gave him a look that could’ve curdled milk. “Shut up,” he said, standing anyway. “Come on. Walk.”

That made Phainon’s grin widen. “Look at you. Man of the people. Out here embracing nature.” He downed the last of his coffee and pushed up from his seat, catching Mydei’s sleeve before he could turn away. “What’re you waiting for, let’s go!”

Mydei froze for just a heartbeat at the touch—barely perceptible, but Phainon caught it. Then Mydei exhaled, the faintest smile ghosting across his lips.

“…Sure.”

His hand slid down in one smooth motion until their fingers brushed. Then, almost absentmindedly—but not quite—he intertwined them, tugging Phainon toward the door.

The café bell gave a soft chime as they stepped outside, light pooling across the pavement in slow, golden ribbons.

Phainon chuckled quietly under his breath, the sound carried off by a passing breeze. Mydei’s expression stayed composed—bored, if you didn’t know better—but his thumb traced a small, steady circle against Phainon’s knuckles.

And that, Phainon thought as they walked into the fading light, was more than enough sky for now.

Turns out, when Mydei said he knew a place, he wasn’t kidding.

The city peeled open around them, the concrete easing into a narrow path that hugged the river. The late afternoon light hit the water just right—warm and gold, the kind that made everything look softer, even the skyline. Cars hummed faintly somewhere above, and a train rattled across a bridge in the distance. The smell of espresso drifted from another café patio nearby, mixing with the faint metallic tang of the river.

It wasn’t nature-nature. But it was the closest thing to peace you could find inside Chicago city limits.

And peace, unfortunately, always made Phainon talk too much.

“See,” he said, waving one hand at the skyline, “this right here’s proof y’all don’t know peace. You stand by a river, see a few clouds, and suddenly everyone’s acting like they achieved enlightenment. Back home, this is just where you go when your cousin flips the four-wheeler and you need a minute to stop laughing before you help him.”

Mydei raised an eyebrow. “That’s your idea of serenity?”

“Absolutely,” Phainon said without hesitation. “You ever had fried catfish straight from the lake? Not that fancy beer-battered junk. I’m talking burn-your-fingers, eaten-on-a-tailgate kind of catfish.”

“That sounds barbaric.”

“It’s tradition,” Phainon said, mock-offended. “You people wouldn’t understand.”

Mydei smirked. “You’re right. I don’t understand willingly eating something that probably came with a tetanus side dish.”

“Blasphemy,” Phainon said, pointing accusingly. “You wound me. I bring you to this beautiful, serene location, and you insult my cuisine?”

“You didn’t bring me anywhere,” Mydei said dryly. “I’m the one who knew the place.”

“Semantics.” Phainon’s grin widened. “You’re just jealous you don’t have proper culinary taste buds.”

“I have standards.”

“Same thing.”

Mydei gave him that long-suffering look he reserved specifically for Phainon.

They passed under a bridge, where the light dimmed to a copper haze. Pigeons strutted along the railing like they owned the place. Phainon slowed, squinted at them.

“See, that’s what I mean,” he said, nudging one with his shoe. “City birds don’t act right. Back home, they’d scatter if you so much as breathed too loud. These ones? They’ve got health insurance.”

“You’re deranged,” Mydei muttered.

“Correct. But you love it.”

Mydei didn’t deny it, though the amusement faded quicker than usual.

For a bit, they walked in silence—the quiet kind that should’ve felt comfortable but didn’t. Mydei’s gaze drifted toward the river, his expression gone unreadable.

Phainon noticed. He always did.

He kept talking anyway, light and easy, watching out of the corner of his eye. “—And that reminds me of the time we tried to turn the barn into a zipline—”

“Mm.”

“Uh-huh.” Phainon stopped mid-step, squinting. “You’re not even listening, are you?”

“I am.”

“Yeah? Then what’d I just say?”

Mydei blinked, caught. “Something about… uh. Ziplining?”

“Wow,” Phainon said, deadpan. “That’s some top-tier listening.”

He crossed his arms, weight shifting. “Alright, spill. What’s up with you? You’ve been weird all day. Usually by now you’ve insulted me at least three times, minimum.”

“I’m fine,” Mydei said too quickly.

“Uh-huh. And I’m the mayor.” Phainon’s tone flattened, skeptical but not harsh. “You sound real fine.”

Silence again, this time heavier.

Phainon let out a breath through his nose, voice softening. “Look, I know you. When you start doing that quiet thing, something’s wrong. So, either tell me or I’ll start making assumptions—and trust me, they’ll be dramatic.”

That earned the faintest glare. Mydei’s jaw tensed, his eyes skimming the water before he sighed.

“…How do you do it?”

Phainon blinked. “Do what?”

Mydei didn’t answer right away. For a while, the only sound was the water pushing against the riverbank and the faint rattle of a train somewhere behind them. His thumb moved along the railing in idle rhythm, eyes following the sunlight as it scattered across the current.

“You ever notice,” he started finally, voice low, “how people like us don’t get much quiet?”

Phainon tilted his head, not interrupting.

Mydei went on, words careful, like each one weighed more than he wanted to admit. “There’s always noise. Schedules. Deadlines. People pulling at you from all sides. And yet—” His jaw flexed. “You still manage to… laugh through it. Like it’s nothing. Like you don’t get tired.”

He exhaled through his nose, a short sound almost like a laugh. “You’re always like this. Joking. Smiling. Talking about food. I don’t know how you do it.” His gaze flicked away. “How do you stay so… happy?”

The question hung there.

Phainon blinked, caught mid-movement. For a second, he didn’t even breathe.

Then Mydei frowned and straightened, already regretting it. “Forget it. That came out wrong.”

“Hey—”

“No, seriously.” Mydei lifted a hand. “You don’t owe me an answer. It’s rude of me to even ask—”

Phainon sighed, pinching the bridge of his nose. “Nah, it’s fine.” His voice came out rough, heavier than usual, like gravel rolling in his throat.

He stepped toward the railing, leaning his weight on his arms. The metal was cool beneath his palms; the river, a restless mirror throwing back the skyline in shaky strips. For a moment, he just watched it move, trying to line up his thoughts into something that didn’t sound like a TED Talk.

This would’ve been the perfect moment for a grand speech. Something about perseverance, grit, and staying strong—the kind of quote that gets embroidered on throw pillows or posted in cursive font over a sunset photo.

Keep your head up. Stay positive. Every storm passes.

He could’ve said all that. He wanted to, even. But it felt too fake, too neat for the real mess in his chest. And lying to Mydei wasn’t something he could stomach.

So instead, Phainon said flatly,

“Well, for one, I fucking hated myself.”

Silence.

Behind him, Mydei blinked. “…What?”

Phainon turned just enough to throw him a crooked grin. “Yeah. Like, professionally. If self-loathing were an Olympic sport, I’d have gold. Probably a sponsorship deal too.”

The corner of Mydei’s mouth twitched despite himself.

“I got bad enough that my sister started nagging me about therapy.” Phainon gave a low whistle and shook his head. “But then we checked the price. And I don’t know if you’ve seen the price of therapy in the U.S., but we both noped outta there faster than a raccoon from a flashlight.”

He sighed.

“Yeah, well, skipping therapy shockingly didn’t cure me.” Phainon’s tone brightened just enough to be self-mocking. “I couldn’t look at mirrors for a while. Or water. Anything that might remind me I was still… me.” He paused, then chuckled dryly. “My sister tried crystals and tarot. I tried whiskey. She won. Barely.”

Mydei exhaled.

“There’s that point,” Phainon went on, “where you start thinking, ‘Maybe I’m the problem.’ And then you realize—yeah, I am the problem, but I’m also the only one who can fix it, and that’s way too much responsibility for a Tuesday.”

He took in a breath, leaning back against the rail. “I once told myself I’d fix my mental health after harvest season. Three years later, still harvesting excuses.”

That earned a genuine frown from Mydei.

Phainon smiled faintly, but didn’t look over. “I don’t know,” he said after a bit. “One day I just got tired. Tired of hating myself. Tired of thinking every bad day was proof I deserved it. So I stopped taking it so damn seriously. Figured if I can laugh at it, maybe it stops winning, you know?”

He shrugged, voice dipping softer. “Plus, statistically, the universe can’t bully me harder than I already do, so… checkmate.”

It landed like a joke but didn’t quite sound like one.

He laughed anyway—a small, tired sound—and shook his head. “So yeah, not exactly the best guy to ask for mental-health tips. I checked therapy prices again last week—still criminal. So if I seem positive, that’s just because sarcasm’s cheaper than antidepressants.”

He turned then, expecting Mydei to throw a jab back, but instead found him quiet—frozen, almost, with one hand half-lifted, like he’d started to reach for him and stopped midway.

Phainon blinked, grin faltering. “…What?”

Nothing. Mydei just looked at him—a mixture of worry, surprise, something too honest for words.

Phainon sighed and turned back toward the river. “Okay,” he muttered, “maybe I should stop joking for five seconds.”

He leaned forward again, elbows propped on the railing. “Didn’t used to be like this,” he said more softly. “Back in high school, I… hell, I hated myself. Got real low. Thought I wouldn’t make it some days.” He rolled one shoulder, forcing a lighthearted tone. “But I kept busy. Kept my hands working. And now I figure, if I can laugh at it, that means I won.”

Mydei stepped up beside him, resting his arms on the railing too. “…You think laughing makes it smaller,” he said.

Phainon’s answer came easy. “Ain’t about making it small. Just remembering I got through it.”

They stayed like that—side by side, city hum behind them, river light in front—until Phainon turned.

“Now that I’ve told you all that,” he said, “it’s only fair you tell me what’s bothering you, right?”

Mydei huffed a faint breath, the ghost of a smile returning. “…I suppose it is.”

And the water kept moving, catching the sunlight in restless shards, like even the river itself was pretending not to listen.

Then Mydei said, so evenly it almost sounded like an opening to another joke,

“My father’s acting like the second coming of Christ and it’s getting to me.”

Phainon nearly choked on air. “…Huh?”

“Yeah.” Mydei didn’t even look up from the river. “Allow me to explain.”

He said it like he was narrating a minor inconvenience. “He’s been on this… reformed streak lately. Calls me just to ask if I’ve eaten. Buys fruit baskets. Gives advice about sleep schedules. Keeps talking about ‘making up for lost time’ like he’s been possessed by a self-help book.” He exhaled softly, the corner of his mouth twitching. “It’s—exhausting.”

Phainon blinked. “That doesn’t sound so bad.”

“It wouldn’t be,” Mydei said, “if he hadn’t spent the last decade pretending I didn’t exist.”

The words were light, but they hit with the weight of a dropped stone.

Phainon opened his mouth, closed it again. “Oh.”

“Mm.” Mydei’s gaze followed the ripple of the water. “To make a long story short, he wasn’t always like this. There was a time he was…” he gave a small shrug, “…actually kind of brilliant. The sort of man who walked into a room and everyone made space. Business, politics, whatever—he could bend things. Until he couldn’t.”

He tilted his head slightly, thinking. “Then came the drinking. Not constant, just… cyclical. He’d stop, swear off it, then start again whenever the market dipped or a deal went wrong. He’d come home smelling like whiskey.” His tone didn’t shift, but the silence that followed did. “At first he wasn’t cruel. Just gone, even when he was there.”

Phainon stayed quiet.

“When I was about ten,” Mydei continued, “he came home drunk out of his mind. I don’t remember what I said—probably something stupid—but he hit me.”

He said it so casually that it almost didn’t register as something that should hurt.

Phainon’s hands tightened on the railing. For a second, all he could see was the flash of that faceless man, heavy-handed, towering—and the sharp, ugly thought that he wanted to find him and make him regret it.

Then Mydei gave this small, wrong-sounding laugh. “It wasn’t even that dramatic. One hit. That’s all.”

Phainon turned sharply, jaw tightening. “That’s not funny.”

“I didn’t say it was,” Mydei said, finally looking at him. His voice wasn’t cold, just tired in a way that felt older than he should be. “I just said it happened.”

He lifted a hand, dismissive, like brushing off a speck of dust. “Anyway. My mother came home, saw him passed out on the couch and me looking like I lost a boxing match. That was it—she told him she was filing for divorce.”

Phainon’s voice was low. “So they—?”

“No.” Mydei cut in, gaze dropping again. “Key word: was.”

He pressed his lips together, thinking. “I didn’t want them to divorce.”

Phainon frowned. “Why?”

Mydei hesitated. His tone softened, lost that polished dryness. “I thought if we stayed a family, he’d get better. That it’d force him to.” A faint smile crossed his face, bitter around the edges. “So my mother moved out instead. Took me with her. They stayed married in name only. Guess that was my compromise.”

The pause that followed stretched long enough for the wind to fill it.

“It worked, eventually,” Mydei said after a moment. “He got sober. Got help. Started trying again. And I’ll give him that—he really has tried. But sometimes…” He exhaled, eyes flicking toward the horizon. “Sometimes he tries too hard. Like he’s auditioning to be someone new. Like if he overcorrects long enough, I’ll forget what it was like before.”

Another pause.

“This morning got to me,” he said finally, voice quieter now.

Phainon looked at him, at the tiny break in his posture, the small sag in his shoulders that Mydei was trying to pretend wasn’t there. It was a look that didn’t belong on him—defeat.

“…I didn’t know,” Phainon said.

Mydei waved a hand vaguely, not meeting his eyes. “Of course you didn’t. Who would?”

It came out like a joke, but the faint catch in his voice betrayed it.

The city wind pressed against them, tugging at jackets and sleeves. Neither spoke again.

But when Phainon shifted closer—just slightly, enough that their shoulders nearly brushed—Mydei didn’t move away.

He nudged Mydei’s shoulder with his own, the motion half playful, half grounding. “You look like you’re thinking yourself into a hole again,” he said. “Don’t do that. Dirt’s hard enough to climb out of.”

Mydei huffed, eyes still on the skyline. “You always talk this much when it’s quiet?”

“Only when someone’s glaring at me like they’re auditioning for a tragic art film.” Phainon leaned his elbows against the railing, gaze turning toward the glinting river. The water caught the city lights in thin, trembling ribbons. “Thing about life is, it don’t care if you’re ready or not. It’ll roll right over you, and you’ll still have to wake up the next day and feed the cat. That’s the secret—keep feeding the cat.”

That got him a faint snort from Mydei.

Phainon continued, softer now. “Well, folks used to say you don’t stop walking just ‘cause the road turns ugly. You patch your tires, you keep going. Sometimes that’s all it takes—keeping steady long enough to see the next bit of sunlight. World don’t get kinder, but you get stronger, y’know?”

A low hum came from Mydei, almost thoughtful. “Stronger,” he repeated, as if testing the word on his tongue.

“Yeah,” Phainon said, smiling faintly. “Even if you’re limping.”

For a while, neither spoke.

Phainon could’ve stayed there for hours. The quiet company, the reflection of city lights in Mydei’s eyes, the way the air finally felt light again after weeks of concrete and chaos—it all fit too comfortably.

Then, his phone buzzed.

He groaned. “You gotta be kidding me,” he muttered, patting his pocket. “Can’t even have one moment without the universe poking me.”

He fished it out, thumb hovering over the screen. The name made him pause.

Cassie: [Have you seen the new email yet?]

He frowned. “What new email—”

He flicked open his inbox, eyes skimming the latest message. His expression shifted from confusion to mild dread as he read.

⸻ From: Administrative Office — Okhema Tech

Subject: Division Integration Meeting – Mandatory Attendance

Dear all,

As part of the ongoing Okhema–Kremnos merger completion, all personnel are required to attend the upcoming Division Integration Meeting at Okhema Headquarters, downtown.

Location: Okhema HQ Conference Hall A Date: Thursday, 4 p.m. sharp Purpose: •Official announcement of leadership transitions •Introduction of consolidated divisions •Overview of new interdepartmental operations and reporting structures

This meeting is mandatory for all staff. Further details, including floor assignments and access credentials, will follow in a separate internal memo.

Thank you for your cooperation as we move forward together into this next chapter of Okhema Tech.

— Okhema Administrative Office

⸻ Phainon clicked his tongue. “Well, that’s one way to ruin a good mood. Sounds like corporate hell in heels.”

Mydei glanced over, eyebrow raised. “The merger meeting?”

“Yeah. Downtown, nine sharp. Guess it’s time for the big song and dance.”

Mydei hummed quietly. “I saw that earlier.”

Phainon blinked. “Oh, right—you’re Kremnos side of things. Means you’ll be there too, huh?”

“Unfortunately.” Mydei’s voice was dry, but his gaze stayed steady on him. After a beat, he added, “Do you want me to drive you?”

Phainon paused mid-scroll. “You what?”

Mydei didn’t look away. “We’re going the same direction. I can pick you up that morning. If you’d like.”

For a second, Phainon just stared, his brain short-circuiting somewhere between he offered and he said if you’d like. His chest did that ridiculous thing again—thudding harder, uninvited—and before he could stop it, the teasing slipped free.

“Well, I didn’t know you could be so generous,” he drawled. “What’s next, you gonna grab me dinner too? Maybe open the door for me? Careful, Mydei—you keep this up and it’s gonna start sounding like a date.”

Mydei blinked once, deadpan. “…Can it, Hayseed.”

Phainon laughed, loud and unrestrained, the sound rolling out across the quiet riverfront. “There he is. I was getting worried you caught feelings for a minute.”

“Keep talking,” Mydei warned, but the corner of his mouth twitched—just enough to betray him.

Phainon leaned back against the railing, grin lingering.

Maybe this was something worth feeding the cat for.

The first thing Phainon noticed was how quiet it was for a room packed with a hundred people.

Not silent—just that strained, pre-speech sort of quiet that hung in the air like static. The kind of quiet that made the faint click of heels sound like a threat and every polite laugh echo too loudly against the marble.

Even the air-conditioning hummed with restraint, as though it knew better than to interrupt a room full of people pretending to enjoy corporate networking.

Phainon shifted in his seat. The chair gave a small, judgmental creak. His tie was crooked—had been since the second he’d put it on—and his blazer was doing its best impression of “formal” while losing a button battle at the cuffs. Around him: rows of sleek suits, polished watches, lanyards that cost more than his rent. The perfume of ambition and expensive coffee.

And then there was him.

A wrinkle in the otherwise ironed-flat picture.

He tugged at his jacket anyway, like the motion could disguise how out of place he looked. Same jacket he’d worn to his cousin’s wedding. Technically also to a court hearing. He was on a streak.

If he were being honest, he still wasn’t entirely sure how he’d ended up here.

Well—he did, technically.

A flash of the morning came to him: stepping out of his apartment building, coffee in hand, blinking at the slick black car parked at the curb. The windows were tinted to the kind of black that whispered classified government operation. The driver stepped out, immaculate and unbothered, holding the door open like he was guarding royalty.

“Compliments of Mydeimos, sir.”

Phainon had just stared for a good five seconds, waiting for a camera crew to jump out.

Then he laughed. “Of course,” he’d muttered. “Of course you’d send a Batmobile.”

He’d considered texting—Did you actually send this or am I about to get abducted by tax agents?—but decided against it.

Rich people probably just did that sort of thing.

So he’d climbed in, sighed at how the leather seat adjusted itself automatically, and tried not to feel too weirdly… disappointed. Mydei had said he’d pick him up himself, but apparently “himself” meant a driver in a three-piece suit. Typical. He hadn’t even had time to roll down the window and complain before they were speeding toward downtown.

Still, it wasn’t all bad. The week had been hectic—Mydei buried in work— but they’d managed to text between meetings, enough that the silence between replies didn’t feel like absence.

So now here he was, in the big glass headquarters that smelled faintly of printer toner and nerves, trying not to yawn himself into unemployment.

At least he wasn’t alone.

“Speech should be starting any minute now,” said a voice to his right.

Phainon turned to find Castorice sitting there—posture immaculate, hair in its usual lavender-grey bun, the picture of composure. Her ID badge hung neatly in placel. She radiated that quiet, efficient energy that made everyone else seem slightly messier by comparison, but Phainon could tell she was just as exhausted and putting on a front so people don’t talk to her.

“Great,” Phainon said. “I was starting to worry I’d have to sit through this alone.”

She asked softly and amused, “No complaints yet about your outfit yet?”

He pressed a hand to his heart. “Hey, this is my formal jacket. I only wear it to weddings and court dates.”

Her laugh was quick and soft but real, enough to earn them a glance from a nearby coworker who clearly hadn’t laughed since the merger announcement.

“You do realize,” she murmured, tilting her head toward the crowd, “half the board’s here today. I even heard some of Kremnos’s top brass flew in.”

Phainon gave a low whistle. “Fancy. Hope they like the existential dread of workers.”

“Mm. I think they prefer cost-cutting,” she replied with a small smile.

He snorted. “Same thing, really.”

Castorice shook her head, amused. “You should at least pretend to care. This merger’s the biggest thing to happen to Okhema in a decade. They’re re-wiring the company.”

“Yeah,” he said, adjusting his tie with exaggerated effort, “and yet somehow I still make the same paycheck.”

She gave him a sidelong glance—sympathetic and grimly in the same boat as him. “Don’t act like you’re not curious who the new management is.”

Phainon hesitated, eyes on the stage as the low murmur of conversation swelled again. “Curious isn’t the word I’d use. More like… cautiously terrified.”

Castorice’s lips twitched. “You and everyone else.”

He smiled faintly but didn’t reply.

Because truthfully, his mind wasn’t on the merger. It kept slipping back—to the texts, the car, the missing presence beside him. He told himself it was stupid to notice, that Mydei had a life, a job, a billion reasons to be busy. But still. The seat next to him felt too empty. The night had felt too quiet without that smug bastard showing up five minutes early and some dumb comment about “country punctuality.”

He shook himself, straightening in his chair as the lights began to dim.

The projector screen blinked to life, white to black to silver, until the logo spread across the stage wall in sleek letters:

OKHEMA TECHNOLOGIES × CASTRUM KREMNOS Division Integration Summit

A hush rolled over the auditorium. Phones slipped away, backs straightened, conversations cut off mid-sentence. The stage lights flared, sterile and perfect.

Phainon gave a low whistle, tipping his head toward Castorice. “Speak of the devil,” he said. “Looks like you were right about that speech.”

“Try not to snore through it,” she whispered back, adjusting her blazer.

“No promises.”

He remarked faintly, but as the first executive stepped up to the podium and began their polished introduction, Phainon found his fingers tapping restless against his knee. He wasn’t sure why. The air felt thicker somehow, his shirt collar tighter, like the room itself was holding its breath.

Something told him this wasn’t just another corporate day.

The overhead lights dimmed to a soft amber glow, and the murmur of hundreds of voices settled into expectant silence. The auditorium’s screens flickered awake—Okhema’s logo blooming across the walls, all white and steel blue.

At the center podium, Aglaea adjusted her microphone.

Phainon straightened in his seat before he even realized he was doing it.

He’d been to his fair share of corporate presentations, but Aglaea always managed to make the air feel sharper somehow—clearer. Maybe it was the fact that she’d been the one to pull him out of his old post and into this circus to begin with. Or maybe she was just one of those rare executives who looked like she actually believed in the words coming out of her mouth, though knowing her he doubted it.

“Good afternoon,” she began, her voice carrying easily, every syllable crisp. “It’s a pleasure to welcome you all to Okhema’s Division Integration Summit. Today is quite an important day, a beginning. About what happens when two legacies choose to build something new together.”

A few polite claps rippled through the audience. Cameras flashed. Phainon joined in, slow, rhythmic, as if applause were part of his job description. Beside him, Castorice gave the world’s most efficient three claps, then folded her hands in her lap like she’d trained for it.

“Today,” Aglaea continued, “we celebrate a partnership between Okhema Technologies and Castrum Kremnos—two organizations that have long shared not only a professional history, but a philosophy. We believe in purposeful innovation. In creating systems that outlast us. In a culture where transparency is common.”

The presentation behind her shifted to soft gradients, bold text, buzzwords dressed up in modern font. Phainon squinted up at one of the slides.

‘Driving cross-divisional collaboration.’

‘Leveraging shared infrastructure for scalable growth.’

He could almost hear the corporate drumroll.

“Cross-divisional collaboration,” he muttered under his breath, tasting the words like bad coffee. “Bingo.”

Castorice’s elbow nudged his ribs without her gaze leaving the stage. “Behave,” she whispered.

“I am behaving,” he murmured back. “I’m absorbing the synergy.”

Her lips twitched—barely—but it counted.

Onstage, Aglaea’s rhythm didn’t falter. “This isn’t merely an economic move,” she said. “It’s an investment in people—our engineers, our analysts, our field teams, our partners. We’re shaping not just the technology we use, but the way we connect through it. Because innovation without humanity,” she paused deliberately, letting the weight of the words settle, “isn’t progress at all.”

Another wave of applause. Polite, measured, mechanical.

Phainon clapped again, slower this time. His eyes drifted past the stage lights, to the glass walls beyond the rows of heads—the stars, albeit not much—glinting faintly through. It was too bright in here. Too clean. Every word sounded polished, edited, like something pre-approved by ten departments before leaving anyone’s mouth.

Still, he watched her. Listened enough to catch the tone underneath—the practiced steadiness, the warmth that almost made the buzzwords sound real. Almost.

“We stand on the edge of a decade that will redefine global research and digital ethics,” Aglaea went on. “Our shared goal is simple: not to compete for the fastest innovation, but to cultivate the most meaningful one. Together, we can build a foundation that endures—not just as companies, but as communities.”

That one caught him. He didn’t know why.

Build something that endures.

His thumb brushed over his notepad without realizing it. Maybe it was the phrasing, or maybe it was the fact that his own foundation had been feeling pretty temporary lately—his job, his apartment, the half-empty evenings where he sat talking nonsense on the phone until sunrise. Whatever it was, the words hooked somewhere quiet.

He exhaled through his nose, forced himself back into the room just as Aglaea’s final line rose:

“So—to new ideas, to partnership, and to a future we build together.”

Applause swelled. Cameras clicked. A few people stood.

Phainon clapped, eyes half-lidded. In his head, the words blurred together— cooperation, partnership, vision, growth—all of it melting into a low hum. He smiled faintly to himself, thinking that if someone ever made a drinking game out of this kind of speech, no one would survive past the third slide.

The intermission announcement followed: ten minutes to stretch, grab coffee, or pretend to network.

Phainon was on his feet before the sentence ended.

Castorice noticed immediately. “You’re leaving.”

“I’m stepping out,” he said. “Air, a break.”

“Phainon.”

“What? I’ll be back before she finishes her next PowerPoint transition.”

“You always say that.”

“And I’m almost always right.”

Her sigh was soft but tired. “Fine. Just don’t miss the next presentation. Caenis will have an aneurysm if you’re not here when the investors start their questions.”

“Tell him I’m out gathering cross-divisional inspiration.”

She gave him a look. “Go,” she said at last, waving him off. “Before HR sees your tie.”

He grinned. “Already on that.”

The corridor outside was blessedly empty. The air cooler, heavier with that faint ozone smell of early fall rain. He passed a few stragglers—people on their phones, a couple of assistants whispering by the elevators—but didn’t stop. He wanted open air.

The doors opened with a faint creeks

The city rushed in.

Chicago stretched wide and gleaming, the water cutting silver through the blocks below. Wind sliced past the glass railings, tugging at his sleeves, ruffling his hair. He loosened his tie all the way, draped it around his neck like a casualty. His shoulders unknotted for the first time that morning.

He leaned on the railing, staring out over the sprawl of rooftops and traffic. From up here, everything looked calm—motion slowed by distance, the noise muffled into something like rhythm.

“Five minutes,” he muttered to himself. “Just five minutes without the word ‘innovation.’”

Somewhere below, someone laughed. A trumpet wailed faintly from the street corner. The sound bounced up between the buildings like sunlight on glass.

He closed his eyes briefly, breathed in the cold air. It almost felt like quiet. Almost.

Then he turned.

And paused.

Because a few feet away, framed by the terrace glass, stood a figure that made his brain stutter before the rest of him caught up.

Blond hair—longer now, caught by the wind. Hands tucked into the pockets of a tailored coat. The same posture, the same half-cocked tilt of the head that screamed too composed for his own good.

That stupidly familiar mane.

Phainon’s mouth curved before he could stop it.

“Well,” he breathed, smile tugging wider. “I’ll be damned.”

He whistled low as he stepped out, hands in his pockets.

“Fancy running into you here,” he drawled, voice carrying lazily through the dark.

Mydei didn’t answer right away. He stood at the edge of the terrace, city light gilding the sharp line of his jaw, the wind teasing his hair like it knew him. There was a stillness about him, something distant.

Phainon took his time walking over, smile tugging at the corner of his mouth. “You know,” he said, stopping beside him, “when people say they’ll pick someone up, they usually mean personally. Not by proxy.”

That earned the faintest curve of Mydei’s lips. “And yet, here you are.”

“Didn’t want your driver to feel unloved.”

“Always thinking of others,” Mydei murmured dryly.

“Especially the ones with good air conditioning.”

It drew a quiet exhale from Mydei, almost a laugh, and Phainon felt that ridiculous flutter in his chest again. He leaned forward against the railing, shoulder to shoulder now, close enough to catch the scent of Mydei’s cologne—clean, subtle, maddening.

It wasn’t until then that he noticed the cigarette, unlit, balanced between Mydei’s fingers.

When Phainon’s gaze flicked to it, Mydei followed his eyes, then wordlessly flicked the cigarette away. The motion was casual, thoughtless.

But it hit Phainon harder than it should have.

“You didn’t even light it,” he said.

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You always do.”

“I changed my mind.”

The words were simple, but something in the quiet between them felt more personal than it should have. Phainon cleared his throat, looking for something—anything—to fill it.

“You’re too calm,” he said finally. “Everyone else in there looks like they’re about to get audited.”

“That’s because they probably will.”

Phainon laughed. “God, you’re terrible.”

“I’m realistic.”

“You’re annoying is what you are.”

“Coming from you, I’ll take that as a compliment.”

Their laughter blended into the wind. For a moment, it was easy—too easy.

Phainon looked at him again, really looked this time: the faint glow brushing the slope of his cheekbone, the careful way he stood like even gravity needed his permission. Controlled. Contained. Unreachable.

The kind of person you shouldn’t want but end up orbiting anyway.

“You ever think,” Phainon said suddenly, “that maybe we’re all just pretending we have any idea what we’re doing?”

Mydei turned slightly, brow lifting. “Random but sure. You mean you don’t?”

“I fake it pretty well,” Phainon said, half-laughing. “You’re the only one I can’t bullshit.”

“I’ll take that as a compliment too.”

“You shouldn’t.”

“I just did.”

Their eyes met briefly, and Phainon had to look away before he said something stupid. His heart was doing that dumb thing again—racing like it wanted out.

The silence that followed wasn’t empty; it was charged, almost humming.

“I like being around you,” Phainon said quietly.

Mydei didn’t look at him. “Why’s that?”

“Don’t know,” Phainon said, gaze fixed on the sky. “You make me feel less cold.”

That got him a glance. Mydei’s eyes softened just slightly, like the words had landed somewhere he didn’t expect.

“You make it sound simple,” he said eventually, quietly.

“Maybe it is,” Phainon murmured, a smile tugging at his mouth. “Not everything has to be complicated.”

“You’d be surprised.”

“Try me.”

There was a pause—long enough for the air between them to change.

Mydei turned fully toward him now, one hand resting loosely on the railing, the other brushing close enough that Phainon could feel the heat of it near his sleeve.

“My life doesn’t allow for simple things,” Mydei said quietly. “They tend to get… broken.”

“Then maybe you’re holding them wrong.”

That made Mydei laugh softly, the sound low and quiet and god, unfair.

Phainon smiled at the sound, but his heart was going wild. “Sometimes,” he said, barely above a whisper, “I think if I’m gonna put my whole heart into someone, it oughta be someone who won’t drop it.”

Mydei’s eyes flicked to his. “You’d risk that?”

Phainon shrugged, though his voice was steadier than he felt. “Guess it depends who’s catching.”

The noise blurred into nothing. All that was left was the wind and the faint, almost audible rhythm of his pulse.

Mydei took a small step forward. The distance between them thinned to inches—close enough for Phainon to feel the warmth of his breath.

“You shouldn’t say things like that,” Mydei murmured, but his voice had gone soft at the edges.

“Why not?”

“Because I might believe you.”

And that was it. That was the breaking point.

Neither of them moved first; they just leaned, caught somewhere between instinct and gravity, until Mydei’s hand brushed Phainon’s sleeve—gentle, questioning—and Phainon didn’t pull back.

The air felt electric, delicate, waiting to shatter.

Then—

Mydei leaned in, slow enough to feel every inch of tension drawn between them, until his lips brushed Phainon’s—barely, and softly.

Warm. Careful. Dizzying.

The world outside kept spinning, but for one suspended heartbeat, Phainon swore the everything had gone silent—just lights, wind, and the taste of something he hadn’t realized he’d been waiting for.

For a dizzy second or two, Phainon didn’t move.

The world seemed to go still—the hum of the city below, the faint clatter of traffic, even the wind against his coat—all of it dulled into a low, ringing hush. His brain was trying to catch up with what his body already knew: Mydei was kissing him.

And God, he tasted exactly how Phainon imagined he would—cool air, sweet, something faintly like pomegranates, the kind of taste that lingered.

Then he snapped.

The thought never formed; his body just moved. One second his hands were at his sides, the next he’d fisted the front of Mydei’s coat, dragging him close with unfiltered, reckless need.

Mydei made a sound—half gasp, half swallowed word—before Phainon’s mouth found his again, rougher this time, no second-guessing or hesitation.

This wasn’t polite. It wasn’t measured. It was hungry.

Phainon kissed like he meant it—like a man who’d been holding something back for years and finally let it out. He pressed Mydei back against the terrace wall, the railing just brushing his hip, his free hand sliding to his waist to tilt him forward, deepening the kiss until the line between air and heat blurred.

Mydei’s hands came up reflexively—one gripping Phainon’s arm, the other hovering at his chest, unsure whether to pull him closer or push him away. But the hesitation broke the second Phainon made a low, involuntary sound against his mouth.

That sound did it.

Mydei’s fingers slid up, wrapping behind Phainon’s neck, drawing him closer, deeper. The motion was shaky but genuine, the kind of surrender that burned slow. His control slipped in increments—first the way his head tilted to meet him halfway, then the soft, startled exhale against Phainon’s cheek when he realized he wanted it just as badly.

The space between them disappeared.

Phainon’s pulse roared in his ears, his whole chest aching with how alive it felt—how warm. His thumb brushed the edge of Mydei’s jaw, feeling the tremor that ran through him, and something about it—the contrast, the fact that this man who never lost his composure was trembling under his touch —made him smile mid-kiss, just a small breath of a laugh.

“Hell,” he murmured against Mydei’s lips, voice rough and fond, “you really do know how to shut me up.”

Mydei’s soft, helpless laugh broke against his mouth, and Phainon thought for one wild second that this could be it—the kind of moment that rewires everything.

He kissed him again, slower now, the urgency melting into something deep, dizzying. The city light glinted off the glass behind them, painting them in streaks of amber and blue. It was just them—the skyline, the wind, the warmth of another person’s breath mixing with his own.

It felt like something good.

Mydei’s hand slid up the back of Phainon’s neck, fingertips pressing lightly into his skin. But the longer they stayed, the more the tension returned— small things at first, almost imperceptible. The stiffness of his shoulders. The faltering rhythm of his breath. The way his fingers curled like they were fighting between holding on and letting go.

Phainon noticed, barely—just enough for a flicker of confusion to pass through him before—

A sound.

Small. Barely there. The terrace door creaked from the draft.

Mydei froze.

He went still all at once, every trace of warmth gone from his touch. Phainon felt it before he understood it—the sudden distance, the absence of motion. Mydei’s lips parted against his, breath shuddering once before he pulled away like he’d been burned.

“Mydei—”

The word slipped out on instinct, but Mydei had already stepped back. His expression was unreadable, pale under the city light, his chest rising too fast, eyes darting anywhere but Phainon’s.

“Hey,” Phainon said, voice rough, breath still uneven. He took a hesitant step forward. “What’s wrong? You—did I do something—?”

“I—” Mydei’s voice caught. He tried again, quieter. “I can’t.”

“Can’t what?” Phainon’s laugh came out thin, strained. “Can’t breathe? Yeah, me neither—”

“Phainon.” Mydei said his name like it hurt. Just one word, but it landed sharp. He shook his head, exhaled shakily. “I’m sorry. I have to go.”

“Wait, what do you—Mydei, hold on—” Phainon reached out, catching nothing but air as Mydei turned. “Can we just—talk for a second? You don’t have to—”

But the door opened before he could finish. The slam that followed wasn’t loud, but it cut clean through the air like a line drawn in concrete.

Then silence.

For a few seconds, Phainon just stood there, still half-leaning forward, hand hanging where he’d reached out. The wind pressed cold against his skin, filling the space Mydei had just been standing in. His breath came too fast, too shallow.

He looked down at his hands, still trembling faintly, and it almost made him laugh—the absurdity of it, of feeling this warm.

The night went on around him. The cars below, the low rumble of engines, the heartbeat of the city.

He stayed there long enough for the cold to settle in his jacket, for the buzz of his pulse to fade into something quieter, duller.

When he finally exhaled, it came out uneven, like he’d forgotten how to breathe right.

The railing where Mydei had been pressed against still held the faint scent of his cologne.

Phainon stared at it for a moment, and for some reason, that—more than anything—was what finally made his chest ache.

When the world stitched itself back together, it did so under fluorescent lights.

The air inside was too bright, too clean, too indifferent to what had just happened. The conference hall hummed with the quiet chaos of people returning from smoke breaks and hallway gossip. The smell of catered wine and carpet cleaner mixed in the air. Somewhere across the room, a laugh came a beat too loud, a glass clinked, and life—stubborn as ever—kept moving.

Phainon hadn’t moved since sitting back down.

Same chair. Same half-untucked shirt. Same damn tie that suddenly felt like it had shrunk a size. His name badge hung crooked against his chest like it was mocking him.

On the big screen, the company promo reel kept looping—city hotspots, drone shots, smiling employees shaking hands like the world was a perfectly reasonable place to be in. The music swelled triumphantly for the fifth time in ten minutes.

Phainon stared straight ahead, eyes glassy. His brain, however, refused to cooperate.

It kept replaying that. The warmth of Mydei’s mouth, the press of his hands, the quick, stunned breath they’d shared before the world tilted and crashed. The way the door had sounded when it shut.

He wanted to stop thinking about it. God, he wanted to. But his mind kept spinning the same loop like a scratched record.

I ruined it. He probably hates me. Hell, maybe he ain’t even gay—

The thought hit hard enough he dragged a hand down his face, as if he could physically scrape it off. His palm came away warm. His cheeks were hotter than they should’ve been.

Get it together. You’re a man, damn it. Don’t cry. Be better.

That last part didn’t sound like him. It sounded like his dad. Or his uncle. Or every old-timer from back home who thought stoicism was a survival skill.

He let out a quiet, humorless laugh under his breath. Yeah, that’s right. Be a man. Pretend your heart didn’t just nosedive off a roof.

He sat up straighter, squared his shoulders, tugged at his cuff. Just another guy in a conference hall. Just fine. Perfectly fine.

“Hey.”

The voice beside him was soft. Castorice had finally returned to her seat, the faint smell of her lilac perfume cutting through the stale recycled air. She was smoothing down her skirt, phone tucked between her fingers, before she turned toward him with that gentle frown that meant she actually cared.

“You don’t look so good.”

Phainon blinked, caught between confusion and gratitude that someone noticed. “I’m peachy.”

Her brows lifted slightly. “You sure? You look a little—well.” She hesitated, choosing a word. “Un-peachy.”

That pulled the ghost of a smile out of him. “Nah. Just thinking about how lucky I am to work for such an inspiring company.”

Castorice huffed a small laugh. “That bad, huh?”

“Oh, worse. But you missed the best part,” he said, nodding toward the stage. “Apparently we’re getting new parking passes. Game changer.”

Her eyes brightened. “See? There’s always a silver lining.”

He forced another smile. It almost held this time.

Around them, the chatter began to fade as people drifted back to their seats. Chairs scraped against the floor, the lights dimmed just slightly, and the air settled into that pre-speech hush again.

At the front, Aglaea reappeared—perfect posture, calm smile, half-full glass of wine in hand. She looked like she’d never been rattled a day in her life.

“Alright, everyone,” she began, voice smooth as ever. “Let’s pick up where we left off.”

The room quieted completely. Phones flipped facedown. All eyes turned forward.

Phainon did too, mostly because it was easier than looking anywhere else.

He folded his hands, stared at the stage lights, and let the motion of it all blur—the hum of the AC, the clink of glass, the polite laughter a few rows up. Somewhere, buried under it all, was the phantom memory of a kiss.

His throat ached, but he sat up straighter anyway.

Because that’s what a Midwestern boy does. He doesn’t fall apart under fluorescent lights. He just smiles, nods, and keeps pretending everything’s fine.

And under those too-bright, too-honest lights, that’s exactly what Phainon did.

“Thank you all for your patience,” she began, one hand resting gracefully on the podium. “I know it’s been a long evening, but I promise this last part will make it worth your while.”

Polite laughter rippled through the audience, the practiced, cordial kind that didn’t reach anyone’s eyes.

Phainon managed a faint smile. His jaw hurt from holding it that way. He tried to focus, eyes fixed on the sleek conference stage, but his pulse still hadn’t settled. Keep it together, he told himself. Just a few more minutes. Keepittogetherkeepittogetherkeepittogether.

Aglaea moved seamlessly into her next cue, voice gliding through phrases that sounded important—synergy, integration, growth, mutual trust. The projector behind her rolled through carefully curated slides: a glossy Okhema logo alongside another—Kremnos.

He blinked at it, brain stuttering half a beat behind.

“—and as many of you already know,” Aglaea continued, “this merger marks the beginning of a shared vision. Together, Okhema and Kremnos are paving the way for a more connected, sustainable future.”

Applause spread politely across the room.

Phainon clapped too, his palms stinging, the motion mechanical. The sound barely registered in his ears.

Keep it together. Just keep breathing.

Aglaea smiled, composed as ever, her earrings catching the light. “It’s my absolute pleasure now to introduce the person who made this partnership possible. His leadership, innovation, and commitment to collaboration have truly shaped this moment.”

Another pause.

Her hand lifted toward the side of the stage.

“Please join me in welcoming the CEO of Kremnos.”

The room shifted at once—chairs scraping softly, a murmur of anticipation. Someone raised their phone. Someone else whispered, “Finally.”

Phainon glanced toward the stage, only half paying attention. Just a formality, he thought. He didn’t even care who it was.

Then movement caught his eye.

A man stepped into the light.

He was tall—his shoulders framed perfectly by the sharp cut of a charcoal-gray suit that looked like it cost more than Phainon’s car. The stage lights hit polished shoes, a tie with the faint sheen of silk, cufflinks catching a gleam of silver. His hand lifted in a modest, almost reluctant wave, expression composed but not cold.

The applause swelled.

Phainon’s chest tightened. He didn’t know why at first. Maybe it was the way the man carried himself—not stiff, not cocky, just sure. Or maybe it was the voice, low and even, thanking Aglaea, thanking the audience, talking about partnership and innovation and moving forward.

That voice.

He blinked hard. The lights made it difficult to see clearly, but—

Then the man angled slightly toward the crowd, his profile catching the glow.

Blonde hair, neatly combed back. Strong jawline. Familiar curve of a smile that wasn’t quite one.

No.

No, no, no—

His heart lurched violently, thudding once before forgetting its rhythm altogether.

The rest of the room blurred out. He barely felt the chair beneath him, the glass in his hand, the air in his lungs.

Because standing under those sterile, spotless lights, addressing the audience like he hadn’t just kissed him breathless on a rooftop hours ago—

Was Mydeimos.

Phainon’s blood drained clean out of his face. His fingers went numb. The applause sounded far away now, warped, like it was happening underwater.

Aglaea’s voice cut faintly through it all, still smiling. “And we are so grateful to have him here tonight. Mydeimos, everyone.”

There it was—confirmation, like the universe felt the need to twist the knife.

He couldn’t even process the words Mydeimos was saying. Something about innovation, long-term vision, partnership. He saw his lips move, calm and confident, and all he could hear was silence. His mind filled the space instead—with memory. The press of his mouth. The sound of the door closing.

When he finally blinked, Mydeimos’ eyes were on the crowd—but then, just for a moment, they found him.

It was brief. Barely a second. But Phainon knew it wasn’t an accident.

That look—steady, unreadable, almost pained—hit harder than any word could’ve.

His stomach turned. The air was too hot, too thin.

He turned sharply toward Castorice.

“Castorice.”

She didn’t hear him over the applause.

He said it again, louder, his voice raw. “Castorice.”

Her head jerked toward him, startled. “What? What’s—”

“Get me out of here.” The words came out low and rough, all the steadiness gone. “Now.”

Something in his tone—whatever cracked through—made her move without asking questions.

“Oh—okay,” she said softly, already gathering her purse, concern flickering across her face. She rose and touched his arm, steadying him as he stood. He barely felt it.
