They slipped toward the aisle quietly, their movement lost beneath the applause that followed Mydeimos’ closing line. Each clap echoed sharp and hollow in Phainon’s ears.

Halfway to the doors, he looked back—just once.

Mydeimos was still onstage, shaking hands, smiling faintly for the cameras. But his eyes—his eyes—found Phainon again through the crowd.

Phainon looked away first.

And as the applause swelled again, he pushed through the doors, the sound chasing him out into the hall.

Chapter End Notes

*Boo*, angst, though not too angsty actually so YIPPYYYY!!!!

chapters.title: One
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Phainon’s forced transfer lands him directly under Mydei’s leadership, which is terrible for one simple reason: feelings. After a week of Olympic-level avoidance, a surprise rainstorm and a shared umbrella soften the tension just long enough for a certain someone(s) to stage the most obvious matchmaking trap in recorded history.

Communication happens; dignity does not.

Chapter Notes

Finally finished this up!

If optimism were taxable, Monday mornings would fund the entire city.

The sun was shining, the birds were chirping, and the Windy City was alive with promise. The skyline glittered like ambition, commuters hustled with purpose, and even the pigeons strutted like they had quarterly goals to meet. A new week! A new chance to thrive! The kind of morning that made you believe in employee wellness programs, five-year plans, and the transformative power of a really good LinkedIn post.

Or so the brochure probably said. In full color. With a stock photo of people high-fiving around a salad.

Reality, however, had a much smaller marketing budget. The wind didn’t “whisper through the streets”—it punched them, slapping a damp newspaper against a passing intern’s leg and toppling an iced drink onto someone’s loafers. The sky was technically blue, yes, but only in that “somewhere-above-the-clouds” sort of way. Down at street level, the day was already overworked and underpaid.

And at precisely 8:00 a.m., in the cafeteria of Castrum Kremnos Headquarters, Phainon was doing his best to pretend this was all part of a promising new chapter.

Okhema’s old breakroom machine had sputtered out coffee that tasted like resignation and toner fumes. Kremnos, though—Kremnos had baristas. Polished counters, abstract art, ambient jazz that felt like it was judging your posture, and espresso shots so curated they could qualify for museum display.

Espresso shots, Phainon decided grimly, that tasted like debt.

He stood in line, the hem of his slightly wrinkled blazer refusing to cooperate, his old ID badge still hanging there like a tag from a clearance rack: OKHEMA DIVISION TRANSFER ASSOCIATE. He was supposed to get a new one soon, but apparently “sometime this week” in laymen terms meant “don’t hold your breath.”

Behind him, someone whispered, “Oh, merger transfer?” in the same tone you’d reserve for “infectious rash.”

He ignored it, eyes climbing the price board ahead of him. Ten dollars for a donut. Ten.

Did it come with a certificate of authenticity? Was there a down payment option?

Kremnos people moved differently—like they were late to a yacht meeting or a Pilates retreat. They had designer shoes, charcoal travel mugs, and a collective aura that said, I actually enjoy networking. Phainon shifted his weight, glancing down at his own boots. They had mileage. Character. Possibly dust from three zip codes ago.

He slapped his cheeks lightly, earning a few confused stares. Whatever. He was exhausted. Half the reason he was still upright was pure stubbornness.

His parents always said not to let the world’s mood become yours, but right now, the world was tired, overpriced, and smelled faintly of sanitizer.

“Next!”

The barista greeted him with a refined smile so professional it could’ve been part of the uniform.

“Good morning, sir. What can I get started for you today?”

He tried to sound confident. “Uh… just, uh, normal coffee.”

“One moment,” she said, scanning the screen. “Would that be drip, pour-over, or cold immersion single-origin?”

He hesitated. “…The one that costs less.”

That earned a micro-expression—something between pity and understanding. “Of course. That’ll be ready in about five minutes.”

“Thanks.”

Transaction complete. He stepped aside as the next customer—a guy in an immaculate coat and the confidence of generational wealth—ordered something that sounded like a chemistry equation.

Phainon found a seat at one of the polished chrome tables near the window and sat down, elbows resting against the reflective surface. He wasn’t even pretending to check his phone. He just stared, half-awake, watching the parade of shoes march by.

The place gleamed with ambition. Every sound—the hiss of steam, the faint clink of cups—felt like a reminder that he was now very much fucked.

Folks like him built fences.

Folks like them bought the land.

A match made in heaven, truly.

No wonder he was working here now.

He scrolled aimlessly through his inbox, thumb flicking through unread messages like it was a nervous tic. Half of them were from Kremnos HR— links to onboarding portals, cheery reminders about “integrating with our family,” and training modules that featured actors with unsettling eye contact. The other half were ghosts from Okhema—Re: Re: Re: Q3 Updates (FINAL FINAL), Workflow Review 2.1, Team Appreciation Lunch RSVP (Mandatory)—each one a fossil of better or at least simpler days.

He leaned back in his chair, the cafeteria’s chrome light glinting off the unread count climbing into the hundreds, until one name caught his eye in the sender column.

Caenis.

Of course.

It had all been fine and dandy after the merger. The big bosses had called it “a strategic alignment,” which everyone else correctly interpreted as “half of you will be unemployed by December.” Okhema staff had survived the transition mostly intact. There’d been meetings, rebranding, slightly different email signatures. The free snacks disappeared. The coffee somehow got worse.

Still, Phainon was managing.

Never mind the slow erosion of his mental health—or the quiet ache for a certain someone he’d promised himself not to think about. The new reporting system only crashed three times a week, his supervisor mostly ignored him, and no one had yelled at him in two full weeks. In office terms, that was practically a honeymoon phase.

Which was, naturally, the moment Caenis decided to transfer him out.

She hadn’t sent a formal email about it at first—she’d stopped by his desk in person, which was already a red flag. Caenis was the kind of woman who scheduled everything, including smiles. When she appeared unannounced, perfume the and ghost of a childhood sadness arrived ten seconds before her actual body, Phainon knew something was coming.

“Phainon,” she’d said, voice smooth as butter. “Can you come by my office later? Just ten minutes.”

“Sure,” he’d replied, already mentally writing his own obituary.

Her office, later that day, looked like a furniture catalog and smelled faintly of lavender disinfectant. She sat behind her desk like a queen behind her throne, hands folded neatly over a stack of papers she absolutely didn’t need.

“You’ve been selected,” she began, smile so sharp it could’ve filed patents, “to help Kremnos understand Okhema’s work culture. You’ll be our bridge between divisions.”

Phainon had nodded slowly, pretending to consider it. “Bridge, huh? Do I get a raise if someone decides to burn it?”

She didn’t laugh—just that tight, managerial smirk that meant she’d heard a joke and filed it under unhelpful commentary.

“It’s a good opportunity,” she said. “You’ll be representing our branch. Kremnos values initiative, and I think this will be a great fit for you.”

Translation: Get the hell out of my office and take your weird little energy elsewhere.

He’d tried to match her tone, sitting a bit straighter. “Of course, I’m happy to contribute.”

“Excellent. You’ll start next week. I’ve already put in the request with HR.”

“That fast?”

“Transition periods are smoother when people don’t overthink them,” she said, still smiling.

He’d smiled back. “Right. Wouldn’t want to clutter up the process with feelings.”

She tilted her head, that predatory kind of amusement flickering for a moment. “Exactly.”

By the time he’d left her office, the move was already finalized. Kremnos HQ. “Cultural integration role.” No raise, no warning, and definitely no choice.

He had nodded through it like he didn’t understand the underlying message. Said all the polite, grateful stuff. “Of course, I’m happy to contribute.” “That sounds like an honor.” “Thank you for trusting me with this opportunity.”

What he meant was: Please, for the love of God, let me keep my dental plan.

He’d known it wasn’t random. Caenis didn’t do random. She’d seen him that day with Mydei. He had noticed that after the incident, she’d looked at him differently. Too polite. The kind of nice that came wrapped around a knife.

Guess she figured he’d fit right in up here.

“Order for Phainon!”

He blinked out of the memory and stood up, grabbing his coffee from the counter.

“That’s me.”

He took a sip, grimaced at the bitterness, and smiled anyway.

What a joke.

A week in, and Phainon still wasn’t sure what exactly his job was. He’d finished all the onboarding videos, survived three icebreakers, and spent two days shadowing a guy named Theo who said “touch base” every second. His official title was Process Integration Assistant, which translated to: guy who updates spreadsheets nobody reads.

Every morning he told himself he was getting the hang of it. Every afternoon he proved himself wrong.

His cubicle—technically “a modular workspace,” according to Facilities— was wedged between a potted plant that looked perpetually on the brink and a printer that look wheezed like it had asthma. The walls were half-glass, half-fabric, designed for “collaboration” but perfect for hearing other people’s phone calls. Dual monitors blazed in front of him, both full of tabso he couldn’t remember opening. His Teams chat kept pinging with polite anarchy: people asking questions they could’ve answered themselves, project links leading to nowhere, a string of “welcome aboard!” messages he hadn’t known how to respond to.

Theo—his so-called mentor—had explained the job on day two with the confidence of a man who no longer remembered what his own position entailed. “You’ll be doing light integration cleanup. You know, low-stakes stuff. No pressure.” Which turned out to mean hours of reconciling duplicate entries from Okhema’s ancient systems with Kremnos’s overengineered new ones. It was like being a translator for two dialects of Excel that hated each other.

“Don’t worry,” Theo had said that morning, leaning against the cubicle wall with his third cup of coffee. “After a few weeks, it’ll click.”

Phainon had smiled. “What will?”

Theo had blinked. “You know… it.”

Lunch had come and gone, though he couldn’t really claim he’d eaten. He’d stared at the cafeteria board until everything started to blur—wraps, power bowls, something labeled Harvest Medley—and ended up settling for that one cup of coffee that somehow managed to taste both bitter and burnt.

Now, break time. Officially. Unofficially, the point of the day where everyone tried to act relaxed but still checked their notifications every thirty seconds. Most of his coworkers had already clustered into polite little circles, balancing biodegradable forks and conversation starters: “You settling in okay?”, “Did you see the new branding deck?” That sort of thing.

He didn’t feel like joining. The lounge was too loud, too open, too full of people who seemed to know how to perform friendliness in front of cameras.

So instead, he slipped his ID badge into his pocket and started walking.

The hallways at Kremnos HQ were sleek in that curated, minimalist way that made everything feel temporary. Glass walls everywhere, every surface polished to a quiet gleam. The floor plan was a maze of “collaboration zones” with names like Horizon and Nexus, each outfitted with couches nobody sat on. A digital sign scrolled updates about corporate wellness initiatives—something about mindfulness sessions on Thursdays, sponsored by a vendor whose name sounded suspiciously like a drug.

Phainon passed a small group near the espresso bar—someone from HR, a designer, and a man he vaguely recognized from a town-hall slideshow. They were mid-discussion about “streamlining inter-branch communication.”

“Half our emails get lost in translation,” the designer was saying.

“Between departments or languages?” the HR rep asked.

“Both.”

He kept walking.

It wasn’t that he hated it here. The place ran on order—cold, deliberate order—but there was a strange comfort in that. Things worked. The lights always came on, the air smelled faintly of perfume, and the coffee, while questionable, was consistent. He could adapt to that.

Still, every few steps, he caught himself scanning for exits, half-expecting someone to tap his shoulder and tell him there’d been a mistake.

The elevator was somewhere past the next glass corner. Or maybe two corners. Every hallway looked the same, like it had been designed by a committee that feared individuality.

As he walked, he told himself—again—that he was adjusting. That maybe next week, he’d stop double-checking every email before hitting send. That he’d figure out what “process integration” meant in practice. That he’d stop overthinking the pauses when people said his name like they weren’t sure it was his.

He was fine. Mostly.

And even if he wasn’t, he could fake it for another hour. Optimism, he decided, was just another task on the checklist. Something you renewed before it expired.

He straightened his badge and kept walking toward the elevator.

Phainon pressed the button and leaned against the wall, thumb worrying the corner of his badge. The little circle lit up blue, promising arrival sometime before retirement.

“Alright,” he muttered, “this is fine. You’re fine.”

He said it again, slower, softer, like maybe the words would sound truer if he gave them time to sink in.

He’d been through worse. Plenty worse.

He’d survived the Great Server Meltdown back at Okhema, the one where a week’s worth of data vanished because some intern unplugged the main router to charge their phone. He’d made it through four budget cuts, two audits, and that one all-hands meeting where the CFO cried halfway through the slides.

Before that—Missouri. He’d scraped ice off the inside of a farmhouse window in January, fixed a carburetor in the rain, and spent twelve hours herding cattle across a county line because someone forgot to lock the damn gate.

So no, a slow elevator and a few too many spreadsheets weren’t about to break him.

“Hell, you’ve got health insurance now,” he told his reflection in the metal trim, voice tilting almost cheerful. “Can’t scare me with a few slides and a temperamental management.”

The elevator light stayed stubbornly still. He sighed and tapped his badge against his chest, thinking that if he stared long enough, maybe it’d take pity on him.

“You’ve got this, Phainon,” he said, firmer this time. “You’re adapting. You got a desk, a decent chair, a… uh, Theo. You got direct deposit. That’s right. Every two weeks like clockwork. Look at you—living the dream.”

He almost smiled. Almost.

He’d landed in Chicago with two suitcases, a dying plant, and a savings account that wheezed every time rent was due. But he’d found his footing, mostly. He could navigate the trains without pulling up three maps. He’d stopped saying y’all every third word in meetings—well, mostly.

“Progress,” he told himself, nodding like it was official company policy.

Finally, the elevator dinged—a small, merciful sound.

“See?” he said, grinning as the doors slid open. “You stick it out long enough, life throws you a bone. An empty elevator. That’s a win right there.”

He stepped inside, shoulders loosening, optimism gathering itself for one last push. “That’s right. Nothing to it. You’ve got this. Nothing, and I mean nothing, can stop you now.”

He pressed his floor number. The button glowed a pleasant gold.

And right as he allowed himself that one small, earned breath of peace—

“Hold the door, please!”

The voice carried down the hall, quick and apologetic, shoes scuffing against tile.

Phainon’s eyes closed briefly. He sighed, the kind that came from somewhere deep, then stuck his hand between the doors before they could seal.

“’Course,” he muttered, still polite, still that good-natured steadiness his parents raised into him. “Would’ve been too easy otherwise.”

The elevator paused obediently. Phainon straightened his tie, expression settling back into its practiced calm.

“Alright,” he said under his breath, to the ceiling this time. “You can handle this too.”

The numbers above the door waited, glowing patiently.

Phainon plastered on a polite smile and called out, “No need to rush, I got it!”

It came out too cheerful—like he was auditioning for Employee of the Month—but fine. He could commit to the bit. Might as well.

Everything was alright.

Everything.

He said that, didn’t he?

He’d had worse.

God, he’d had worse.

He’d survived his upstairs neighbor’s month-long country music marathon (same three songs, same volume, all night). He’d figured out how to use the train without getting lost more than twice, survived a team-building retreat in Wisconsin that ended in a collective group cry, and even managed not to combust when his first paycheck bounced the same week his sister’s tuition was due.

He’d gotten through all of that. He could get through anything.

He was an adult. He paid taxes. He owned three identical button-ups and a microwave that only caught on fire once. He couldn’t keep falling apart over minor inconveniences.

“See?” he murmured, shoulders straightening as he waited by the elevator. “You’re okay. You’re okay. You’re—”

He paused, let out a breath, nodded at his reflection in the polished steel. “Alright, champ,” he told himself quietly. “Let’s take it easy today. No overthinking. No emotional breakdowns in public hallways. You got this.”

Everything was fine.

Perfectly fine.

Totally fine.

Which, naturally, is when the universe decided to test that theory.

He heard the echo of quick footsteps down the corridor—the brisk, businesslike kind that screamed “late for a meeting” and “probably important.” Phainon smiled faintly, the kind of automatic, polite curve of the mouth you gave coworkers in passing. He reached to hold the door—

“Thank—”

The voice hit him first.

Familiar. Calm. Just a little deeper than memory had kept it.

Then came the pause.

And the heartbeat that followed it.

Phainon looked up.

The world didn’t stop, exactly—it just went still in that quiet, cruel way a dream does right before it turns on you.

Because of course.

Of course.

Standing there, perfectly real and perfectly impossible, was the man he had maybe—probably—cried about on the phone with Stelle.

Stelle, who’d listened without interrupting while he rambled about fate and bad timing and “how the hell was I supposed to know he’s the goddamn CEO?” Stelle, who’d told him, “You’re living in a Wattpad story, babe,” and then, softer, “You’re an idiot, but I love you.”

The man he’d kissed.

The man who’d left.

No goodbye. No reason.

And Phainon had told himself it didn’t matter. That Mydei had his reasons. That maybe there was a world where CEOs disappeared mid-sentence because of work emergencies or divine intervention or—hell, he didn’t know. Anything was easier than believing it meant something.

But now—standing here, with light spilling harsh across polished marble floors—it mattered. Because Mydei was right there.

And he looked good.

Unfairly, cosmically good.

Binder in one hand, jacket folded over his arm, stride purposeful and steady. His sleeves rolled up, his tie loosened just enough to look human, and that faint frown—focused, impatient, utterly him. He looked like the kind of man who never lost his footing. Who never had to.

And Phainon hated how his heart leapt anyway.

“Thank y—” Mydei started again, looking up mid-step.

Their eyes met.

A breath.

Then another.

Two full seconds of recognition stretching far too long.

“…” Phainon said, eloquently.

“...” Mydei retorted, smartly.

Oh.

That was it—the flicker. Surprise, dawning understanding, and then that quiet, horrified oh no as the pieces clicked together in his head.

And through it all, Phainon’s smile didn’t move.

“Morning,” he said pleasantly, voice steady in that way only a man on the brink could manage.

Mydei opened his mouth—maybe to apologize, maybe to explain—but Phainon was already moving. His thumb found the “close doors” button with the singular conviction of a man choosing flight over fight. He pressed it once. Then again. Then several more times in what could only be described as moral panic disguised as composure.

“Wait—!”

Mydei’s binder hit the floor with a slap of scattered paper as he lunged forward. It wasn’t even graceful—he just ran for it, one hand outstretched like pure instinct had taken over.

DING.

The doors slid shut in his face.

The soft, soulless hum of elevator music filled the silence.

Phainon stared at the floor numbers blinking slowly upward. Inhale. Exhale. A polite, tight smile tugged at his mouth—the kind that said, I’m fine. This is fine. Nothing’s on fire.

Three floors passed like that.

At the fourth, the doors opened with a gentle chime. A chipper intern stepped in, coffee in hand, eyes bright. “Morning!”

Phainon didn’t move. “Mm,” he managed, still staring straight ahead like a hostage in a wellness ad.

The elevator hummed on.

Everything was fine.

That was what he kept telling himself anyway. It sounded better than “mostly functional.”

Phainon gripped his visitor badge a little too tight as the security gate hiccuped, buzzed, and tried to eat his ID. He tugged it free with a smile that barely qualified as polite.

“Welcome aboard, Phainon!” chirped the receptionist—bright, terrifyingly awake, and far too sincere for eight-thirty.

She remembered his name. Out of everyone walking through those glass doors, his.

Not reassuring at all.

“Thanks,” he said, a little flat. “Trying not to make a mess yet.”

Her laugh followed him past the lobby, light and genuine. It shouldn’t have stung, but it did.

Kremnos HQ was a maze pretending to be a building, every hallway identical, every surface too clean to feel real. Who designed this place— Sisyphus, with a grudge?

You’d think he’d know his way around by now.

He really should’ve.

But the universe—or maybe middle management—had a sense of humor. Someone was always asking him to deliver something to the other side of the building. Always across, never next door. If the company wanted to boost efficiency, they could start by issuing maps or hiring a sherpa.

Still, it was almost nostalgic. Almost.

Like his first weeks at Okhema—back when getting lost felt like an accident, not a pattern.

He got lost three times before lunch.

First: wandered into an HR wellness seminar. Someone pressed a stress ball into his hand and told him to “breathe through the tension.” He didn’t have the heart to say the tension had tenure.

Second: dead-ended into what he thought was a hallway but turned out to be a very convincing pane of glass. He stood there a beat too long, palm stinging, before muttering, “Jesus, you people really do love your glass.”

Third: wrong turn into a C-Suite Strategy Briefing. Twenty executives looked up in perfect synchrony. He froze mid-step, raised his coffee in silent apology, and backed out like a raccoon realizing it had wandered into daylight.

After that, he stuck to the stairwells. At least concrete didn’t lie.

By the time he finally found his department again, his phone was littered with three missed messages, two “where are you” pings, and one cheerful calendar invite titled Orientation Follow-Up (Optional 😊).

He dropped into his chair, exhaled, and stared at his monitor until his reflection blurred into the screen’s glare. Then he smiled.

The only real difference between this and his old routine at Okhema was that now he had to work a little harder to avoid a certain someone who knew he worked here.

Not that hard, right?

He could do that.

He could absolutely, definitely, without question do that.

Right.

Phainon had learned early that ignoring things was a legitimate workplace skill. The trick was to look busy enough that no one questioned your silence.

Like right now.

Two desks over, the kind of gossip that never actually stayed quiet drifted through the air.

“It’s just me, or has Mydei—ahem, boss—been moody again lately?”

“Moody?” someone snorted softly. “He’s not sleeping much. I saw him in at six this morning. Man’s got the kind of dark circles that scream existential crisis.”

“Didn’t something happen at that merger meeting?”

Phainon took a measured sip of water and pretended to scroll. The paper cup gave a brittle pop between his fingers.

“Wouldn’t know a thing about that,” he murmured, mostly to the water cooler, and dropped the cup in the bin before he could shred it completely.

He told himself it didn’t sting. He was fine. He was functioning. He even smiled when people talked to him. See? Thriving.

His coworkers were a treat.

“I love your accent!” someone chirped later that morning, eyes bright with that particular brand of curiosity that felt like touching glass with bare hands.

Phainon exhaled through his nose. “Thanks,” he said lightly, even though every muscle in his face wanted to fold in on itself.

“Oh, you’re from Okhema, right? Must’ve been… fun.”

“That must’ve been quite the adjustment for you.”

He nodded, smiled the practiced kind of smile that said please stop before I start crying or laughing, and quietly re-organized a file he’d already submitted. The sound of keyboard clacks made for decent white noise, at least.

It hadn’t taken long to figure out Mydei’s routine. Corporate calendars were an open secret, and people had a way of dropping details when they thought you weren’t listening.

So he built a system. Something neat and efficient—on paper.

Coffee breaks: two minutes after Mydei’s, assuming he actually took those.

Elevators: avoided entirely; stairwells didn’t ask questions.

Hallways: mapped to minimize risk.

Conference rooms: occasional hiding spots, though explaining why he was “reviewing acoustics” got awkward fast.

For a few days, it worked. The universe almost seemed merciful.

But every so often, he’d glance across the atrium or into a glass corridor and catch sight of someone—tall, coat slightly rumpled, binder tucked under one arm—pausing mid-stride. Searching, maybe. Looking around like he’d lost something he didn’t want to admit he had.

If Phainon didn’t know better, he’d swear Mydei was looking for him.

Not directly. Never directly. But there was a rhythm to it—the half-turn when a door opened, the distracted nods in meetings, the faint crease between Mydei’s brows when his gaze swept past a crowd and didn’t find what he wanted.

Yeah. No. Definitely was.

Which was exactly why Phainon doubled down on his escape artistry. If he moved fast enough, ducked at the right time, stayed just behind the reflective glare of glass, maybe he could pretend none of this existed.

By the time he collapsed back into his cubicle chair, the fabric squeaking in complaint, he let out a sigh that sounded suspiciously like surrender. He slumped until only his eyes cleared the top of the desk divider.

The screen’s glow reflected him faintly—rumpled tie, tired face, the picture of composure if you squinted hard enough.

Another day done.

Another day survived.

And for now, that was as close to peace as he was going to get.

His phone buzzed against the desk.

Phainon ignored it at first, chin propped on one hand, staring at the writing that had long since stopped making sense. Whoever it was could survive five more seconds without him.

Then it buzzed again—longer this time, stubborn.

He groaned, dragging himself upright, every vertebra in his back cracking like the soundtrack of defeat. The screen glared up at him, far too bright for someone whose soul had already clocked out for the day.

Unknown number. No—wait. Not unknown.

He blinked, leaning closer.

Dan Heng.

Oh.

Well, that was new.

His bad mood loosened, like the day suddenly remembered how to breathe again. It had been months since they’d talked properly—long enough that he’d half-assumed the archivist had gone off the grid again to dig through some forgotten library or commune with a stack of ancient scrolls.

Funny thing, how they even met. He had Caelus to thank—or blame—for that. The man somehow managed to be unemployed and cosmopolitan at the same time, drifting through Europe until one day he stumbled into March and Dan Heng somewhere in the U.K. (because of course he did). March had been photographing some cathedral, Dan Heng was there for research, and Caelus—well, Caelus was there because he “followed the cheap flight.”

One weird afternoon turned into a week of pub food and train hopping, and when Caelus finally wandered back home to Missouri, the friendship stuck. March and Dan Heng started visiting whenever they passed through the States, which meant Phainon eventually got pulled into the chaos too— Stelle and Caelus made sure of it.

Dan Heng had always been the calmest of them. The kind of calm that didn’t come from stillness but from quiet focus—like he could fit whole worlds into a sentence if he wanted to.

So yeah, seeing his name flash across the screen now… it did something funny to Phainon’s chest.

He scrubbed a hand over his face, half-smiling despite himself. “Of course it’s you,” he muttered. “Time zones don’t exist, do they?”

He swiped to answer. “Hello?”

Dan Heng was calling. Which, in Phainon’s world, meant one of two things: either the man had a question only the universe’s most obscure database could answer, or he just wanted to check in.

And somehow, the latter always caught him more off-guard.

The line clicked.

“Hello?”

“Dan Heng!” Phainon straightened automatically, grin breaking across his face before he could stop it. “Man, it’s been forever since we actually called each other.”

A quiet laugh. “It has. I was starting to think you forgot what my voice sounded like.”

“Please,” Phainon said, leaning back in his chair, “you think I’d forget that sleep-deprived poet tone of yours?”

“I’ll take that as a compliment,” Dan Heng replied, perfectly even—though Phainon could practically hear the smile hiding behind it.

“Yeah, yeah. How’ve you been anyway? Last I heard you were in—wait, was it Spain? Or that train museum in France? The one where you nearly got locked inside?”

“Switzerland,” Dan Heng corrected. “But yes, I stopped in France for a day. The archives there are… quiet. You can hear the wind moving through the cracks in the stone.”

Phainon huffed out a laugh. “Only you could make a drafty hallway sound poetic.”

“You’d change your mind if a stack of parchment fell on your head.”

He snorted. “Yeah, well, that’s what you get for touching things older than my grandpa.”

Dan Heng made a soft, amused sound. For a moment it felt like they were back on the couch in Stelle’s apartment again, several years ago, arguing about whose thesis was better.

“So,” Phainon said, the grin returning to his voice, “what’s the special occasion? Lost a bet? Got lonely? Or are you secretly dying and this is your final call to me?”

“Actually,” Dan Heng said, tone gentling, “I just wanted to see how you’re doing. March had mentioned you transferred departments.”

Phainon groaned, letting his head fall back against the chair. “Of course she did.”

“You settling in?”

“Trying,” he said, rubbing the back of his neck. “Building’s bigger than my hometown.”

“That’s not saying much, Phainon.”

“You’re right,” he admitted, smiling. “I’m being generous.”

That earned him another quiet laugh.

They slipped into easy chatter again—the kind that filled the quiet without needing to mean much. Dan Heng talked about train rides across Europe, the way the dawn light cut across the windows, the steady rhythm of the tracks beneath him.

“I swear,” Dan Heng said.  “it’s the only time the world feels balanced. Just motion and air and no reason to rush anywhere.”

“Sounds peaceful,” Phainon murmured.

“It is. But it’s strange.” A pause. “The more places you go, the more you start missing people instead.”

Phainon stared at the ceiling tiles, listening to the hum of the office beyond the cubicle walls. “Yeah,” he said softly. “Ain’t that a bitch.”

There was a long beat before Dan Heng spoke again, tone deceptively light. “Speaking of people—are you seeing anyone lately?”

Phainon blinked. “That’s a hell of a topic change.”

“I’m making conversation.”

“Uh-huh.” He pushed off from the desk, chair rolling a few inches. “Let me guess. March—or Cyrene, said something again.”

“I might have heard a few things.”

“Oh, for—of course you did.” Phainon dragged a hand down his face. “What was it this time? That I’m being dramatic again? In denial? That I cried to an Adele song?”

“‘Phainon’s pretending he’s not still hung up,’” Dan Heng quoted smoothly.

Phainon groaned so loud it echoed. “Lord help me if I end up falling for this man twice.”

Silence—then the quietest smile in Dan Heng’s voice.

“…You already did, didn’t you?”

“Go to hell, Dan Heng.”

“Geographically speaking,” he said mildly, “I might already be close.”

Phainon laughed despite himself, pressing a hand over his mouth. “You’re the worst.”

“And yet,” Dan Heng said, gentle as ever, “you still answer when I call.”

“Yeah,” Phainon admitted after a moment, voice softer now, the grin lingering even as it faded at the edges. “Guess I do.”

For a while neither of them spoke. The hum of static filled the silence— easy, comfortable, familiar. Phainon spun his chair once, the world blurring around him, before letting it drift to a stop.

In hindsight, he really should’ve seen this coming.

Especially after that conversation.

What conversation, you ask?

Well. Picture this: mid-afternoon at Castrum Kremnos HQ—the lull where people either scroll through docs pretending to work or stand in front of the fridge pretending to think. Phainon was doing the latter, except he wasn’t even pretending. He was just hiding.

He had one hand on the fridge handle, reading the same yogurt label for the third time, when the door swung open behind him. Two voices filtered in, that easy, clipped cadence of people who’ve survived too many meetings together and are now bonded through corporate trauma.

The first voice—impossible to mistake.

Ptolemy.

Loud, charming, the human equivalent of a LinkedIn post that actually gets engagement. Phainon had met him months ago at the mingling event, right before the whole “car ride with Mydei” fiasco. He’d hoped never to see him again.

The second voice was smoother, calm with a faint Balkan lilt. It had the practiced neutrality of someone who spent more time in airports than at home. He caught the name a second later.

“Leonnius,” Ptolemy said, somewhere near the espresso machine.

Right. That guy.

If Phainon had to guess, Leonnius was one of those diplomats—title vague, influence terrifying. The kind of man who could sit through a seven-hour negotiation without a single hair moving out of place.

“—He’s been miserable for weeks,” Ptolemy was saying, voice bouncing off the glass tiles. “You’d think someone ran over his cat.”

Leonnius didn’t miss a beat. “He doesn’t own a cat.”

“Exactly! That’s the problem. No emotional outlet. He’s haunting the office like a man one sad song away from writing a manifesto.”

The sound of a spoon clinking against a mug. “He drinks chamomile like it’s whiskey,” Leonnius added, dry as copy paper.

“God, yes. And that stare.” Ptolemy let out a theatrical sigh. “You ever see a grown man look that tragic before noon? I started apologizing before I even knew what for.”

Phainon blinked.

He didn’t know who they were talking about, but he had the sinking feeling he was about to.

“Apparently,” Leonnius went on, “it’s all over some… Phainon, was it? Guy?”

Phainon nearly dropped the yogurt.

He froze, half crouched, the refrigerator light glaring on his face like a spotlight. “Different Phainon,” he muttered to himself. “Common name. Happens all the time. Statistically possible.”

Ptolemy snorted. “Phainon? That’s not even remotely common. You ever met another Phainon, Leo?”

“Not personally,” Leonnius admitted, “but I’ve read one in a myth. Does that count?”

“Not really. Theo, maybe. Even an Alex. But Phainon? C’mon.”

Phainon mouthed a soundless oh my god to the dairy section.

“I remember Mydei mentioned something,” Leonnius said thoughtfully. “A falling out, perhaps. He didn’t elaborate. Just stared at the window like he was composing an elegy.”

“Classic,” Ptolemy muttered. “He’s got work, friends, actual things to do. But no—let’s brood by the window like an unpaid intern in a perfume ad.”

“You’re assuming he hasn’t written poetry about it.”

“…Has he?”

“I wouldn’t know,” Leonnius said in a tone that absolutely meant he did. He stirred his coffee with deliberate calm. “But if he starts quoting tragic verse at lunch again, I’m staging an intervention.”

Phainon’s stomach sank. Again?

That meant it already happened. Which meant they weren’t exaggerating.

“Oh, you’d love that,” Ptolemy laughed. “Standing there like, ‘Mydei, you are loved, but please stop reciting Sappho to the salad bar.’”

Leonnius made a dignified noise. “You’re mocking me, but it worked last time. Temporarily.”

“I’m not mocking, I’m admiring the commitment,” Ptolemy said. “But seriously—man’s in deep. Over some Phainon, no less.”

“Who,” Leonnius said mildly, “may or may not work here.”

Phainon went very still.

Ptolemy perked up. “Wait, that’s right! Didn’t I see that name in an internal memo last week? Something about an onboarding in the Kremnos division?”

He paused suddenly, tilting his head. “Could be coincidence, though.”

“Yeah, and I’m the CEO.”

“Traveling might’ve scrambled your memory again,” Ptomely said, taking a slow sip. “You really shouldn’t do six time zones in a week.”

“I’ll have you know I’m sharp as ever.”

“Of course,” Ptomely said smoothly. “Sharp as a butter knife.”

“Ha-ha. You know, some of us still have functioning brains.”

“Functioning? Debatable.”

Their banter trailed toward the door, still trading half-sincere insults as they left. The sound of the automatic lock clicking behind them was almost merciful.

Phainon straightened slowly, staring at his reflection in the stainless steel fridge.

“…Yeah,” he muttered, setting the yogurt back. “Should’ve seen that coming.”

And that, as it turned out, was the beginning of the end.

For whatever reason, afternoons at Castrum Kremnos had a way of testing one’s commitment to employment.

The air-conditioning always dipped too low after three. The lights buzzed faintly. Emails multiplied like they’d been left unsupervised. It was the hour when the soul grew tired before the body did.

So really, it shouldn’t have surprised Phainon that the next memorable event in his day was, apparently, an intervention.

It began innocently enough.

He was heading toward the elevators, rubbing the growing ache at the bridge of his nose and mentally negotiating with himself about whether he had the stamina for one more budget review, when someone called out behind him.

“Hey—you’re that transfer, right?”

Phainon turned. Halfway through putting on his polite corporate face, he found himself looking at two men who radiated the kind of practiced competence that came from surviving years of corporate trench warfare.

The first was tall, dark-haired, and wore a suit that somehow managed to look both expensive and lived-in—like he’d been in ten meetings already and still had energy for ten more. His smile was smooth, confident, and the kind that made people instinctively like him.

“Hephaestion,” he said, offering a firm handshake. “Corporate Strategy. Welcome to the circus.”

Phainon shook it. “Phainon. Accounting.”

The second man stepped forward with considerably less enthusiasm. Shorter, broader shouldered, with a relaxed slouch and headphones hanging around his neck like an accessory he forgot to take off.

“Peucesta,” he said. “AV and Cultural Operations.”

Which, based on his tone, translated to: I fix broken projectors, manage sound systems for events, and tolerate everything else.

Hephaestion’s smile only widened. “We’ve been meaning to say hi. Transfers usually get a whole welcome packet and a tour, but I think HR misplaced you in the system.”

“Wouldn’t be the first time something ate my name,” Phainon said, amused. “Still appreciate the effort.”

“Oh, trust me, we’re professionals,” Hephaestion said. “Castrum Kremnos has a reputation for being a maze. Half the departments don’t even know each other exist. You’d think they designed it this way on purpose.”

“Would explain the staircases,” Phainon mused. “Every day feels like a obstacle course.”

Hephaestion tapped his temple. “That’s the spirit. Only the strong survive.”

Peucesta snorted quietly. “You’re making it sound like a cult again.”

Hephaestion glanced at him, utterly unfazed. “Only a friendly one. We have snacks.”

Phainon cracked a smile despite his fatigue. These two were…oddly refreshing.

Conversation drifted easily after that—commutes, cafeteria food (“edible, but only in theory”), which departments were secretly gremlins, which ones held grudges. Peucesta chimed in occasionally with the dry comments of a man who’d seen too much malfunctioning equipment to be impressed by anything.

Phainon relaxed. They weren’t pushy. They weren’t intense. They weren’t —

“Heard you made quite an impression on our CEO.”

Oh.

There it was.

Phainon blinked once. “Pardon?”

Hephaestion’s smile didn’t falter, but there was a spark there—amused, perceptive. “Mydei. People talk, you know.”

Peucesta didn’t even pretend to be invested. “He says that to everyone,” he told Phainon, sipping from a mug. “Don’t let it get to you.”

Phainon stared at him, expression politely blank in the way that absolutely screamed: it has already gotten to me.

“Anyway,” Hephaestion continued breezily, “we were heading to lunch. Figured we’d bring you along. It’s practically tradition to make sure transfers don’t eat alone on their first month.”

There was no graceful way to decline without sounding rude, so Phainon followed—reluctantly, but resigned.

They took the elevator up to the 27th floor, where the “Client Hospitality Dining Room” lived. Technically not an executive cafeteria, but it might as well have been: quiet, polished, soft lighting, furniture that whispered fancy.

The moment they sat, the interrogation began.

“So,” Hephaestion said lightly, swirling his fork through his salad, “how do you feel about jazz?”

Phainon stared. “Jazz?”

“Any kind,” Hephaestion said. “Smooth, big band, fusion—very atmospheric genre.”

Peucesta lifted his eyes to the ceiling with the weariness of someone who had lived through this conversation at least five times. “Hephaestion, subtlety.”

“This is subtle,” Hephaestion insisted.

“No,” Peucesta said flatly. “It’s not.”

Phainon tried a polite smile. “Is this… some kind of survey?”

“Of course not,” Hephaestion said, much too quickly. “Though—speaking of scenery—have you been up to the 32nd floor garden yet? Spectacular spot. Very private. Great for… conversations.”

Phainon set his fork down and gave him a leveled stare.

“You boys takin’ a survey or matchmaking?”

Hephaestion didn’t blink. “Why not both?”

Peucesta sighed, long-suffering. “This is why HR blocks your emails.”

“It’s called team morale,” Hephaestion said, entirely unbothered. “Some of us care about fostering connection.”

“Some of us should be supervised,” Peucesta muttered.

Phainon groaned and let his head fall briefly into his hands. A tired laugh escaped him. “Lord, just smite me next time.”

He straightened, wiped any visible despair from his expression, and managed a strained smile. “Pardon me, but I think I’ll take my lunch to go.”

Hephaestion’s face fell, halfway into a protest—

—but Peucesta, moving with the resigned reflexes of someone who had done this before, calmly reached over and clapped a hand across Hephaestion’s mouth.

“We get it,” Peucesta said, muffled but comprehensible. “See you around.”

Phainon nodded, gathered his tray, and escaped with all the speed and dignity of a man fleeing an emotional ambush.

He didn’t slow down until he reached the glass doors at the end of the hall. Sunlight caught the floor, too bright after the dim dining room. He checked the time.

5:30.

“Figures,” he muttered.

Maybe a walk would help—air, distance, a little space to unclench his soul after whatever that lunch had been.

If divine smiting wasn’t available, fresh air would have to do.

Funnily enough, the sky had that flat, heavy look it got right before the clouds decided to punish everyone at once. Phainon noticed it the moment he stepped out of Castrum Kremnos’ revolving doors—still spinning a hair too fast, still threatening to smack someone’s backpack straight into traffic if they weren’t paying attention. He escaped without incident today, badge intact, dignity mostly intact, and he’d made it a full two minutes down the street with the illusion that maybe—just maybe—the universe had clocked out with him.

Then, inevitably, the universe remembered it had his number.

A cold drop hit the back of his neck. Another on his shoulder. Then a whole constellation of them.

“…Of course,” he muttered, staring up as the drizzle thickened into rain that meant business. “Sure. Why not. Was overdue anyway.”

Umbrella? Absolutely not. He’d left it at home in a rare burst of optimism. Jacket? In his locker. And he was not—under any circumstances—spending fifteen hard-earned dollars at the kiosk on the corner for something that looked like it would disintegrate the moment wind touched it.

He breathed in slowly, the kind of long inhale grown adults take when they’ve run out of creative swear words.

“Well,” he said to no one, “ain’t nothing rain can do that someone else hasn’t already tried.”

He rolled his shoulders back, braced himself, and stepped forward—

fwip.

An umbrella opened above his head.

Phainon jerked like it was thunder cracking right over him.

For half a second—one small, desperately human second—his chest loosened. Someone being kind. Someone stepping in. After a week that felt like getting sanded down on all emotional fronts, the tiny gesture hit him harder than it should’ve. His throat tightened. He blinked quickly, trying not to look like a man on the verge of crying over a piece of nylon fabric.

He turned, words already spilling out in relief.

“Thank y—”

They fell apart the moment he saw who it was.

Mydei stood there.

If the universe was throwing punches, this one was straight to the gut.

Rain slid along Mydei’s collarbone, sank into the loosened knot of his tie, clung to the rolled sleeves of his dress shirt. His hair was damp, not quite disheveled, but definitely far from the immaculate CEO look Phainon expected. He looked like a man who had walked out of a boardroom, down twenty flights of stairs, and straight into the storm without stopping long enough to breathe.

He also looked like a man who had not exhaled properly since the night everything had gone to hell.

“…You’ll catch a cold,” Mydei said softly.

Phainon blinked at him. Once. Twice. Slowly. His face barely moved, but something in him bristled.

“You’ll catch trouble if anyone sees you talking to me,” he answered, tone flat but not quite gentle. Not quite angry either—just tired. Depleted. The kind of tired that wasn’t from lack of sleep but from too much everything.

Rain filled the silence between them, soft and steady.

Mydei’s grip on the umbrella tightened. “I didn’t know you were… here,” he tried, voice quiet, like he was starting a conversation in a library instead of a storm. “At Kremnos , I mean. They didn’t tell me about the transfer list for the merger until last week and I—well. I figured you’d still be at Okhema.”

It wasn’t exactly small talk, but it wasn’t a justification either—just him reaching, clumsily, for anything Phainon might take.

Phainon let out a dry exhale that could’ve been a laugh if it had any strength left. “Didn’t plan to advertise it. Figured you had a company to run.” A beat. “And a panic button to hit, apparently.”

That hit. Mydei’s jaw twitched; he swallowed once, sharp and visible.

“I panicked,” he admitted. “That night. I know how it looked. I know it was —” His voice cracked, just barely. “It’s not an excuse.”

Phainon looked away, toward the reflections wobbling in the puddles on the street.

“I’d normally listen,” he said, quieter now. “But I’m real tired. And I just wanna go home before this rain decides to baptize me.”

Mydei’s expression softened, pained but not dramatic. He understood.

“Hell of a way to start a merger,” Phainon added, tone dry as the street wasn’t.

Mydei flinched like someone had tugged a string in his spine.

Then he breathed in, steadied himself, and said, “At least let me walk you. Wherever you’re going next.”

“Walking me out’s exactly the problem, ain’t it?” Phainon muttered. But there was less bite now, more weary honesty.

“Please.”

One word. Sincere in a way Mydei rarely allowed himself to be.

Phainon closed his eyes for half a second. Then sighed—the kind of sigh that sagged from bone to boots. He wasn’t strong enough right now to fight someone genuinely trying.

“…Fine.” He lifted one hand and gestured vaguely ahead. “I’m heading to the stop on Fourth. It’s close. Don’t panic—I’m not makin’ you trail me across the whole city.”

He started walking, deliberately not looking at Mydei.

Which, of course, meant he saw everything in his peripheral vision.

The way Mydei’s posture brightened, subtle but impossible to miss. The way his shoulders lifted just slightly, almost like a cat whose ears perked at its name. The way he had to catch himself from stepping too quickly to keep up, smoothing the motion into something normal.

It was almost cute.

Almost.

“Of course,” Mydei murmured, falling into step beside him. And without hesitation, he angled the umbrella to cover Phainon. Rain clung to Mydei’s exposed shoulder, but he didn’t even blink.

Phainon said nothing.

He didn’t need to.

The rain softened around them—not stopping, but easing into something gentler, as if the city had decided to give them five minutes of grace.

They fell into step the cautious way people did when they weren’t sure who was following whose lead. The umbrella forced them a little closer than either would’ve chosen, shoulder to shoulder whenever the sidewalk narrowed, their steps syncing only because the alternative was bumping elbows every three seconds.

Neon signs blurred like watercolor behind the wet air. Cars hissed by in the distance. It wasn’t awkward. Not yet. But it wasn’t comfortable either.

Mydei kept glancing over—quick, guilty peeks, never longer than a heartbeat. Phainon counted the fifth one before sighing through his nose.

“Most folks,” he muttered, “tend to look forward when they’re walking. Helps keep the hospitals empty.”

Mydei’s face turned pink so fast Phainon almost forgot he was irritated.

“Yes, I know,” he said. “I was making sure you weren’t freezing.”

Phainon side-eyed him. “Mydei, I grew up in a place where the wind’ll take your hat and your dignity in one blow. I’ll survive a drizzle.”

“That doesn’t answer the question.”

“It wasn’t a question.”

“…Well, it felt like one.”

A reluctant huff escaped Phainon—not quite a laugh, but close.

They turned onto a quieter street where puddles shimmered under yellow streetlamps. Mydei angled the umbrella toward him again, which forced his own sleeve into the rain. Phainon noticed, and irritation tugged at him—not angry, but tired, the kind of tired that came from months of not knowing where he stood with someone.

“You ain’t gotta do that,” he said. “I’m not gonna shrivel up because my shoulder gets wet.”

Mydei’s mouth twitched, not quite a smile. “I know. But it’s rude to offer someone shelter and then hog it.”

“That ain’t shelter. That’s you holding an umbrella like it’s a peace treaty.”

“A peace treaty implies we were at war.”

Phainon snorted. “We kinda were.”

That shut Mydei up.

Phainon shoved his hands in his pockets, fighting the sting of frustration rising up again.

He kissed me, he ran, he’s my damn CEO, and now he’s here playin’ umbrella escort like this ain’t complicated as hell.

He tamped the thought down before it showed on his face.

“You know,” he said after a moment, “you don’t gotta walk me home. I’m a big boy. Been walkin’ in storms since I was eight.”

“I know.”

“So why’re you still here?”

Mydei hesitated—visibly, audibly, almost painfully.

“…Because I didn’t want you walking alone in the rain.”

Phainon’s jaw clenched. Not because it was a bad answer—not because it was untrue—but because it was too gentle, too careful, too close to everything he’d been trying not to think about.

He didn’t respond.

They walked the last block like that: Mydei quietly attentive; Phainon pretending he wasn’t noticing.

The street split at a wide corner. One path toward Phainon’s stop; the other back toward the business district. Phainon stopped beneath a dim streetlight, water dripping from the brim of the umbrella.

Mydei stopped with him, instinctively.

“Well,” Phainon said, rubbing the back of his neck, “this is me.” His voice came out rougher than he meant. “Thanks for the—uh—overhead protection. And, I dunno. The company, I guess.”

“Anytime,” Mydei said.

Phainon tried a smile. It wobbled like a bad table leg.

“Right. Well. Have a good evening.”

He stepped back.

Mydei reacted without thinking—his hand caught Phainon’s wrist. Warm. Surprising. Firm enough that Phainon froze, heartbeat lurching like someone had kicked it out of rhythm.

Mydei seemed to realize what he’d done a second too late; he released him instantly, clearing his throat, fingers flexing once in apology. Then he held out the umbrella handle.

“Take it.”

Phainon blinked at him. “You’re wetter than I am.”

“It’s fine.”

“Mydei, your shirt is plastered to you like you’re auditionin’ for a sad music video.”

“My walk’s close.”

“You’re still—”

“Yes,” Mydei cut in, “I’m still giving it to you.” He nudged the handle toward him. “Return it when you can.”

Phainon opened his mouth to protest. He wasn’t sure if he was more annoyed or more touched, and either way he didn’t want it to show. But Mydei didn’t give him the chance—he placed the umbrella into Phainon’s hand, wrapped his fingers around the handle with a careful, deliberate press of his palm, and stepped back with a nod.

“Good evening, Phainon.”

Before Phainon could respond—before he could decide whether to say thank you or ask him why the hell he cared so much—Mydei turned and walked away.

Phainon stood at the corner, soaked and staring after him, the umbrella limp in his hand.

“…He really just—” He tipped his head back, letting out a tired, breathless laugh. “Damn sneaky bastard.”

Later—hours later, after dripping his way into his place and shaking off the night—he noticed the initials lightly carved into the wooden handle.

It wasn’t fancy. Wasn’t even intentional, probably. Just his name.

But it was enough.

Just an excuse to see him again.

The bar looked like it had already put one boot in bed.

Most of the lights had been dimmed to that warm, syrupy amber that clung to the wooden beams and made shadows stretch slow across the floor. The jukebox hummed low, a lazy old thing refusing to fully quiet down, and every table had its chairs flipped upside down—every table except the one in Phainon’s corner.

Cipher had left that one alone for him. Whether it was pity or poor judgment was anyone’s guess.

The fryer clicked as it cooled, the sound sharp in the otherwise settled hush, and a mop bucket sat forgotten in the corner from when Cipher decided she’d “handle that later.” She never did.

And on that one lonely chair sat Phainon, hunched forward like he was trying to fold himself in half and disappear.

His elbow dug into the varnished counter, cheek mashed into his palm. The cocktail in front of him had gone mostly water, ice floating like it had given up a long time ago. He stared at it with the single-minded misery of a man who absolutely did not need another drink but desperately wanted one.

A low mutter escaped him—half sigh, half complaint, all pitiful.

Cipher caught it instantly.

She was only a couple feet away, wiping foggy glasses with the smooth, practiced rhythm of someone who’d survived far too many closing shifts. Her bracelets clinked together in light metallic ticks, and her tailored suit jacket shifted as she leaned one hip against the bar, giving him a stare sharp enough to cut.

“Lord above, you are just a picture,” she drawled, amusement sliding warm under her tone. “What’re you even doing, Deliverer boy? Tryingvto win the award for Most Dramatic Man Alive?”

She tapped his glass with a fingernail—once, twice—as if checking for signs of life.

Phainon didn’t lift his head. Just groaned deeper into his palm, voice muffled.

“Cipherrrr. What do I doooo…”

“You stop mopin’ in my bar like a kicked possum, that’s what.” She swapped glasses, slung a towel over her shoulder. “Mercy. You’re gay as hell, sugar, it ain’t that complicated.”

He made a wounded grunt, the kind he’d probably deny making later. “I am not—well—I mean—that’s not—okay but—”

Cipher flicked a hand, dismissive, tolerant, fond.

“Hush. You like him. Big shocker. Men that pretty turn all of us stupid sooner or later. Nature’s never been kind in that department.”

She shelved another glass. Her tone settled into that soft scolding she reserved for stray dogs and men who didn’t know what to do with their feelings.

“And don’t you dare act like you ain’t been pacin’ around here all evening like you’re halfway through writin’ sad country lyrics. You came because you needed to vent. Lucky for you, I’m a generous woman.”

“Are you?” Phainon muttered, barely lifting his eyes.

“Debatable,” she said breezily. “But I let you in after hours, didn’t I?”

He gave a small grunt—a grunt that carried mild gratitude, mild skepticism, and mild suffering all smashed into one sound.

Cipher leaned her hip harder into the counter, squinting at him like she was debating whether to shake him or hug him. She eventually settled for neither, plucking his glass away instead.

He immediately reached for the bottle.

“Nope.” She smacked his hand with a practiced crack. “Yeah, no. You’re cut off ’fore you start crying on my counter. Got enough stains I regret.”

Phainon groaned again, dragging his fingers down his face. “You’re cruel.”

“Mm-hm. I sleep fine.” She propped her hands on the counter and looked him over. “And now real talk—how in the hell did you not know who he was?”

That sliced straight through the fog.

Phainon’s head snapped up, eyes wide. “Wait—what?”

Cipher raised a brow like this was common knowledge.

“Boy works half the business circles I deal with. Hell, we were at the same university for a hot minute.”

Phainon choked, coughed, slammed a fist to his chest like he’d swallowed a shard of glass. “You—you WHAT—”

“Sit still,” she said, already turning away. “Gettin’ you some water before you pass out on my shoes.”

“That’s—not—Cipher, hold on—what do you mean you were—”

“Well how else you think I know him?” she called, rummaging for a clean glass. “Ain’t like handsome men rain from the damn ceiling.”

Phainon opened his mouth, ready to argue, but the thought tangled up on itself and stalled.

Because—actually—that tracked. All of it. The weird timeline, the Massachusetts comments, the short-lived dropout period she never explained, the sudden return years later with two degrees and a smug grin. It… made sense.

Too much sense.

Cipher slid the water toward him and rested her arms on the counter, posture loose, almost contemplative. When she spoke again, her voice dipped quieter—not sad, just reflecting something she rarely let anyone see.

“I didn’t finish at the time,” she said, thumb running over a faint scratch in the bar. “Life got… complicated.” A short huff of breath. “Went back a few years ago—you remember that. Got my degrees proper.”

Phainon did remember. He remembered her calling him, breathless and triumphant. He remembered how proud he’d been, even now, drunk and miserable.

Cipher tapped the counter, the click steady and sure.

“Hospitality, consumer psych… little marketing tricks. Enough to make grown men empty their wallets if I smile right.”

Her voice kept drifting—half to him, half to herself—as she wiped at spots that weren’t there.

“Anyway—it ain’t a story worth fussin’ over. Met your man in one of those elective seminars. Logistics or somethin’. Quiet, mature boy, smart as hell.” She waved a hand lightly. “Now, if you’ll allow me, I’ll recount our exact meetin’ in exquisite detail, loverboy. It started when—”

Phainon blinked.

Her voice softened at the edges, curling in that familiar Southern cadence she didn’t use as much anymore. Somewhere between the alcohol, the dim lighting, and the warmth in her tone, everything blurred.

Her accent wasn’t nearly as thick as when he first met her.

He hadn’t noticed the change until now.

What a strange thing to realize.

Phainon stared at her, glassy-eyed, as Cipher continued on—completely unaware she’d lost him to memory and liquor both.

Phainon wasn’t sure if he was getting sentimental, or if the whiskey had finally decided to wring his heart out like a dish rag. Either way, something loosened in him—just enough for old memories to start peeling up around the edges, curling back like wallpaper in a humid room.

His head dipped onto his folded arms. A low sound—half sigh, half growl —slipped out before he could stop it.

“Why’s it always you I end up cryin’ to,” he muttered, voice thick and muffled by the crook of his elbow.

Cipher didn’t even pause wiping the bar. “Because you ain’t got an ounce of pride left in you once you’re drunk.”

He made a noise that could’ve been a laugh or a wounded cough.

“And,” she continued, flicking a crumb into her palm, “because I don’t let you run off and do somethin’ stupid.”

“Well,” he said, dragging the word, “that’s kind of you.”

“I’m an angel,” she deadpanned.

“Mm.”

She snorted—light, dismissive, fond. No judgment, no pressure. Just the quiet hum of the closed bar around them and the low amber lighting pooling on their faces.

And maybe it was the warmth, or the silence, or the fact his guard was already slipping—but his thoughts drifted toward her again. Not Cipher as she was now—propped on one hip, plenty of attitude, lecturing him about hydration—but the Cipher he’d met years ago—or more accurately—pieced together. A story made out of scraps she’d dropped accidentally or let slip when she was tired, when her walls had hairline cracks in them.

He remembered the first time she’d mentioned her birthplace. New Orleans. Some tight-knit Greek neighborhood tucked between tourist traps and trouble. She’d talked about it the way old folks talked about their favorite church pew—familiar, frayed, and stubbornly theirs.

Her parents were gone by the time she could remember anything clearly. Car wreck, storm damage—she switched explanations depending on who she was talking to and how nosy they were being. What mattered was simple: she refused to get swept into foster care, refused to be taken from her block, from the people who fed her more often than they lectured her.

So she survived the only way a kid in that kind of place could.

Quick fingers, quicker eyes.

Small cons, small lies.

Charm used like a bottle cap, flicked open whenever she needed something.

Phainon found himself smiling—crooked, reluctant, but warm.

Cipher glanced over. “What’re you smilin’ at, beefcake?”

“Somethin’ dumb,” he murmured.

“You think about plenty dumb things.”

“Appreciate the reminder, sweetheart.”

She pointed her towel at him. “Call me sweetheart again and I’m puttin’ lemon in your next beer.”

“Pumpkin,” he countered lazily.

She narrowed her eyes. “You’re playin’ with God’s animals.”

He huffed a tired laugh, the kind that softened the lines around his mouth. With Cipher, it was easy—too easy—to slip back into the way he talked growing up. Maybe it was the liquor. Maybe it was her. Or maybe it was the fact he still remembered those damn coworker from earlier who’d told him they “loved his accent,” and he was still mildly irritated about it.

Pa always said: Be polite to women, even when they’re bein’ weird as hell.

So he’d thanked her, stiff as a two-by-four.

Didn’t mean he liked it.

His eyes drifted back to Cipher. He thought of the secondhand pieces he’d gathered over time—the only three things she’d ever said about her first arrest.

“I stole stuff. Not proud. Needed to.” ”Juvie sucks.” “Missouri was better.”

That was all she’d given him.

Everything else, he had filled in with his own imagination—pictures of a teenage Cipher tearing down broken New Orleans sidewalks, cops on her heels, her grinning like she’d invented trouble. He could see it clear as day: her rounding a corner, skidding on beat-up sneakers, clutching stolen hoop earrings like trophies.

The image made him snort into his arm.

Cipher shot him a look. “What now?”

“Nothin’, Pumpkin.”

She groaned. “I will end you.”

He just smirked into his sleeve.

His thoughts wavered again, drifting to the morning years ago when Cipher had stayed with his family. He’d woken to the smell of coffee and found her in the kitchen with his mother, talking soft—too soft for Cipher. He’d only caught the tail-end of it, but he remembered the name.

The “older Greek lady.”

Aglaea.

Back then, Cipher had tried to play it off—pretended no one knew who that woman would become in her life. Pretended Phainon hadn’t heard anything.

Aglaea still ran her garment shop—fancy now, all draped windows and mannequins with elegant necks—but that had always been her first love, long before Okhema and its gleaming tech swallowed her schedule. Maybe that was why she’d been quick to merge the companies. Maybe she wanted her hands back in fabric. Needles. Silk. The things that made her light up.

If that was the Aglaea Cipher met as a kid, then she must’ve been younger, newer—traveling state to state, hustling for suppliers, stitching together the bones of a dream.

Cipher had once let slip—just once—the outline of their first meeting.

Aglaea was in New Orleans.

Cipher lifted her wallet.

Aglaea caught her instantly.

And instead of pressing charges, the woman bought her a meal and talked to her the way adults should talk to kids: steady, gentle, real.

Something about that must’ve struck deep. Cipher never explained what.

When they finished eating, Aglaea gave her a burner phone.

According to Cipher, the advice was simply:

“Call if you need me, Cifera.”

Cipher didn’t call.

Not until years later—after something went wrong back home. Something she never talked about. She ran north on grit and panic, hitchhiking through Arkansas, limping through Missouri, sick and starving and stubborn as hell.

He hated remembering the end of that journey.

A teenager collapsing on the rural highway outside his hometown.

Skin dull. Eyes too big.

Clothes hanging on her like she’d been washed out by rain.

His parents found her first.

Cipher always insisted she “just fell over a lil’ bit.”

He’d seen the photos.

She had been gone.

Phainon blinked hard, jaw tightening. The bar lights blurred faintly at the edges.

“Hey.” Cipher snapped her fingers. “Quit starin’ holes in my countertop. You’re thinking too loud.”

He lifted his head a little, cheeks flushed from alcohol, eyes tired and a little raw.

“M’not thinkin’.”

“Uh-huh. And I’m the Queen of France.”

A rough, unwilling laugh slipped out of him.

Cipher placed a hand on one hip, smug. “There he is.”

He didn’t answer, just sank back down again, cheek pressed to his arm, letting the room tilt gently like a rocking boat. The quiet wrapped around them—warm, familiar, lived-in.

And despite everything—despite the road she’d crawled through to get here —he was grateful.

Maybe it was fate she ended up in Missouri.

Maybe—

She stayed with them a long while after that.

Him and his family, he meant—though in that first month, Cipher acted like the whole house might vanish if she breathed wrong. His parents didn’t make a fuss about it. They were the type who believed in feeding someone before interrogating them, and they fed her like she’d walked in starving. Maybe she had.

Cipher didn’t know what to do with that kind of gentle consistency. Phainon, at thirteen, didn’t know what to do with her either.

He remembered her then as this brilliant-chaos older girl who could lie smoother than sugar water but still cried silently in the bathroom while wrapping gauze around her own hand. She’d curse under her breath in some tangle of half-Louisiana vowels and half-something-foreign, trying not to drip blood on his mom’s floor. She swore she’d stay “just a week, promise.”

A week became three.

Three became months.

Nobody mentioned it.

Not his father. Not his mother. Not Cyrene, who simply started leaving out an extra bowl at dinner.

And just like that, a year folded itself quietly behind them.

No dramatic speeches about family or belonging. Just dishes drying on the rack, winter boots by the door, Cipher and Cyrene arguing over who got the last piece of cornbread. Little moments that stacked into something solid.

They sheltered her, fed her, eased her back into being young again. And they talked. Lord, there was so much talking.

Especially from Phainon.

Back then he was a relentless chatterbox, a one-boy radio station. Cipher called him “loud as a damn cicada,” but she still listened every time. She’d sit at the kitchen table with her arms crossed, pretending she didn’t care about his rambling play-by-play of school drama, or his theories about why the neighbor’s goat hated him, or his earnest pride about Cyrene winning her science fair.

Cipher pretended she didn’t like those stories—but her eyes always softened somewhere around the middle.

It was the first steady friendship either of them had.

Though, neither had the vocabulary to say so.

Eventually the morning came when Cipher decided to leave.

She didn’t make an announcement. Phainon just woke up to find her by the counter, backpack slung over one shoulder, face a careful blank. The kind of blank people wear when they’re bracing for something.

Before she went, she made a call.

Aglaea arrived that afternoon.

Their meeting wasn’t dramatic either. The older woman stepped through the door, introduced herself, thanked his parents with a quiet sincerity that made even his dad straighten up. She looked around the house—not judging, not pitying, just… acknowledging it. Respectfully. Like she was filing away the fact that these were the people who kept Cipher alive this long.

Phainon remembered thinking she didn’t look like the type who’d pick up kids off the street. But she talked to Cipher like she’d been waiting to see her again for a long time.

Maybe that was why, years later, when Phainon dragged himself to Chicago broke, raw, and newly dumped, Aglaea didn’t hesitate before offering him a job. One phone call, one favor, and suddenly he had rent money.

Almost made him jealous.

Almost.

But when it came to Cipher, jealousy never stuck. She deserved good things. And if good things meant people showing up for her, then fine— he’d take his pride and sit on it.

Funny thing was, Cipher had been jealous of him too, back in the early days. Not out loud, but in the tightness of her shoulders whenever his parents hugged him, or the way she went quiet when Cyrene ran to show him something. Two kids with two different kinds of missing pieces. They didn’t talk about it then. They barely talk about it now.

Cipher left Missouri with her health back but nothing else.

She thanked his parents until her face turned red. Tried to thank Aglaea too —softly, like someone unused to gratitude. Promised she’d pay them back even though everyone insisted she didn’t owe a cent.

She headed east.

That was the last time he saw her in person until adulthood, though she kept calling the house. She’d ring up Cyrene asking about school, or ask his mother for recipes, or pretend she wasn’t checking on Phainon when she very obviously was. Once he got his own phone, she blew that up too.

Then came Massachusetts—“far, civilized, full of places nobody knows you,” she’d said. She collected scholarships like stray pennies; Aglaea covered the rest.

Cipher claimed she studied “somethin’ that makes folks spend money wrong.” Marketing, psychology, economics—Phainon never got them straight. Just knew she was damn good at it.

Turned out she attended the same elite university Mydei later graduated from, which he just discovered. It explained a lot about the way she talked around certain polished types.

He remembered the night she called him four states over sobbing—real crying, not her usual annoyed sniffles—because she’d actually graduated. He’d sat on the back porch staring at the Missouri stars, tearing up right along with her. Cyrene pretended not to notice, but left tissues by his elbow anyway.

Then came Chicago.

Cipher liked the city because it let her build something without drowning in East Coast noise. Close enough to Missouri that she didn’t lose that part of herself. Cheap enough to invest. Rough enough to respect her.

Aglaea funded her early. Cipher hustled the rest. She knew everyone now— bartenders, bouncers, accountants, corporate sharks and shadowy characters who owed her favors. Loved money, sure, but loved her people more.

When she called and breathed, “I’m opening  it. A real place. Mine,” he cheered—whooped in a full-body, obnoxious type of joy—and Livia, whose spare room he was staying in, hollered through the wall for him to shut up.

He felt that pride again now—sharp, warm, a little drunk.

A laugh escaped him, sudden and bright.

Cipher looked up from cleaning the bar. “What’s funny with you?”

He exhaled, slow and heavy, heart right at the surface. Before he could swallow them, the words slipped out:

“I’m… I’m so proud of you…”

Soft. Slurred. Honest.

Cipher went still like someone hit pause.

Her eyes widened. Her cheeks flushed hot. She stared at him like he’d just offered to adopt a stray possum on the spot.

“The hell you sayin’?” she muttered, scandalized.

He tried to explain, but the attempt melted into nonsense.

“You’re jus’… y’know… good. An’—I’m—proud. Real proud. Me. You. Somethin’.”

Garbage. Complete linguistic trash.

Cipher sputtered, ears red all the way to the tips. “Alright—okay—enough. Don’t—look, thank you, damn.” She scrubbed a glass like she was trying to polish a hole straight through it. “Hate when you get sentimental,” she grumbled, voice a little wobbly.

She checked the clock, sighed, and moved through her final closing sweep —flipping stools onto tables, wiping sticky rings off the counter, muttering about “men who drink my sweet tea liquor and turn philosophical.”

Phainon watched her, one eye open, mostly slumped in his chair. He felt a touch guilty for keeping her after hours.

A touch.

Almost.

“So,” Cipher drawled, one hip braced against the counter, towel slung over her shoulder like a warning sign, “weren’t you yappin’ ’bout your boytoy earlier?”

Phainon’s head shot up so fast the overhead lights streaked.

“Cipher—no, come on—don’t call him that,” he groaned, stretching her name like it was stuck to his tongue. “Why would you—why would you even say it like that?”

Cipher winced, eyes closing as if bracing for impact.

“Should’ve kept my mouth shut,” she muttered.

Too late.

Phainon inhaled once—then the dam broke.

“I thought he was such an asshole,” he started, waving one arm like he was directing traffic, “and he is, don’t get me wrong, he absolutely is. He’s got that look—you know the one—where he’s starin’ at you like he’s calculating the weight of your soul? That face? I hate that. I hate him.”

Cipher made a quiet, unimpressed “mm,” wiping a glass that had never been dirty.

“But then,” Phainon continued, shoulders slumping as the honesty spilled out, “he’ll go and do somethin’ stupidly kind outta nowhere. Not even normal kind—like quietly thoughtful. Like he thinks I won’t notice.” He scoffed. “Please. I grew up fixin’ fences in the dark, I can hear a mouse breathe in a hayloft. I notice everything.”

“Hm,” Cipher acknowledged, switching to a glass that also didn’t need attention.

“And he’s got this—this sense of responsibility that makes the rest of us look like we’re just playin’ at bein’ adults. I swear, he carries every problem like it’s a fragile little bird he’s scared of crushing! Doesn’t complain. Doesn’t make a show of it. Just—handles it.” He laughed once, low and disbelieving. “And when he goes quiet? That’s him thinking. Not checking out. Thinking. And you can feel it in the air like a storm coming. It’s—hell, I dunno. It does somethin’ to me.”

He sagged down onto his folded arms, fingers idly tapping the wood in a rhythm he didn’t notice.

Cipher didn’t interrupt. She didn’t have to.

Phainon was long gone.

“And—God help me—his body,” he said, half-whispering it as if the Lord Himself might walk in. “What in the world is he even built for? He’s got shoulders like he was put together by someone real fond of overkill. And those arms—good Lord. I’m not even exaggeratin’. I’ve seen tractors with less horsepower.”

Cipher’s towel paused mid-wipe.

Phainon kept going, helpless.

“And it’s like—how is any man supposed to think straight when he leans over you? He’s tall for no reason. He stands next to me and suddenly I’m back on the farm starin’ up at the water tower feelin’ like I’m about to get baptized by God himself. He’s not even taller than me! And nobody needs a chest like—”

Cipher slammed the glass down.

“Alright. Enough.”

Her eyebrows climbed halfway to the ceiling.

“That’s too much information for one poor woman to bear.”

Phainon blinked up at her. “You asked.”

“No,” she corrected. “I made the mistake of speakin’. Don’t twist it.”

He sighed, face dropping back to his arms. “I’m doomed.”

Cipher stilled.

Utterly.

Towel halfway to the sink.

Eyes narrowed, mouth tightening, brain spinning in slow circles like a dog realizing it’s about to do something real stupid.

“Oh, Lord,” she muttered. “I cannot believe I’m even thinking ‘bout helping you two fools with your little lover’s mess.”

Phainon raised his head an inch. “…what?”

“Nothing,” she said instantly, snapping the word like a mousetrap.

But she kept muttering, pacing behind the bar—quiet curses, soft groans, the sound of a woman preparing to commit to a mistake she’d deny in court.

Phainon squinted blearily. “Cipher… somethin’ wrong?”

She dragged a hand down her face. “Angels above, I cannot believe I’m about to get dragged into this. Y’all are givin’ me gray hairs faster than hurricanes roll in.”

“Cipherrr—”

“Fine,” she snapped. “I’ll help. There. Happy?”

Phainon blinked, utterly lost. “Help with… what?”

“Nevermind,” she repeated with finality. “If you ask again, I’m leavin’ you in the alley.”
