Before he could untangle that sentence, she reached beneath the counter, grabbed a bottle of water, and thunked it in front of him with the force of righteous judgment.

“Drink.”

He reached. Missed. Reached again. Got it.

And promptly managed to choke on the first swallow.

Cipher sighed, long and deep. “Pitiful.”

She rounded the bar, slid his arm over her shoulder, and hauled him upright. He did not help.

“You’re stayin’ at my place,” she informed him. “Ain’t lettin’ you wander off and get yourself flattened by a bus. And don’t forget to pay your damn tab later.”

Phainon leaned on her like a wet coat. “Cipher… you’re a good woman.”

“Don’t butter me up, farm boy. You’re heavy.”

They reached the door.

Cipher shoved it open with her hip.

“Tomorrow,” she muttered, “is gonna be real eventful, Deliverer boy.”

Phainon, drunk and miserable and sloppy-honest, whispered, “That… sounds ominous.”

Cipher snorted. “That’s ‘cause it is.”

The door swung shut behind them, leaving the bar in peace for the first time all night.

Wind skimmed off the river like it was trying to make a point.

Phainon walked anyway, shoulders tucked against the cold and the weight of the umbrella strapped to his bag—a sleek, stupidly over-engineered thing with reinforced ribs and a grip molded so clean it felt like it should come with a warranty card. Too nice for him. Too nice to ignore. Too nice to forget who handed it to him in the first place.

He really wanted to return it.

Returning it meant seeing him.

Seeing him meant—

Yeah, no. Not here. Not where his face could do something stupid and end up in a stranger’s Instagram background.

He tightened the strap and muttered, mostly to the wind, “Should’ve left it with you, jackass.”

A little too honest, a little too weary. Whatever. The river wasn’t gonna judge.

The whole day had been like that—tiny reminders he didn’t ask for, nudging him in the ribs. And Cipher, apparently not content with letting him stew in peace, had swung by his desk that morning like a specter of obligation.

No greeting. No knock. She just snapped her fingers in front of his face when she realized he’d spaced out, then dropped a glossy brochure across his keyboard. Something with flowers. Bright ones.

“Fresh air’s good,” she’d said. “Go touch some grass.”

And she’d walked off like she hadn’t just said something that unhinged.

He’d stuffed the brochure into his bag without looking. With Cipher, it could’ve been a pamphlet for a gardening workshop or a multi-level marketing scheme for artisanal moss. Hard to tell.

Twilight edged over the river by the time he drifted toward a food cart with a hand-painted sign and a guy behind the grill who looked like he’d been working the same corner for twenty years.

“One chili dog,” Phainon said, “extra onions.”

The vendor gave him a look halfway between challenge and amusement.

“Extra onions? On a weekday night? You trying to lose friends or keep ’em?”

“I got a durable constitution,” Phainon said. “And nobody worth impressing tonight.”

“Attaboy.” The man constructed the thing with the care of a surgeon.

Phainon took the first bite and genuinely felt his knees loosen. Food had always done that to him—been his best cure-all since he was a kid with an appetite that made grown relatives stare in disbelief. Chicago hadn’t helped. Too many hole-in-the-wall places serving comfort in paper boats. He still needed to go back to that gyro spot he found last week, the one where the owner called him “darlin’” in a voice that brooked no argument and served tzatziki like it solved moral failings. Maybe tomorrow. Or—

“PHAAAAINON!”

He froze mid-chew.

God. No. Not now.

He turned like a condemned man and, of course, found Hephaestion waving both arms overhead like Phainon was a long-lost cousin returning from war. Peucesta trailed behind him with the graceless tranquility of a man carrying two cups of steaming herbal tea that smelled like someone had boiled an entire front yard.

Phainon closed his eyes, muttered a prayer that went unanswered, and opened them again.

Still there.

“Lord help me,” he said. “Y’all followin’ me?”

Hephaestion flashed a grin that could power streetlights.

“No! …Not in a weird way!”

Peucesta lifted one cup in greeting, expression unreadable. “We were in the area.”

“In the area?” Phainon repeated. “This ain’t even close to your area.”

Peucesta took a slow sip. “We expanded.”

Uh-huh. Sure.

Phainon narrowed his eyes. “Do y’all need a kidney or a witness statement? Just tell me upfront.”

Hephaestion sputtered. “What—no! Absolutely not. Mostly not.”

Peucesta considered this with a tilt of his head. “A witness statement could be handy.”

“Stop talking,” Hephaestion hissed at him.

Phainon took another bite of chili dog to protect himself.

“Anyway,” Hephaestion said, bouncing back like a golden retriever in human form, “we’re going somewhere, and you’re coming with.”

Phainon’s stomach dropped. “That’s a terrible introduction.”

“It’s an invitation,” Hephaestion corrected. “Fairview Botanical Conservatory. Night Bloom. Lights, heat, food, plants pretending to be mystical—”

“Pretentious plants,” Peucesta added. “Very calming.”

Phainon stared at them over the edge of his chili dog.

“Sounds like a date.”

“Exactly,” Peucesta said without blinking.

Hephaestion smacked him hard. “He means it’s not—we’re not—look, just come with us. Worst case, you hate the whole thing and hold it over us forever. That’s a bonding experience.”

Before Phainon could protest, Hephaestion looped their arms like this was legally binding. Peucesta drifted to his other side like an assigned escort.

“I didn’t agree to—”

“No time!” Hephaestion sang.

“I’m eating,” Phainon protested weakly.

“Walk and chew,” Peucesta advised. “Basic motor skill.”

Phainon glared at him. “You know I can outrun both of you.”

Peucesta shrugged. “Not if Hephy over there tackles you.”

Hephy????

Hephaestion brightened. “I could.”

This was happening. Against every natural law of the universe, this was happening.

They were halfway down the path when Peucesta casually dropped, “Cipher said you’d love it.”

Phainon stopped dead. They did not.

He stood there, chili dog suspended mid-air, something low and suspicious coiling in his gut.

Cipher.

Great.

That meant something was brewing, and he was smack in the middle without a clue.

He jogged after them with the resigned energy of a man accepting his fate.

“Y’all better not be luring me into a cult,” he called.

Hephaestion raised a hand without turning. “Too late!”

Peucesta lifted his cup. “Welcome.”

Phainon groaned into his bite, already regretting everything.

The Fairview Botanical Conservatory rose out of the dark like a cathedral that accidentally got built out of greenhouse parts. Glass panes arched overhead, catching little shards of Chicago’s skyline, and warm bulbs hung in loose zigzags across the entryway—like the decorators gave up halfway through but somehow made it charming.

The moment they stepped inside, the air wrapped around Phainon in a damp, floral hug. Humidity clung to him instantly, softening the edge of his hair and sticking his shirt faintly to his chest.

It wasn’t bad per se.

Just… like walking straight into someone’s lungs.

Soft jazz drifted through the greenery—old, warm, and so unobtrusive it almost felt like the plants were the ones humming. Thin fog rolled near the ground from hidden humidifiers. The walkways glimmered under amber spotlights, and couples kept drifting around them like this was the city’s unofficial date-night pilgrimage.

And Phainon hated—hated—how romantic it was.

“This is a damn trap,” he muttered, tugging at his collar. “A good-lookin’ one, but still a trap.”

Peucesta had already peeled off toward some sign about a rare orchid, reading the fact card like it was a midterm exam. Hephaestion hovered nearby with the exact posture of a man pretending he understood words like epiphyte.

Phainon wiped a bead of moisture off his cheek. “Why’s it hotter than July in here? In Chicago. In November.”

“It’s tropical,” Hephaestion offered.

“That ain’t an answer.”

“It’s the intended climate,” Peucesta added, still staring at the sign.

“That’s less comforting,” Phainon said. “Feels like the devil’s greenhouse in here.”

They didn’t respond. They just kept giving each other quiet looks—pointed, secret, very we’re definitely lying right now looks.

The weirdness escalated fast.

Hephaestion started checking every door they passed like he expected one to whisper plot-critical secrets. Peucesta took out his phone, angled it toward a fern, and proceeded to “take pictures” of… absolutely nothing. At one point the phone was pointed at the floor drain. He even nodded at it thoughtfully.

Phainon squinted. “You two ain’t slick. If y’all sell drugs, just say that.”

Hephaestion stumbled over a sago palm. “We don’t—no one sells anything —there is no selling happening—”

“That’s exactly what a dealer’d say.”

Peucesta cleared his throat. “Please ignore him. He gets nervous in public spaces.”

“Nervous?” Phainon scoffed. “I’m observant. There’s a difference.”

But truthfully, they were acting strange. Whispering. Checking their phones. Whispering again. They moved like interns trying to coordinate a surprise party with no rehearsal.

If they pull out matching trench coats, he thought, I am walking out of here. Calm and collected. Like a man escaping a pyramid scheme.

Statistically, he was eighty percent sure he was being sold.

Twenty percent sure they were dodging taxes.

Sixty-forty, realistically.

Still, when Peucesta wandered back to him, he tried not to judge. No one deserved suspicion just for acting weird… even if they were acting weird as hell.

Peucesta actually made good conversation—quiet, unhurried, gently distracting. He asked if Phainon had tried the little empanada cart near the entrance. Mentioned a room of succulents that apparently smelled like orange peel. Grumbled that the humidity was making his curls “inflate like a balloon quartet mid-performance,” which was admittedly more poetic than expected from him.

Phainon laughed—genuinely, low in his chest.

He even forgot, for a moment, to keep side-eyeing Hephaestion.

That was probably the only reason he didn’t notice sooner when they turned a corner and—

Oh.

A hallway stretched in front of them, long and glass-ceilinged, flanked by tall palms trimmed in fairy lights. The lights shimmered like stars tangled in fronds. At the far end, a fountain whispered to itself, water falling into a marble basin with soft, rhythmic sound.

No couples.

No staff.

Nobody.

Just them.

Phainon blinked. “Okay… this is pretty. Pretty in the ‘someone paid a lotta money renting this’ way. Or the ‘we are trespassing and about to be escorted out’ way.”

He took one step back. “I think we should leave—”

Hephaestion raised a hand. “Just a moment.”

Those three words again. A curse. A prophecy.

Phainon heard a rustle—light footsteps, fabric shifting—and turned automatically.

And froze.

Mydeimos stood down the hallway, half-turned, mid-sentence to two other men. One was Ptolemy, wearing an expression like someone had handed him a subpoena. The other was a medical guy Phainon vaguely recognized from the hospital halls—a nurse? tech?—who instantly slapped his phone to his ear as if international diplomacy required his presence right now.

Mydei finished his sentence, turned toward the sound—

And completely stilled.

The lighting hit him unfairly well. Soft gold across his cheekbones, faint reflections in his light hair, the kind of glow that made Phainon’s stomach do something irritated and lovesick at the same time.

Their eyes locked.

Shock cracked across Mydei’s features first. Then resignation. Then a silent, city-bred you have got to be kidding me.

Phainon was not feeling any more graceful; heat crawled up his throat, embarrassed and furious at how good Mydei looked in fairy lights.

For a full second, no one breathed.

Then realization hit them both at once, sharp and synchronized.

Phainon raised a brow.

You too?

Mydei gave him a look, tired and apologetic.

You have no idea.

Mydei turned toward Ptolemy and the nurse.

Phainon turned toward Hephaestion and Peucesta.

And all four conspirators reacted like someone had hit the Raccoon Emergency Button.

Hephaestion made a strangled noise—somewhere between a blender and a broken clarinet.

Ptolemy clapped once, loudly. “WOULD YOU LOOK AT THAT—”

The nurse declared into his silent phone, “MY SHIFT—YES—STARTING —RIGHT NOW—SEE YOU.”

Peucesta said, perfectly calm, “Bye,” and vanished.

They scattered in four different directions, limbs flying, pure chaos.

Like the Chicago wildlife Mydei always complained about—the alley cats that sprinted when porch lights flicked on.

Phainon stared at the empty hallway. “What in the Scooby-Doo hell was that.”

He turned back.

Mydei was still looking after Ptolemy, jaw tight, muttering under his breath in the most Chicagoan exasperation possible—something about idiots running like raccoons after a garbage truck.

Then slowly—slowly—he turned toward Phainon.

There was hesitation there. Uncertainty. Maybe regret. Maybe hope.

He took a step toward him.

Then another.

Phainon’s breath caught tight in his chest.

Oh God.

Mydei stopped a few feet away at first, hands loose at his sides, as if he wasn’t sure whether stepping closer counted as trespassing. For a second, he looked like he might just stand there forever and hope the air did the talking for him.

But then he let out a slow breath, squared himself, and closed the gap until he stood fully in front of Phainon.

Close enough for Phainon to catch the faint flush blooming across his cheekbones. Close enough to see humidity catching in the strands of his hair. Close enough to see—because fate had a sick sense of humor—that his collar was crooked.

Phainon clamped his arms across his chest so he wouldn’t reach up and fix it.

He raised an eyebrow instead. “Knew it,” he said. “I’ve been ambushed.”

A fleeting grimace crossed Mydei’s face. “Yeah. Same. Sorry about them.”

He paused, then added dryly, “They mean well. Unfortunately.”

Phainon snorted. “Could’ve fooled me.”

The greenhouse fans hummed. Palm fronds rustled overhead. Mydei swallowed once—something small but noticeable—and seemed to steady himself.

Then he reached behind him.

He hesitated, just long enough for Phainon to get suspicious, and pulled out —like he was revealing contraband—a bouquet.

If one could call it that.

Wildflowers. Not store-made, not trimmed, not arranged. Stems uneven but chosen with care. Leaves bent in places, a few petals frayed at the edges. A little earth still clung to the roots of one that had clearly been replanted into the bunch. Purple blossoms tucked between faded yellow ones, not messy so much as earnest—clearly handled by someone who refused to buy anything he hadn’t tried to fix himself.

Phainon stared at it. Then at Mydei.

“…Mydei. What in the hell is that.”

Mydei looked at the bouquet like it had personally betrayed him. “A mistake,” he said.

A beat.

“A meaningful one.”

Phainon’s mouth twitched. “Did you mug a meadow?”

Mydei sighed through his nose. “No. I needed flowers today, all the shops were closed, so I got in my car, drove out past the suburbs, found a field, and walked around until I saw something that looked… cheerful.”

Phainon’s jaw dropped. “You went where? At night? Past the suburbs? For flowers? Are you—have you lost your damn mind?”

“Yes,” Mydei replied flatly. “Obviously.”

Phainon opened his mouth again—ready to ask Wait, so you planned this? —but Mydei lifted a hand, cutting him off before he could get the words out.

“Before you jump to conclusions,” he said quickly, eyes skittering away, “these weren’t for tonight.”

That caught Phainon.

Stopped him clean.

“…Mydei?” he said, quieter.

No answer.

“Mydeimos.”

That did it.

Mydei folded like someone had pressed a palm between his shoulder blades. His posture sank a fraction, gaze slipping toward the floor. Color crept up the back of his neck, his ears turning a shade that looked almost painful. Embarrassed in a way that made him look startlingly real and— against Phainon’s will—endearing.

“I’ve been carrying them around like an idiot for three days,” he admitted, voice embarrassed. “In case I ran into you.”

Phainon stared. Heat dragged up his throat, settling high and warm in his cheeks.

“You… carried dead plants around town for days?”

“I replaced them,” Mydei muttered. “A few times.”

A beat.

“I’ve acquired more wildflowers this week than the rest of Illinois combined.”

Phainon let out a choked laugh—first a snort, then a full, helpless cackle that bowed him slightly forward. It echoed off the greenhouse rafters, startling a bird somewhere above them.

It was the first time he’d laughed like that in weeks. Maybe months.

When he finally managed to catch his breath, he wheezed, “How’d you even know I liked these ones?”

Mydei shut his eyes briefly, bracing.

Then:

“I didn’t,” he said. “So I asked around.”

“…Around where?”

“Everywhere.”

He huffed. “Coworkers. Former coworkers. Some guy from Okhema who picked up on the second ring. A lady from the bookclub set in Anaxa’s cafe. The mail carrier. A barista I cornered during their break. I think someone’s aunt chimed in at one point.”

Phainon stared at him like he had grown a second head.

“You didn’t.”

“Oh, I absolutely did.” Mydei rubbed a hand over his brow. “People started texting me pictures of random plants. It turned into a neighborhood watch, except for your taste in flowers.”

Phainon pressed his palm to his forehead. “Oh my god.”

“My favorite was the cactus,” Mydei continued grimly. “Someone told me you liked ‘stubborn plants.’ I still don’t know what that means.”

Under his breath, Phainon murmured, “Means they were right…”

“And,” Mydei finished, resigned, “I have a spreadsheet now.”

That was it.

Phainon burst out laughing again—loud, bright, uncontrollable. His shoulders shook with it, breath catching. Mydei watched him with a look that hovered between offended and something privately grateful for the sound.

By the time Phainon wiped a bit of moisture from his eye, he realized Mydei was smiling. Barely there, but real.

The tension between them didn’t vanish—but it loosened, softened at the edges, became something breathable.

For a moment they stood like that, suspended in the warm greenhouse light: one holding a crooked bouquet, the other looking at him with a heart beating too loud in his ears.

Finally, Phainon exhaled, slow and steady. “Alright,” he said, voice gentler. “Let’s not let everyone’s scheming go to waste.”

The smile slipped from Mydei’s mouth—not gone, just overshadowed by something more serious.

Their eyes met.

Mydei inhaled once.

“Alright, Phainon,” he said quietly. “Let’s… talk.”

Mydei didn’t rush it this time.

“When you kissed me,” he began, choosing each word carefully, “I reacted badly.”

Phainon lifted a brow. You think?

Mydei continued. “Not because I didn’t want it. That wasn’t the issue.” His mouth twitched in a dry, self-aware smile. “If anything, I wanted it more than I knew what to do with. And that… scared me a little. Or a lot. I didn’t know how to hold something like that without dropping everything else I’ve been carrying.”

Phainon didn’t say anything, but he shifted his weight, like he was giving him space to keep going.

“So I panicked,” Mydei said. “And I left. And then I tried to go back, but you weren’t there, and every hour that passed made it easier to tell myself I just needed a plan, or a script, or something so I wouldn’t screw anything up.” He shook his head once. “That was cowardice, I admit it.”

Phainon’s gaze sharpened. “You could’ve told me any of that. Instead, you dropped off the face of the earth.”

A muscle jumped in Mydei’s jaw. “I know,” he said, and there was no defense in it. “I know,” he repeated, softer. “And I’ve had plenty of time to sit with how unfair that was to you.”

He didn’t fidget but his hands opened and closed at his sides like he was grounding himself.

“It wasn’t fair,” he said again. “I kept trying to think of some explanation that didn’t sound like a flimsy excuse. I don’t have one. Just… the apology.”

Phainon let out a slow breath. “You talk like that and people might start thinking you’re responsible.”

Mydei blinked, surprised enough that a small, helpless laugh escaped him. “Please don’t spread that rumor. I’ve got shareholders.”

“Shareholders of what? Poor life decisions?” Phainon said, deadpan.

Mydei took the hit clean, though the edges of his eyes softened in a way that said he was grateful for the levity, even if it came wrapped in sass.

“Look,” Phainon said, crossing his arms loosely, “I’m not gonna pretend I’m made of stone. But you better not think you’re getting forgiven just because you showed up with some flowers and your best sad puppy face.”

“I don’t expect that,” Mydei said immediately. “I’m not here for instant forgiveness, or a clean reset. I’m here because… I don’t want us to go back to being strangers who’d just pass each other.”

Mydei carefully set the wildflowers down on a potting table. The conservatory hummed around them—a faint fan, the layered scent of wet leaves—and then a soft tapping began overhead.

Phainon glanced up. “Is it raining?”

“It started about ten minutes ago,” Mydei said. “You always get chilled after walking in cold weather, so I moved us closer to the fern.”

That was small, but thoughtful in a way that wasn’t showy—just something instinctive and gentle. Phainon’s expression flickered, something warmer threading through the guarded look.

Mydei straightened slightly. “There’s an exhibit this weekend,” he said. “At the museum downtown. Solid curation. Interesting pieces. Thought it might be something you’d… enjoy.”

Phainon’s eyes narrowed, suspicious. “You know I’m into that stuff?”

“Of course I do,” Mydei said, sounding almost offended at the implication that he wouldn’t. “I asked Caelus to find someone who worked with you during your old apprenticeship when I remembered you mentioning it a few months back. Needed some intel.”

Phainon let out a single, disbelieving laugh. “You’re kidding.”

“I wish I were,” Mydei muttered. “The man talked for thirty minutes about pottery shards. Thirty. Full minutes.”

Phainon covered his face. “That man loves pottery.”

“He really does,” Mydei said, exhaling like he’d survived a war.

For a moment they just stood there, listening to the rain deepen overhead. The conservatory lights reflected soft gold across the glass panes, and something in the air eased between them—still tentative, still careful, but moving.

Phainon’s voice came quieter, more honest. “I should’ve talked to you sooner, too. I kept telling myself you made your choice, so why bother? But maybe I should’ve just said what I needed to say instead of avoiding you. Could’ve saved us a whole lot of stupid.”

Mydei nodded once. “Maybe. But you don’t owe me the clean-up for my mistakes. I should’ve faced you the morning after. That’s on me.”

The quiet held—comfortable now, not brittle.

Then, almost shyly, Mydei extended a hand. Not demanding. Just offering. “Walk with me?”

Phainon glanced down at the familiar navy handle peeking out of his bag. Mydei’s umbrella. The one he’d never given back.

He snorted under his breath. “Of course you want to walk in the rain.”

“It’s a good rain,” Mydei said, voice soft as the falling water.

Phainon looked at him for a long moment—really looked—and something settled.

“Alright, lover boy,” he said, letting a smile pull at his mouth. “Let’s walk.”

Mydei didn’t hide the way his breath eased out in relief.

But Phainon reached for his hand first, lacing their fingers with deliberate steadiness before tugging him toward the conservatory doors, rain waiting just outside.

Phainon didn’t even realize he’d snagged the bouquet until they were already halfway to the doors. His hand had closed around the stems on instinct—like some part of him already knew he wasn’t leaving without them. The flowers brushed his leg with every step, a small, warm reminder.

Outside, the rain had settled into a soft, steady fall, turning the glass walls behind them into sheets of gold where the lights hit. Mydei flicked open the umbrella and angled it just enough to cover both of them. Their shoulders brushed as they stepped into the damp evening, and neither made any effort to shift away.

From a distance, the scene would’ve looked almost storybook: the conservatory glowing behind them, rain glimmering in the light, two silhouettes moving in quiet sync beneath one umbrella.

Naturally, the moment lasted all of twelve seconds.

Because behind a giant fern—one that was absolutely not large enough to hide anything—Hephaestion and Peucesta crouched like two children filming a low-budget nature documentary.

Peucesta whispered (badly), “He kept the flowers. That’s a win.”

Hephaestion dabbed theatrically at the corner of his eye with the sleeve of his hoodie. “Our boy’s in love.”

Mydei and Phainon stopped in perfect unison.

Turned.

And delivered a synchronized glare potent enough to curdle milk.

Hephaestion froze mid-gesture, then sighed with the drama of a man surrendering to fate. “Okay—wow—hostile. Fine. Whatever.” He stood with languid resignation and waved them off. “Not my problem anymore. I retire from matchmaking. Effective immediately.”

Peucesta scrambled upright after him. “He doesn’t mean that,” he stage-mwhispered to Mydei. “He’ll come back Monday with a color-coded PowerPoint on communication styles.”

“Go,” Mydei said flatly.

They went—Hephaestion dragging Peucesta by the back of his jacket like someone hauling off a misbehaving pet. Their bickering faded into the rain.

Silence settled again. The soft kind.

Phainon adjusted the flowers under his arm, the stems tucking neatly into the crook of his elbow. And there it was—that small, stupid smile tugging at Phainon’s mouth, the one he’d been trying to smother all night.

Mydei noticed, of course. He didn’t call it out, but something in his expression gentled, like he might tuck the smile somewhere safe if he could.

They fell into step once more, side by side, the night carrying them forward.

And Phainon thought, quietly:

Maybe folks like him don’t buy land. But every now and then, someone asks if they wanna walk a little of it together.
